facts.statement: A pressure instrument's measurement range, permissible operating/working or static-pressure limit, overpressure limit, proof-pressure rating, and burst pressure are distinct product ratings and must not be substituted for one another. Operation within an overpressure limit may exceed specified accuracy even if permanent damage is avoided; exceeding the model-specific pressure boundary can cause irreversible damage or rupture. Check the exact datasheet definition and the lowest-rated component in the installed pressure boundary.

verification_refs.citation: WIKA, What does maximum operating pressure or working pressure mean with pressure sensors?
verification_refs.locator: Definitions of measuring range, overload range, and burst pressure
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that working/operating pressure is not uniformly defined across manufacturers and distinguishes measuring range, overload range, and burst pressure.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 3154N Nuclear Qualified Pressure Transmitter Product Data Sheet, §Specifications
verification_refs.locator: Maximum Working Pressure; Static Line Pressure Limits; Overpressure Limits; Burst Pressure
verification_refs.supports_claim: Lists maximum working pressure, static line pressure, overpressure, and minimum burst pressure as separate specifications, with limits differing by range code and application.

verification_refs.citation: WIKA, Frequently Asked Questions: Pressure instruments and overpressure limits
verification_refs.locator: Answer: effects of reaching or exceeding overpressure limit
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that pressure up to the overpressure limit may not cause permanent damage but can exceed datasheet error limits, while pressures above the limit can cause irreversible damage.

facts.statement: Pressure instrument range selection must cover the intended process pressure envelope and the required calibrated span, while remaining within the selected model's URL/LRL, minimum-span, overpressure, and accuracy specifications. A narrower span may increase turndown/rangedown and can change the stated accuracy or resolution; therefore assess normal, minimum, maximum, transient, and calibration conditions against the product datasheet rather than maximizing range or turndown alone.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 2090P Pressure Transmitter Product Data Sheet
verification_refs.locator: Reference accuracy, calibrated-span accuracy and turndown specifications
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines accuracy against calibrated span and gives accuracy behavior across specified turndown ratios, showing that usable range and performance are model-specific.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, TechView User's Guide D5131, URL/LRL and URV/LRV discussion
verification_refs.locator: Upper/Lower Range Limit and Upper/Lower Range Value; turndown example
verification_refs.supports_claim: Distinguishes fixed sensor URL/LRL from configured URV/LRV and explains that values outside the defined limit cannot be considered accurate.

verification_refs.citation: WIKA, The Optimal Pressure Range for Pressure Sensors
verification_refs.locator: Measuring range and its effect on accuracy; zero-related errors and operating range example
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that too-wide a measuring range can compromise accuracy or output signal, while usable accuracy depends on the sensor's measurement range and error terms.

facts.statement: A zero/low trim is a single-point offset adjustment and generally preserves the sensor-characterization slope; it is not a substitute for full-range calibration. A two-point sensor trim uses lower and upper pressure standards to correct offset and slope/span over the intended range. Trim type and valid reference condition are instrument-dependent—for example, absolute-pressure transmitters cannot use a zero-based gauge-pressure zero trim—and line/static pressure or mounting effects may require calibration under the installed operating condition.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 2051 Pressure Transmitter Reference Manual, §4.4
verification_refs.locator: Sensor trim overview; zero trim and two-point sensor trim descriptions
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines zero trim as single-point offset adjustment preserving curve slope, and sensor trim as two-point calibration with lower trim for offset and upper trim for slope; warns against zero trim on absolute transmitters.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 4051S Pressure Transmitter Manual, Calibration and Trimming sections
verification_refs.locator: Calibration overview; zero trim; upper/lower sensor trim; applied line pressure during field zero trim
verification_refs.supports_claim: Distinguishes sensor offset/range correction and analog-output trim, recommends line pressure during field zero trim to eliminate line-pressure errors, and notes inaccurate trim equipment or procedure can degrade performance.

facts.statement: A pressure transmitter's reference-accuracy specification may combine linearity, hysteresis, and repeatability under stated reference conditions; it does not by itself represent all installed measurement error. Product specifications may separately state temperature effect, static-pressure effect, vibration effect, and long-term stability, and the definitions and included terms vary by model. Evaluate expected performance using the selected model's specification and operating conditions; do not assume a universal additive total-performance formula unless the manufacturer defines one.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 2088 Pressure Transmitter Product Data Sheet, Performance Specifications
verification_refs.locator: Reference accuracy, ambient temperature effect, stability, vibration effect
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines reference accuracy as including combined linearity, hysteresis, and repeatability, while listing temperature effect, stability, and vibration effect separately.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 3051N Pressure Transmitter Product Data Sheet, Performance Specifications
verification_refs.locator: Reference accuracy, ambient temperature effect, drift, overpressure effect and range-down conditions
verification_refs.supports_claim: Specifies reference accuracy with stated included terms and separately quantifies ambient-temperature, drift, and overpressure effects under range-specific conditions.

facts.statement: Impulse piping can bias or slow pressure transfer through leakage, obstruction or deposits, friction loss, trapped gas in liquid service, liquid in gas service, unequal hydrostatic heads or density between DP legs, and unequal leg temperatures. Installation controls depend on phase and service: route and slope lines to manage gas/liquid pockets, keep paired legs thermally and hydrostatically balanced, vent or drain as appropriate, prevent sediment/freezing, and verify leak-tightness. The transmitter and manifold must be installed and operated according to their model-specific procedures.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 4051S Pressure Transmitter Manual, Hardware Installation §Impulse Piping
verification_refs.locator: Impulse piping sources of error and service-specific installation guidelines
verification_refs.supports_claim: Identifies pressure-transfer problems, leaks, friction loss, trapped gas/liquid, and density variation between legs; prescribes service-specific slopes, avoiding gas/liquid pockets, equal leg temperatures, suitable pipe diameter, venting, and equal sealing-fluid levels.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 2051 Pressure Transmitter Reference Manual, Hardware Installation §Impulse Piping
verification_refs.locator: Impulse piping guidelines: deposits, process freezing, hot/corrosive media and leak prevention
verification_refs.supports_claim: Adds instructions to prevent sediment deposits and process fluid freezing, and to keep hot or corrosive process material away from the sensor module; requires proper flange bolt installation to prevent process leakage.

facts.statement: Pressure pulsation and mechanical vibration can cause pointer flutter, reduced readability, accelerated movement/Bourdon-element wear, or damage in mechanical gauges. A transmitter's damping and finite response time can smooth rapid input variations but also delay response; select damping, mounting, sampling/update rate, and any remote or pulse-damping arrangement against the required loop dynamics and measurement objective. Signal damping is not proof that the underlying process fluctuation has been removed.

verification_refs.citation: Ashcroft, Is Your Pressure Gauge Safe for Chemical Applications?
verification_refs.locator: Effects and mitigation of pulsation and vibration on mechanical pressure gauges
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes pointer flutter, reduced readability, gear wear, stress on Bourdon tubes, shortened gauge life, and mitigation options including liquid fill, dampeners, and remote mounting.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 2051 Pressure Transmitter Reference Manual, §3.7.4 and SIS damping note
verification_refs.locator: Damping changes response time and smooths rapid input changes; configured damping plus response time must meet loop requirements
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that damping introduces delay and smooths output variations caused by rapid input changes, and that damping plus response time must not exceed loop requirements.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 3051 Pressure Transmitter Reference Manual, Advanced Pressure Diagnostics
verification_refs.locator: Impulse-line resonance, frequency response and RC low-pass behavior
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that impulse-line length and fluid properties can produce resonance or low-pass response, and that trapped gas changes impulse-line response; supports evaluating installation/sampling response against process dynamics.

facts.statement: Select pressure-instrument wetted materials, process connection, and any seal/isolator against the actual process composition and operating conditions. Corrosiveness/chemical compatibility, process and ambient temperature, pressure, viscosity, solids or crystallization that can plug a pressure port, and cleaning or containment requirements can change the suitable material and connection. Flush diaphragms, diaphragm seals, flushing, or drain provisions are application-specific options—not universal requirements—and must preserve the required accuracy, response, and process compatibility.

verification_refs.citation: WIKA, How to Select a Pressure Gauge
verification_refs.locator: Selection factors: temperature and media; wetted material and diaphragm-seal use
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that media contacting wetted parts determines material choice, temperature affects wetted material selection, aggressive media require compatible materials, and a diaphragm seal can isolate media that clog gauge mechanisms.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 1199 Diaphragm Seal Systems Product Data Sheet, Material Selection notice
verification_refs.locator: Material selection and purchaser responsibility for chemical composition, temperature, pressure, flow, abrasives and contaminants
verification_refs.supports_claim: Requires analysis of process chemical components, temperature, pressure, flow rate, abrasives, and contaminants when specifying materials/options, and cautions that compatibility depends on the selected application configuration.

verification_refs.citation: WIKA, Model S-11 Flush Pressure Sensor
verification_refs.locator: Applications and description for viscous, crystallizing, particle-laden and contaminated media
verification_refs.supports_claim: Identifies viscous, adhesive, crystallizing, particle-laden, and contaminated media as cases where conventional pressure ports may clog, and describes a flush diaphragm and cleanable connection for those cases.

facts.statement: Select a pressure transmitter's enclosure, mounting, and approvals against the actual installation environment and jurisdiction. Check the model's ambient/process-temperature limits, ingress/environmental protection, vibration and EMC specifications, and—where the area is classified—the applicable gas/dust classification, protection concept, temperature class, certificate conditions, and installation requirements. A general hazardous-area label or enclosure IP/NEMA rating alone does not establish suitability for every site.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 3051 Pressure Transmitter Quick Start Guide, Hazardous Locations and Special Conditions for Safe Use
verification_refs.locator: Hazardous-location certification, ambient temperature, grounding, cable glands, blanking plugs, and installation conditions
verification_refs.supports_claim: Shows that suitability depends on the selected approval, ambient-temperature range, grounding, certified cable glands and plugs, and special installation/use conditions.

verification_refs.citation: WIKA, IS-3 Pressure Transmitter Product Information and Datasheet PE 81.58
verification_refs.locator: Product approvals, hazardous-area variants and ingress protection
verification_refs.supports_claim: Lists distinct approvals for gas/dust zones and mining, and identifies minimum IP65 with IP68 variants; the accompanying datasheet lists EMC and jurisdiction-specific approvals.

verification_refs.citation: WIKA, IS-3 Pressure Transmitter Datasheet PE 81.58
verification_refs.locator: Approvals table: EMC directive and industrial-environment immunity; ATEX/IECEx area markings
verification_refs.supports_claim: Separately enumerates EMC compliance and multiple area-specific hazardous approvals, reinforcing that each relevant environmental and certification requirement must be checked for the product variant and installation.

facts.statement: For an installed pressure-measurement application, selection may also consider calibration and maintenance access, isolation/manifold arrangement, diagnostics, spare and replacement strategy, expected outage or process-interruption consequences, and lifecycle cost in addition to measurement and process requirements. These are project-specific operability and economic tradeoffs; no single weighting or universally optimal configuration follows from the instrument type alone.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 4051S Pressure Transmitter Manual, Installation Considerations and Diagnostics Overview
verification_refs.locator: Considerations: easy access, safety, practical field calibration; diagnostics and shutdown-risk rationale
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explicitly includes access, personnel safety, and practical field calibration in installation considerations; describes diagnostics as a means to identify upsets and reduce potential shutdown/failure.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Pressure Transmitters Product Guide and Maintenance Cost FAQ
verification_refs.locator: Ongoing maintenance costs: battery replacement, calibration, field labor; built-in diagnostics and verification tools
verification_refs.supports_claim: Identifies battery replacement, calibration and field labor as ownership/maintenance cost drivers and discusses diagnostics and verification tools as factors affecting maintenance strategy.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 4051S Pressure Transmitter Product Announcement
verification_refs.locator: Rangedown effect on number of stocked models; diagnostics/calibration logs and maintenance access
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes high turndown as reducing unique models needed in stock and built-in diagnostics/calibration logs as maintenance and root-cause-analysis inputs.

facts.statement: For shaft speed n in revolutions per minute, angular velocity is ω = 2πn/60 radians per second because each revolution is 2π radians and one minute is 60 seconds. Pulse-based speed or position calculations must use the effective counts per revolution defined by the encoder output and the selected counter decoding (for quadrature, X1/X2/X4 count different signal edges); the encoder's stated PPR/lines-per-revolution must not be silently equated with decoded counts per revolution.

verification_refs.citation: Unit conversion from revolution/minute to radian/second
verification_refs.locator: n rev/min × 2π rad/rev × 1 min/60 s = 2πn/60 rad/s
verification_refs.supports_claim: The revolution unit cancels and minutes convert to seconds, yielding ω = 2πn/60 rad/s.

verification_refs.citation: National Instruments, NI Hardware Encoder Measurements: How-To Guide
verification_refs.locator: Pulses per shaft revolution and X1/X2/X4 quadrature edge-counting definitions
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines N as pulses per shaft revolution and explains that X1 counts one edge per cycle, X2 counts two edges, and X4 counts all four A/B transitions; thus the configured decode factor determines effective counts per revolution.

facts.statement: Hydraulic or pneumatic power should be selected against the application rather than by a universal ranking. Relevant requirements include force/load, speed and motion profile, response or positioning behavior, working-fluid compressibility, leakage and contamination consequences, installation environment, energy supply and efficiency, safety, and maintenance capability. The relative advantages depend on circuit design and duty; for example, gas compressibility differs materially from liquid behavior, while energy and maintenance outcomes depend on the complete supply and actuator system.

verification_refs.citation: U.S. Navy, NAVEDTRA 14050A, Basic Principles of Hydraulics and Pneumatics
verification_refs.locator: Hydraulics and pneumatics definitions; liquid and gas compressibility
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines hydraulics as use of liquids and pneumatics as use of gases; explains that gases are highly compressible while liquids are treated as practically incompressible for ordinary system analysis.

verification_refs.citation: Festo, How to Select the Optimal Linear Motion Technology
verification_refs.locator: Application requirements: payload, force, repeatability, footprint, energy source, lifecycle cost, efficiency, motion control and support expertise
verification_refs.supports_claim: Recommends choosing motion technology according to application-specific technical and economic criteria, rather than asserting one technology is universally best.

verification_refs.citation: ISO/TR 22164:2020, Hydraulic fluid power — Application notes for the optimization of the energy efficiency of hydraulic systems
verification_refs.locator: Scope and abstract: efficiency optimization while maintaining intended machine functionality
verification_refs.supports_claim: Confirms that hydraulic-system energy efficiency is an engineering design objective to be optimized while preserving the machine's intended function, not an intrinsic fixed ranking independent of duty.

verification_refs.citation: U.S. Department of Energy, Compressed Air Systems
verification_refs.locator: Compressed air system energy assessment and management guidance
verification_refs.supports_claim: Treats compressed air energy performance as a system-level issue and recommends energy-management practices and equipment evaluation.

facts.statement: A Safety Instrumented System (SIS) is the instrumented system used to implement one or more Safety Instrumented Functions (SIFs); the SIS is the system-level implementation context, while each SIF is a specified safety function.

verification_refs.citation: IEC 61511-1:2016, Functional safety — Safety instrumented systems for the process industry sector
verification_refs.locator: Clause 1, scope, items j and l; Figures 1 and 4
verification_refs.supports_claim: The standard describes functional safety achieved using one or more SIFs and requirements for implementing SIFs within SIS arrangements.

verification_refs.citation: UK Health and Safety Executive, Functional safety
verification_refs.locator: SIS section
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes SIS as instrumented systems that provide risk reduction and typically include sensors, logic functions, and final elements.

facts.statement: A Safety Integrity Level (SIL) is a discrete level for specifying the safety integrity requirements of a safety function; it is not a product model or a standalone certificate for an arbitrary device.

verification_refs.citation: International Electrotechnical Commission, Overview of IEC 61508 & Functional Safety
verification_refs.locator: Safety Function: Safety Integrity Levels (SILs)
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines SIL as one of four possible discrete levels for specifying safety requirements of safety functions allocated to safety-related systems and depicts SIL as a property of a safety function.

verification_refs.citation: IEC 61511-1:2016, Functional safety — Safety instrumented systems for the process industry sector
verification_refs.locator: Clause 1, scope, items g, j, and n
verification_refs.supports_claim: Requires identification of functional and safety-integrity requirements for each SIF and hazard/risk analysis to define the SIL of each SIF.

facts.statement: A SIF is evaluated as the instrumented safety-function path that detects a hazardous condition and initiates the action needed to achieve or maintain the defined safe state; its implementation includes the relevant sensing, logic, and final-element functions rather than a single device alone.

verification_refs.citation: UK Health and Safety Executive, Functional safety
verification_refs.locator: SIS section
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes SIS sensors and logic as detecting dangerous conditions and final elements such as valves as being manipulated to achieve a safe state.

verification_refs.citation: ISA dTR-84.00.07 preview, terminology sourced from IEC 61511-1:2016
verification_refs.locator: Definitions: safety function and safety instrumented function
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines a SIF as a safety function implemented by an SIS and a safety function as achieving or maintaining a safe process state for a specific hazardous event.

facts.statement: Hazard and risk analysis identifies the safety functions and their required safety-integrity levels, taking account of risk reduction assigned to other protection measures; the resulting functional and integrity requirements are allocated to each SIF and documented for implementation.

verification_refs.citation: IEC 61511-1:2016, Functional safety — Safety instrumented systems for the process industry sector
verification_refs.locator: Clause 1, scope, items g and n; Figure 1, framework
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that functional and safety-integrity requirements are identified for each SIF taking into account risk reduction by other methods, and that hazard and risk analysis defines safety functional requirements and SIL for each SIF.

facts.statement: Safety-related SIS application software is managed within a lifecycle that includes requirements and design, implementation, verification, integration, validation, operation and maintenance, and controlled modification; the applicable activities and evidence depend on the system lifecycle phase and standard scope.

verification_refs.citation: IEC 61511-1:2016, Functional safety — Safety instrumented systems for the process industry sector
verification_refs.locator: Contents, Clauses 12–17; Figures 7–8 and Table 3
verification_refs.supports_claim: Identifies SIS application program development, design, implementation, verification, SIS validation, operation/maintenance and modification, and explicitly lists an application-program safety lifecycle related to the SIS lifecycle.

verification_refs.citation: UK Health and Safety Executive, Functional safety
verification_refs.locator: Functional safety lifecycle principles
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes the process-sector lifecycle from hazard/risk assessment and specification through design, implementation, validation, operation, maintenance, modification and decommissioning.

facts.statement: For the IEC/Fisher liquid valve-sizing definitions, P1 and P2 are absolute static pressures, Pv is the liquid absolute vapor pressure at inlet temperature, and Pc is absolute thermodynamic critical pressure; pressure comparisons and equations must use consistent units and an absolute-pressure basis.

verification_refs.citation: Fisher, ANSI/ISA/IEC Valve Sizing, Catalog 12, Section 2
verification_refs.locator: Table 1, Abbreviations and Terminology
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines P1 and P2 as upstream/downstream absolute static pressure, Pc as absolute thermodynamic critical pressure, and Pv as absolute liquid vapor pressure at inlet temperature.

facts.statement: The vapor pressure Pv used for liquid control-valve sizing is the liquid's absolute vapor pressure at the specified inlet/operating temperature; when that temperature changes, the corresponding Pv input must be reassessed.

verification_refs.citation: Fisher, ANSI/ISA/IEC Valve Sizing, Catalog 12, Section 2
verification_refs.locator: Table 1, definition of Pv
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines Pv as the absolute vapor pressure of the liquid at inlet temperature.

facts.statement: In the Fisher/IEC liquid-sizing notation, Pc denotes the liquid's absolute thermodynamic critical pressure; it is distinct from the valve liquid pressure-recovery factor FL.

verification_refs.citation: Fisher, ANSI/ISA/IEC Valve Sizing, Catalog 12, Section 2
verification_refs.locator: Table 1, definitions of Pc and FL
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines Pc as absolute thermodynamic critical pressure and FL separately as rated liquid pressure recovery factor.

facts.statement: For flow through a control-valve restriction, the vena contracta is the region immediately downstream of the restriction where the flow stream reaches its minimum cross-sectional area; local velocity is high and static pressure can reach its minimum there.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th edition
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 5, liquid sizing and vena contracta pressure profile
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines the vena contracta as the minimum flow-stream cross-sectional area downstream of the physical restriction, with increased velocity and reduced static pressure.

facts.statement: In liquid flow through a control-valve restriction, when local static pressure at the vena contracta falls below the liquid vapor pressure at that temperature, vapor bubbles can form; the resulting phase-change regime downstream depends on pressure recovery and outlet pressure.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th edition
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 5, Cavitation and Flashing
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that bubbles form when pressure at the vena contracta drops below liquid vapor pressure and that the subsequent state distinguishes cavitation from flashing.

facts.statement: Downstream of the vena contracta, as the flow area expands and velocity decreases, part of the static pressure can recover toward the valve outlet pressure; irreversible losses mean recovery is not generally complete back to upstream pressure.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th edition
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 5, pressure profile through a valve restriction
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes flow expansion and velocity decrease downstream of the vena contracta, with static-pressure recovery that is incomplete because of dissipated energy.

facts.statement: For a liquid control valve at fixed upstream conditions, choked flow is the limiting-capacity regime in which further increase in pressure differential does not produce the corresponding increase in flow; it is a flow-capacity limit, not zero flow.

verification_refs.citation: Fisher, ANSI/ISA/IEC Valve Sizing, Catalog 12, Section 2
verification_refs.locator: Sizing valves for liquids, qmax definition and choked-flow description
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines qmax as maximum flow at given upstream conditions and states that choked flow is manifested by no additional increase in flow with increasing pressure differential.

facts.statement: In the conventional liquid control-valve classification, cavitation involves vapor-bubble formation as local pressure approaches or falls below vapor pressure near the vena contracta, followed by pressure recovery that raises pressure and collapses bubbles; a vapor-forming condition alone does not establish that damaging cavitation occurs.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Cavitation in Control Valves
verification_refs.locator: Understanding Cavitation; Definition
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines cavitation as formation and collapse of vapor bubbles and explains their formation near vapor pressure and collapse as pressure increases downstream.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th edition
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 5, cavitation and flashing pressure profile
verification_refs.supports_claim: Separates local vapor formation at vena contracta from the downstream pressure condition that determines whether bubbles collapse or persist.

facts.statement: For a liquid control-valve application, flashing is classified when liquid vaporizes near the vena contracta and downstream pressure remains below the liquid vapor pressure, so the vapor phase persists downstream rather than collapsing within the valve outlet pressure recovery.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Control Valve Flashing
verification_refs.locator: Understanding Flashing in Control Valves
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines flashing as vaporization with vapor remaining and states a flashing application has downstream pressure below vapor pressure (P2 < Pv).

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th edition
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 5, cavitation and flashing
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that vaporization begins near the vena contracta and downstream outlet pressure determines whether vapor persists.

facts.statement: Cavitation and flashing in liquid control valves share the initial event of local vapor formation when pressure near the vena contracta falls below the liquid vapor pressure; their distinction is determined by subsequent downstream pressure behavior and bubble persistence or collapse.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th edition
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 5, Cavitation and Flashing
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes vapor formation at the vena contracta as common to both conditions and distinguishes the regimes by outlet pressure and bubble behavior.

facts.statement: In Fisher/IEC liquid-valve sizing notation, FL is the rated liquid pressure-recovery factor for the valve; use the value applicable to the selected valve and specified sizing conditions rather than treating it as a universal fluid constant.

verification_refs.citation: Fisher, ANSI/ISA/IEC Valve Sizing, Catalog 12, Section 2
verification_refs.locator: Table 1, definition of FL; liquid sizing procedure
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines FL as the rated liquid pressure-recovery factor and directs users to published coefficient tables for the selected valve.

facts.statement: The Fisher/IEC liquid critical pressure-ratio factor FF is calculated from the ratio Pv/Pc; the published relation uses FF = 0.96 − 0.28√(Pv/Pc), with Pv and Pc on an absolute, consistent pressure basis.

verification_refs.citation: Fisher, ANSI/ISA/IEC Valve Sizing, Catalog 12, Section 2
verification_refs.locator: Liquid sizing procedure, equation for FF
verification_refs.supports_claim: Gives FF = 0.96 − 0.28√(Pv/Pc) and defines Pv and Pc as absolute pressures.

facts.statement: For the standardized liquid sizing procedure for a valve without attached fittings, the allowable choked sizing pressure drop is ΔPmax(L) = FL²(P1 − FF·Pv). This is a sizing limit, not a claim that every valve/application has the same numerical limit.

verification_refs.citation: Fisher, Valve Sizing Calculations (Traditional Method), D351798X012
verification_refs.locator: Determining allowable sizing pressure drop, equation for valves without fittings
verification_refs.supports_claim: Provides the allowable liquid sizing pressure drop equation ΔPmax(L) = FL²(P1 − FF Pv) for valves installed without attached fittings.

facts.statement: In Fisher/IEC liquid-valve sizing, FP is the piping-geometry factor used to account for the capacity effect of relevant fittings attached directly to the control valve; it is not a correction for arbitrary remote piping without applying the prescribed method.

verification_refs.citation: Fisher, ANSI/ISA/IEC Valve Sizing, Catalog 12, Section 2
verification_refs.locator: Table 1, FP definition; determining FP with attached fittings
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines FP as piping geometry factor and provides a procedure for attached reducers, expanders, and fittings.

facts.statement: For a valve with attached fittings, FLP is the combined liquid pressure-recovery factor and piping-geometry factor used by the standardized sizing method; when there are no attached fittings, the catalog states FLP equals FL.

verification_refs.citation: Fisher, ANSI/ISA/IEC Valve Sizing, Catalog 12, Section 2
verification_refs.locator: Table 1, definition of FLP; attached-fitting procedure
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines FLP as the combined liquid pressure-recovery and piping geometry factor for attached fittings and states FLP=FL when no fittings are attached.

facts.statement: For the standardized liquid sizing procedure with directly attached fittings, the allowable choked sizing pressure drop is ΔPmax(LP) = (FLP/FP)²(P1 − FF·Pv); use the fitting-adjusted coefficients from the selected calculation rather than the bare-valve FL formula.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th edition
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 5, liquid sizing with attached fittings
verification_refs.supports_claim: Gives the fitting-adjusted choked pressure-drop relation ΔPchoked = (FLP/FP)²(P1 − FF Pv).

facts.statement: In the standardized liquid sizing procedure, when the calculated allowable choked pressure drop is below the actual service pressure drop, the lower allowable choked pressure drop is used for sizing; equivalently, ΔPsizing is the lesser of the applicable actual pressure drop and the calculated liquid choked limit.

verification_refs.citation: Fisher, ANSI/ISA/IEC Valve Sizing, Catalog 12, Section 2
verification_refs.locator: Determining allowable sizing pressure drop; liquid valve sizing procedure
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that actual pressure drop is compared with allowable ΔPmax and the lesser value is used in the sizing equation.

facts.statement: Liquid choked flow means the flow has reached a limiting capacity under the specified upstream conditions; it does not mean that flow has stopped or become zero.

verification_refs.citation: Fisher, ANSI/ISA/IEC Valve Sizing, Catalog 12, Section 2
verification_refs.locator: qmax definition and liquid choking discussion
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines qmax as maximum flow rate at given upstream conditions and describes choking as no further increase in flow with increasing pressure differential, rather than zero flow.

facts.statement: Control-valve cavitation damage is associated with vapor-bubble collapse; reported mechanical attack mechanisms include high-velocity microjets and shock-wave loading, which can contribute to rough pitting, vibration, and erosion. The detailed damage process is multifactorial and is not captured by a single universal severity threshold.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook—Oil and Gas, Chapter 6
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 6, Material Damage
verification_refs.supports_claim: Reports damage association with bubble collapse and discusses microjet impingement and shock-wave attack, while noting that the detailed mechanisms are not completely understood.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Cavitation in Control Valves
verification_refs.locator: Definition and effects
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes collapse of vapor bubbles and potential noise, vibration, material damage, and reduced flow effectiveness.

facts.statement: Both cavitation and flashing can begin with local vapor formation near the vena contracta; cavitation is associated with subsequent pressure recovery and bubble collapse, whereas flashing is classified when downstream pressure remains below vapor pressure and vapor persists downstream.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th edition
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 5, Cavitation and Flashing
verification_refs.supports_claim: Distinguishes the shared vaporization near vena contracta from downstream pressure recovery and persistent vapor behavior.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Control Valve Flashing
verification_refs.locator: Understanding Flashing in Control Valves
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines flashing as vaporization with vapor remaining and gives the downstream-pressure-below-vapor-pressure classification.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Cavitation in Control Valves
verification_refs.locator: Definition
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines cavitation through vapor bubble formation and collapse as pressure rises downstream.

facts.statement: Persistent flashing can cause erosive wear of valve trim and adjacent downstream surfaces; erosion is often greatest where the two-phase stream velocity or droplet impingement is high. The amount of damage is application-dependent and is not determined by flashing classification alone.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th edition
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 5.14.2, Valve Selection for Flashing Service
verification_refs.supports_claim: States flashing can cause serious erosion of trim, normally greatest near highest velocity, and recommends geometry/material choices to limit erosion.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Control Valve Flashing
verification_refs.locator: Understanding Flashing; Damage Potential
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes the liquid-vapor mixture as highly erosive and flashing damage potential as dependent on multiple process and material factors.

facts.statement: Liquid choked-flow capacity, local vapor formation, and physical damage severity are distinct assessments: choked flow is a capacity limit, vapor formation depends on local pressure relative to vapor pressure, and damage depends on the subsequent flow regime and service/material conditions.

verification_refs.citation: Fisher, ANSI/ISA/IEC Valve Sizing, Catalog 12, Section 2
verification_refs.locator: qmax/ΔPmax choked-capacity definitions and liquid sizing procedure
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines choking by limiting flow capacity and separately treats vapor pressure/phase change in liquid sizing.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Control Valve Flashing
verification_refs.locator: Understanding Flashing; Damage Potential
verification_refs.supports_claim: Separately describes flashing's flow limitation and erosion concern, and says damage intensity depends on multiple factors and has no universal prediction coefficient.

facts.statement: For a specified liquid-valve operating case, increasing downstream backpressure reduces the valve pressure drop and can raise vena-contracta pressure, potentially avoiding cavitation if the resulting local pressure remains above vapor pressure. The downstream device itself and other operating cases must also be checked.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook—Oil and Gas, Chapter 6
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 6, System Design
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that a downstream backpressure device raises valve downstream pressure and vena-contracta pressure; if correctly sized such that vena pressure stays above vapor pressure, cavitation at the valve can be avoided. It also warns that cavitation may occur at the device, conditions may vary, and wear can reduce backpressure.

facts.statement: A properly selected and sized multistage liquid-valve trim divides the total pressure drop among stages; under its design conditions, the partial drop per stage can keep local liquid pressure from reaching vapor pressure and thereby prevent vapor formation/cavitation within the trim.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Product Bulletin Cavitrol III Trims 80.2:030, D100196X012
verification_refs.locator: Principle of Operation, Cavitrol III Two- and Three-Stage Trims
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that each stage takes a portion of total pressure drop and that partial drops in a properly sized valve normally prevent liquid pressure from reaching vapor pressure.

facts.statement: Under otherwise comparable liquid-service conditions, a valve with lower pressure recovery (typically a higher applicable FL) may maintain a higher vena-contracta pressure and have less cavitation susceptibility than a high-recovery valve; actual selection still requires valve-specific coefficients and service analysis.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th edition
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 5, pressure-recovery profiles and valve selection for cavitation service
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that high-recovery valves tend to be more subject to cavitation because vena-contracta pressure is lower and more likely to reach liquid vapor pressure; recovery factor and selection data are valve-specific.

facts.statement: Anti-cavitation trim can control or prevent cavitation by managing pressure reduction and bubble collapse within its design envelope, but it cannot change an application condition in which downstream pressure remains below the liquid vapor pressure; in that flashing service the design must manage persistent two-phase flow and erosion rather than assume the trim recondenses the vapor.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Control Valve Flashing
verification_refs.locator: Understanding Flashing in Control Valves; Damage Potential
verification_refs.supports_claim: States flashing occurs when downstream pressure is below vapor pressure, vapor remains, and flashing cannot be prevented by the valve; geometry/materials mitigate damage rather than change the phase condition.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Product Bulletin Cavitrol III Trims 80.2:030, D100196X012
verification_refs.locator: Principle of Operation, two-/three-stage trim
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes staged pressure reduction as preventing vapor formation/cavitation when properly sized, which is distinct from the application-defined persistent flashing condition.

facts.statement: A characterized anti-cavitation trim can have travel-dependent cavitation-control performance because its pressure-staging geometry changes with plug travel; the applicable result is specific to the trim design and its intended process characteristic.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook—Oil and Gas
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 6, Characterized Cages
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes a characterized Cavitrol III trim whose cage changes from pressure-staging to straight-through geometry as travel increases, with cavitation-control ability greatest at low travel and decreasing as travel increases; the manual cautions that its use depends on the application pressure-drop characteristic.

facts.statement: For water in liquid-vapor equilibrium, saturation vapor pressure decreases as temperature decreases. At otherwise unchanged pressure and composition this increases the static pressure margin above vapor pressure, but it does not by itself establish that a control-valve application is free of cavitation, flashing, or damage.

verification_refs.citation: International Association for the Properties of Water and Steam (IAPWS), FAQs About Water and Steam, vapor pressure and temperature
verification_refs.locator: Vapor pressure increases with temperature; saturation-pressure table
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that vapor pressure increases with temperature and provides saturation-pressure values for water at increasing temperatures; the recorded fact is explicitly scoped to water and static pressure margin.

facts.statement: For the continuous-time linear state model x_dot = Ax + Bu, applying full-state feedback u = -Kx changes the closed-loop state matrix to A - BK; if a reference feedforward term is included, it affects the input/reference term, not this state matrix.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare, 2.154 Maneuvering and Control of Surface and Underwater Vehicles, Lecture 19: Linear Quadratic Regulator
verification_refs.locator: §19.2 Full-State Feedback
verification_refs.supports_claim: Derives x_dot=(A−BK)x+BKx_desired and identifies A−BK as the closed-loop A-matrix.

facts.statement: For a finite-dimensional continuous-time LTI state model with n states, the pair (A,B) is controllable if and only if the controllability matrix [B, AB, ..., A^(n−1)B] has rank n.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare, 16.31 Feedback Control Systems, Topic 12: State-Space Models
verification_refs.locator: Controllability matrix and necessary/sufficient rank condition
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines the controllable subspace as the range of the matrix formed from B, AB, … and states the necessary and sufficient full-rank condition for controllability.

facts.statement: For a finite-dimensional continuous-time LTI model with n states and output y=Cx, the pair (A,C) is observable if and only if the observability matrix [C; CA; ...; CA^(n−1)] has rank n; then the initial state is uniquely reconstructible from ideal input-output history over a finite observation interval.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare, 16.323 Principles of Optimal Control, Lecture 11: Estimation Schemes
verification_refs.locator: Estimation Schemes and Estimator Example 10-1, observability matrix test
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines the observability matrix using C, CA, ... and tests its rank in an estimator example; the general rank-n equivalence follows from the finite-dimensional LTI observability theorem, with the stated ideal-model assumptions.

facts.statement: For the nominal continuous-time LTI plant x_dot=Ax+Bu, y=Cx and Luenberger observer xhat_dot=Axhat+Bu+L(y−C xhat), the estimation error e=x−xhat satisfies e_dot=(A−LC)e; observer error poles are the eigenvalues of A−LC.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare, 16.323 Principles of Optimal Control, Lecture 11: Estimation Schemes
verification_refs.locator: Closed-loop Estimator, estimation-error derivation
verification_refs.supports_claim: Derives x_tilde_dot=(A−LC)x_tilde by subtracting the Luenberger observer equation from the plant equation and identifies the eigenvalues of A−LC as estimator poles.

facts.statement: For a finite-dimensional LTI realization, the input-output transfer function is determined by its reachable and observable subsystem; in a minimal realization all states are reachable and observable, so the eigenvalues of A appear as transfer-function poles, while a nonminimal realization can contain uncontrollable or unobservable internal modes absent from that transfer function.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare, 6.241 Dynamic Systems and Control, Lecture 21: Minimal Realizations
verification_refs.locator: Kalman decomposition, transfer-function realization, and minimal-realization theorem
verification_refs.supports_claim: Shows that the transfer function is entirely defined by the reachable and observable part and states that a realization is minimal iff reachable and observable; the eigenvalue/pole implication follows for the minimal subsystem from its state-space transfer representation.

facts.statement: For a finite-dimensional continuous-time LTI pair (A,B), controllability is equivalent to rank[λI−A, B]=n at every eigenvalue λ of A. The pair is stabilizable iff this rank condition holds for every eigenvalue with Re(λ)≥0; equivalently, every uncontrollable mode must lie strictly in the open left half-plane.

verification_refs.citation: MIT, 16.31 Feedback Control Systems, Fall 2005, PBH Test—Controllability
verification_refs.locator: Slides 18–19, Popov–Belevitch–Hautus controllability test
verification_refs.supports_claim: States (A,B) controllable iff rank[(sI−A),B]=n for all s and proves loss of rank at an eigenvalue when an uncontrollable left eigenvector exists.

verification_refs.citation: Technion, Control Theory (00350188), Lecture 7
verification_refs.locator: Uncontrollable modes and stabilizability
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines stabilizability as all uncontrollable modes being stable, explicitly the open left half-plane.

facts.statement: For a finite-dimensional continuous-time LTI pair (A,C), observability is equivalent to rank[[λI−A];C]=n at every eigenvalue λ of A. The pair is detectable iff this rank condition holds for every eigenvalue with Re(λ)≥0; equivalently, every unobservable mode lies strictly in the open left half-plane.

verification_refs.citation: MIT, 16.31 Feedback Control Systems, Fall 2005, PBH Test—Observability
verification_refs.locator: Slide 24, Popov–Belevitch–Hautus observability test
verification_refs.supports_claim: Gives the equivalent full-rank PBH observability tests using [sI−A; C] at all complex s.

verification_refs.citation: S. Pohland, Linear Systems, Chapter 7: Controllability/Observability—Continuous LTI Systems
verification_refs.locator: §7.2.3–7.2.4, PBH observability and detectable systems
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines detectability as all unobservable modes being stable and gives the modified PBH condition on eigenvalues in the closed right half-plane.

facts.statement: For a finite-dimensional continuous-time LTI pair (A,B), if (A,B) is completely controllable, full-state feedback u=-Kx can assign the closed-loop characteristic polynomial det(sI-(A-BK)) to any real monic polynomial of degree n (equivalently, any conjugate-symmetric set of n desired poles). In a noncontrollable realization, state feedback cannot move the uncontrollable modes; arbitrary assignment of all n poles is therefore not guaranteed.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare, 16.30 Feedback Control Systems, Lecture 11: Full-State Feedback Control
verification_refs.locator: §Ackermann's Formula and pole-placement examples
verification_refs.supports_claim: Presents pole placement through full-state feedback and states Ackermann's formula applies to higher-order controllable systems; the formula constructs K for the requested closed-loop characteristic polynomial.

verification_refs.citation: MIT, 16.31 Feedback Control Systems, Fall 2005, PBH Test—Controllability
verification_refs.locator: Slides 18–22, PBH controllability proof and uncontrollable decomposition
verification_refs.supports_claim: Gives the controllability decomposition with an uncontrollable block and proves rank loss at an uncontrollable eigenvalue; state feedback acts through B and cannot alter the autonomous uncontrollable block's eigenvalues.

facts.statement: For a finite-dimensional SISO LTI pair (A,B) with n states, Ackermann's formula computes a state-feedback gain for a specified characteristic polynomial when the pair is completely controllable; its expression uses the inverse controllability matrix. Numerical reliability is condition-dependent: poorly conditioned pole-assignment problems can produce sensitive or inaccurate computations, so the formula must not be described as inherently reliable merely because it is algebraically valid or the model has high order.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare, 16.30 Feedback Control Systems, Lecture 11: Full-State Feedback Control
verification_refs.locator: §Ackermann's Formula, formula and controllability matrix definition
verification_refs.supports_claim: Gives K=[0 … 0 1] Mc^-1 Φd(A), defines Mc=[B AB … A^(n−1)B], and explicitly says the system must be controllable because the formula inverts Mc.

verification_refs.citation: N. J. Higham, M. Konstantinov, V. Mehrmann, and P. Petkov, The Sensitivity of Computational Control Problems, IEEE Control Systems Magazine 24(1), 2004, pp. 28–43
verification_refs.locator: Abstract and pole-placement conditioning discussion
verification_refs.supports_claim: Peer-reviewed paper treats pole-placement conditioning, identifies ill-conditioned cases where standard numerical methods can fail, and emphasizes condition/error estimation; this supports a condition-dependent caution, not a blanket claim that every high-order system is ill-conditioned.

facts.statement: For a nominal finite-dimensional continuous-time LTI plant with observer-based state feedback u=-K xhat and Luenberger observer gain L, a change to plant-state and estimation-error coordinates makes the combined closed-loop matrix block triangular with diagonal blocks A-BK and A-LC. Its characteristic polynomial is det(sI-(A-BK))det(sI-(A-LC)), so the closed-loop poles are the union of the controller and observer pole sets. Arbitrary independent placement of those sets additionally requires controllability of (A,B) and observability of (A,C), respectively.

verification_refs.citation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, ECE 486 Control Systems, Lecture 23: Combining Full-State Feedback with an Observer
verification_refs.locator: Coordinate transformation to state/error form; closed-loop characteristic polynomial
verification_refs.supports_claim: Derives xdot=(A−BK)x+BKe and edot=(A−LC)e, factors the characteristic polynomial into controller and observer factors, identifies their pole union, and states controllability/observability conditions for arbitrary placement.

facts.statement: State-feedback pole placement determines the eigenvalues of A-BK, but does not by itself impose unity closed-loop DC gain or zero steady-state error to a constant reference. For a stable, feasible LTI tracking problem, reference precompensation can calibrate the steady-state gain using a sufficiently accurate model; integral-error augmentation is an alternative for eliminating constant-reference error under its stability and feasibility assumptions.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare, 16.30 Feedback Control Systems, Lecture 11: Full-State Feedback Control
verification_refs.locator: §Reference Inputs, step response without N correction and reference scaling
verification_refs.supports_claim: Separates pole/stability design from reference tracking, shows a pole-placed example with non-unity DC gain and nonzero step error, then introduces a reference scaling N computed from closed-loop DC gain to achieve zero steady-state step error.

verification_refs.citation: MIT 6.310 Feedback Systems, Spring 2026, Prelab 5: Integral State
verification_refs.locator: Integral state motivation and state-space augmentation
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that model errors can make a state-feedback reference precompensator leave persistent steady-state error and introduces an integral state as an alternative; the fact explicitly retains stability and feasibility assumptions.

facts.statement: For C_lead(s)=Kc(1+Ts)/(1+αTs), with Kc>0, T>0, and 0<α<1, the zero is at −1/T and the pole at −1/(αT), so the pole is farther left on the real axis. On the positive imaginary-frequency axis the zero contributes more phase than the pole, giving a positive phase contribution over finite positive frequencies.

verification_refs.citation: Texas A&M University, ECEN 667, Lecture 21: Stabilizers—Lead-Lag Compensators
verification_refs.locator: Slides 17 and 33, normalized lead-lag transfer function
verification_refs.supports_claim: Gives the normalized first-order transfer function (1+sT)/(1+αsT) and parameter convention for a lead compensator.

verification_refs.citation: Direct pole/zero and frequency-phase derivation from the stated transfer function
verification_refs.locator: Factor numerator and denominator; compare arctan(ωT) and arctan(ωαT)
verification_refs.supports_claim: Roots are −1/T and −1/(αT); because 0<α<1, 1/(αT)>1/T. For ω>0, atan(ωT)>atan(ωαT), so the net phase is positive.

facts.statement: For C_lead(s)=Kc(1+Ts)/(1+αTs), Kc,T>0 and 0<α<1, the maximum phase lead satisfies sin(φmax)=(1−α)/(1+α), equivalently α=(1−sin φmax)/(1+sin φmax).

verification_refs.citation: Texas A&M University, ECEN 667, Lecture 21: Stabilizers—Lead-Lag Compensators
verification_refs.locator: Slides 17 and 33, maximum phase relation
verification_refs.supports_claim: States α=(1−sin φ)/(1+sin φ) and sin φ=(1−α)/(1+α) for the normalized lead network.

verification_refs.citation: Differentiate φ(ω)=atan(ωT)−atan(ωαT)
verification_refs.locator: Set derivative to zero for ω>0 and substitute ωT=1/√α
verification_refs.supports_claim: Differentiation gives the interior maximum at ωT=1/√α; substituting into the phase difference yields sin φmax=(1−α)/(1+α).

facts.statement: For C_lead(s)=Kc(1+Ts)/(1+αTs), Kc,T>0 and 0<α<1, the frequency of maximum phase lead is ωm=1/(T√α), and the compensator magnitude at that frequency is |C_lead(jωm)|=Kc/√α.

verification_refs.citation: Texas A&M University, ECEN 667, Lecture 21: Stabilizers—Lead-Lag Compensators
verification_refs.locator: Slide 17, maximum phase design frequency
verification_refs.supports_claim: Gives T1=1/(2πf√α) for maximum phase at frequency f, equivalent to ωm=1/(T√α).

verification_refs.citation: Substitution into the normalized lead transfer function
verification_refs.locator: Evaluate |Kc(1+jωT)/(1+jωαT)| at ωT=1/√α
verification_refs.supports_claim: At ωT=1/√α the squared magnitude ratio is (1+1/α)/(1+α) = 1/α, giving Kc/√α for Kc>0.

facts.statement: For C_lag(s)=Kc(1+Ts)/(1+βTs), with Kc,T>0 and β>1, the zero is at −1/T and the pole at −1/(βT), so the pole is closer to the origin. The low-frequency gain tends to Kc and the high-frequency gain tends to Kc/β; the network contributes negative phase for positive finite frequencies.

verification_refs.citation: Texas A&M University, MEEN 364, Lecture 26: Lag Compensation
verification_refs.locator: pp. 3–4, lag transfer function and frequency response
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines a lag network with parameter greater than one, states its pole break frequency is below its zero, and describes greater low-frequency gain and negative phase.

verification_refs.citation: Limits of the stated lag transfer function
verification_refs.locator: Evaluate C_lag(0) and limω→∞ C_lag(jω)
verification_refs.supports_claim: The limits are Kc and Kc/β. The pole/zero locations follow by solving denominator/numerator roots; β>1 puts the pole closer to zero.

facts.statement: In stable unity-feedback tracking with a finite, positive, nonzero plant DC gain, a lag factor whose DC gain is β>1 multiplies the low-frequency loop gain by β and reduces the finite unit-step steady-state error 1/(1+Kp). Because its pole and zero are both at nonzero finite frequencies, an ordinary lag compensator does not add an integrator and does not change system type; zero error is not guaranteed.

verification_refs.citation: University of Washington, Xu Chen, Lecture 18: Lead and Lag Compensators
verification_refs.locator: §How a lag compensator reduces the error
verification_refs.supports_claim: Derives stable-loop step error from DC loop gain and shows a lag factor increases that gain and decreases the error; describes the lag network as approximating, but not being, an integrator.

verification_refs.citation: Final-value-theorem step-error derivation for stable unity feedback
verification_refs.locator: E/R=1/(1+L), e_ss=1/(1+L(0)); C_lag(0)=Kc and no pole at s=0
verification_refs.supports_claim: For the stated stable finite-DC-gain conditions, multiplying L(0) by β>1 decreases positive finite 1/(1+L(0)); the lag's finite nonzero pole/zero add no origin pole, so system type is unchanged.

facts.statement: For C_lag(s)=Kc(1+Ts)/(1+βTs), Kc,T>0 and β>1, the phase contribution is atan(ωT)−atan(ωβT)<0 for ω>0. Therefore a lag section adds phase lag at a finite crossover frequency, and the compensated loop phase margin must be recalculated rather than assumed unchanged.

verification_refs.citation: Texas A&M University, MEEN 364, Lecture 26: Lag Compensation
verification_refs.locator: pp. 3–4, lag phase response and design procedure
verification_refs.supports_claim: States the lag network introduces phase decrease and its design procedure explicitly redraws compensated frequency response to check phase margin.

verification_refs.citation: Frequency-domain phase of the lag transfer function
verification_refs.locator: arg(C(jω))=atan(ωT)−atan(ωβT)
verification_refs.supports_claim: For β>1 and ω>0, atan(ωβT)>atan(ωT), so phase contribution is strictly negative.

facts.statement: For the standard lag section C_lag(s)=Kc(1+Ts)/(1+βTs), with Kc,T>0 and β>1, the low-frequency gain is Kc and the high-frequency asymptotic gain is Kc/β; their ratio is β. This ratio is the lag-section gain change only and is not by itself a guarantee of a specified closed-loop error or crossover response.

verification_refs.citation: Zero- and infinite-frequency limits of the standard lag transfer function
verification_refs.locator: C_lag(0)=Kc and limω→∞|C_lag(jω)|=Kc/β
verification_refs.supports_claim: Taking the two limits gives Kc/(Kc/β)=β; the statement explicitly excludes any automatic closed-loop performance conclusion.

verification_refs.citation: Texas A&M University, MEEN 364, Lecture 26: Lag Compensation
verification_refs.locator: pp. 3–4, lag asymptotic frequency response
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes larger low-frequency gain and the corresponding attenuation at higher frequency for the lag network.

facts.statement: In a standard linear feedback loop, a lead section can add positive phase near its design frequency, while a lag section can increase low-frequency loop gain and reduce finite steady-state error; cascading sections can therefore address both transient and steady-state objectives. These effects interact through the full loop transfer function, so their achievement is not guaranteed without recomputing stability margins and response for the combined design.

verification_refs.citation: Texas A&M University, MEEN 364, Lecture 26: Lag Compensation
verification_refs.locator: pp. 1–4, lead design parameters, lag design, and combined compensation
verification_refs.supports_claim: Treats lead as phase-margin/transient shaping, lag as low-frequency gain/steady-state improvement, recommends combined compensation for both objectives, and requires checking compensated frequency response.

verification_refs.citation: Cascade transfer function and unity-feedback characteristic equation
verification_refs.locator: L(s)=C_lead(s)C_lag(s)G(s); closed-loop characteristic equation 1+L(s)=0
verification_refs.supports_claim: Cascade multiplication combines the sections in the loop transfer function; both frequency response and closed-loop characteristic equation depend on the combined product, supporting the requirement to analyze the combined design.

facts.statement: For a fixed linear plant G(s), controller C(s), and unity negative feedback, the loop transfer function is L(s)=C(s)G(s). Root-locus analysis examines roots of 1+kL(s)=0 as scalar gain k varies, while frequency-response analysis evaluates the same loop transfer function on s=jω; adding compensator poles and zeros changes this common mathematical model, though the two analyses answer different questions.

verification_refs.citation: Texas A&M University, MEEN 364, Lecture 26: Lag Compensation
verification_refs.locator: Lead-lag transfer functions and compensated frequency response
verification_refs.supports_claim: Shows compensator pole/zero sections modifying the loop frequency response and calls for compensated response rechecking.

verification_refs.citation: Unity-feedback characteristic equation and frequency-response substitution
verification_refs.locator: Closed-loop denominator 1+L(s); evaluate L(jω) for frequency response
verification_refs.supports_claim: The unity negative-feedback characteristic equation is 1+L(s)=0; frequency response is L evaluated at s=jω. Thus these are distinct analyses of the same loop transfer function.

facts.statement: For a linear time-invariant plant G(s) and a cascaded compensator C(s), the loop transfer function is L(s)=C(s)G(s); the compensator's poles and zeros alter the loop magnitude and phase and thereby affect closed-loop behavior. Lead and lag sections are commonly selected to address different design objectives, but no single section guarantees all stability-margin, bandwidth, tracking-error, control-effort, noise, and robustness requirements simultaneously.

verification_refs.citation: Texas A&M University, MEEN 364, Lecture 26: Lag Compensation
verification_refs.locator: pp. 1–4, lead and lag design parameters and compensation objectives
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes lead and lag compensator transfer functions and their effects on phase margin, crossover, low-frequency gain, steady-state error, and transient response; the design procedure checks the compensated loop.

verification_refs.citation: Series interconnection and unity-feedback transfer-function identities
verification_refs.locator: L(s)=C(s)G(s); closed-loop transfer denominator 1+L(s)
verification_refs.supports_claim: For a well-defined series connection, transfer functions multiply; the resulting open-loop product determines the unity-feedback closed-loop denominator, so compensator poles/zeros affect the combined response rather than independently guaranteeing all objectives.

facts.statement: A standard frequency-response lead-design procedure starts from the uncompensated loop's gain crossover and phase margin, calculates the additional lead with an explicit design margin, selects the desired compensated crossover, derives α and T to place the maximum phase contribution near that frequency, adjusts gain as needed, and recomputes the compensated frequency response and phase margin. This is a design procedure, not a guarantee that one pass will satisfy every plant constraint.

verification_refs.citation: Texas A&M University, MEEN 364, Lecture 26: Lead Compensation Design
verification_refs.locator: pp. 1–2, Design procedure for Lead Compensation
verification_refs.supports_claim: Lists required open-loop error gain, uncompensated phase margin, required phase lead with safety margin, α, new crossover and corner-frequency selection, and checking/iterating the compensated frequency response.

verification_refs.citation: Texas A&M University, ECEN 667, Lecture 21: Stabilizers—Lead-Lag Compensators
verification_refs.locator: Slide 17, maximum-phase frequency design relation
verification_refs.supports_claim: Relates the selected maximum-phase frequency to T and α, the placement step in the stated design sequence.

facts.statement: For the standard continuous-time infinite-horizon LQR regulator, the objective is to minimize J=∫₀∞(xᵀQx+uᵀRu)dt subject to ẋ=Ax+Bu. Q weights state deviation and R weights control effort; this unconstrained objective defines the regulator and does not itself specify nonzero-reference tracking.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare, 16.323 Principles of Optimal Control, Lecture 4: Linear Quadratic Regulator
verification_refs.locator: §LQR cost and infinite-horizon CARE
verification_refs.supports_claim: Derives the LQR cost with state and control quadratic penalties and the infinite-horizon CARE for LTI dynamics.

facts.statement: In the standard continuous-time LQR problem without a state-input cross term, Q is symmetric positive semidefinite and R is symmetric positive definite. Q weights state components in the quadratic cost; positive definiteness of R makes the control-effort penalty strictly positive for every nonzero input.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare, 16.30/16.31 Feedback Control Systems, Recitation 7
verification_refs.locator: §Assumptions for LQR
verification_refs.supports_claim: States Q must be positive semidefinite and R positive definite, explaining their roles in state and control-effort penalties.

facts.statement: For the standard continuous-time infinite-horizon LQR problem with no state-input cross term, the symmetric matrix P satisfies AᵀP+PA−PBR⁻¹BᵀP+Q=0. The regulator gain is formed from a stabilizing solution; among algebraic solutions, the stabilizing solution is the one for which A−BR⁻¹BᵀP is Hurwitz.

verification_refs.locator: §Assumptions for LQR and CARE solution selection
