facts.statement: Given the stabilizing CARE solution P for the standard continuous-time LQR problem, K=R⁻¹BᵀP and u=−Kx yield the closed-loop state matrix A−BK. Its eigenvalues are the regulator's closed-loop poles and are selected indirectly by Q, R, and the plant matrices, rather than prescribed directly as target poles.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare, 16.323 Principles of Optimal Control, Lecture 4: Linear Quadratic Regulator
verification_refs.locator: §Steady-state feedback and closed-loop dynamics
verification_refs.supports_claim: Gives u=−R⁻¹BᵀPss x and derives the closed-loop matrix A−BK.

verification_refs.citation: MIT, 16.31 Feedback Control Systems, Lecture 15: Pole Placement
verification_refs.locator: pp. 1–3, closed-loop pole selection and state-feedback design
verification_refs.supports_claim: Treats pole locations as selected design targets for state-feedback pole placement, distinct from LQR's cost-based design.

facts.statement: For the standard continuous-time infinite-horizon LQR with Q=Qᵀ⪰0 and R=Rᵀ≻0, if (A,B) is stabilizable and (Q¹ᐟ²,A) is detectable, there is a unique symmetric positive-semidefinite stabilizing CARE solution P; the associated gain makes A−BR⁻¹BᵀP Hurwitz. Controllability and observability are stronger conditions than stabilizability and detectability and are sufficient but not necessary.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare, 16.30/16.31 Feedback Control Systems, Recitation 7
verification_refs.locator: §Assumptions for LQR, unique PSD CARE solution
verification_refs.supports_claim: States Q⪰0, R≻0 and that stabilizability/detectability selects a unique positive-semidefinite solution; the associated solution is used for stable feedback.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare, 16.323 Principles of Optimal Control, Lecture 4: Linear Quadratic Regulator
verification_refs.locator: §LQR Observations, stabilizable and detectable performance output
verification_refs.supports_claim: States the unique PSD symmetric CARE solution under stabilizability and detectability and the equivalence of these conditions to asymptotic closed-loop stability for the steady-state feedback.

facts.statement: For the same standard LQR problem, multiplying both Q and R by the same positive scalar γ multiplies every admissible trajectory cost by γ and therefore leaves the set of minimizing controls, including the optimal state-feedback gain K, unchanged. The stabilizing Riccati solution scales to γP; changing the relative scaling of Q versus R is not covered by this invariance.

verification_refs.citation: Direct cost-functional and CARE scaling derivation
verification_refs.locator: Jγ=γJ; substitute Pγ=γP into CARE and Kγ=(γR)⁻¹Bᵀ(γP)
verification_refs.supports_claim: A positive common factor does not change the minimizer; the CARE scales consistently with Pγ=γP and the gain expression simplifies to the original K.

facts.statement: Bryson's rule is a heuristic initial choice of diagonal LQR weights: Qii=1/(maximum acceptable state/output excursion i)² and Rjj=1/(maximum acceptable input j)². It normalizes each selected maximum acceptable excursion to unit quadratic contribution; it is a starting point for tuning, not a theorem that guarantees desired closed-loop performance.

verification_refs.citation: João P. Hespanha, Advanced Undergraduate Topics in Control, §11.2 Bryson's Rule
verification_refs.locator: pp. 127–128, Bryson's rule
verification_refs.supports_claim: Gives the inverse-square maximum acceptable state/output and input formulas, explains their unit-normalization purpose, and describes Bryson's rule as an initial choice often followed by iterative design.

facts.statement: Classical full-state pole placement specifies desired eigenvalues of A−BK and computes a gain to meet them, subject to controllability. Standard LQR instead specifies a quadratic cost and obtains K by solving the Riccati equation; the resulting closed-loop poles are consequences of the optimized gain and are not independently prescribed as arbitrary targets.

verification_refs.citation: MIT, 16.31 Feedback Control Systems, Lecture 15: Pole Placement
verification_refs.locator: pp. 1–3, selecting desired closed-loop poles
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes selecting desired closed-loop pole locations and computing state-feedback gains to place them.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare, 16.323 Principles of Optimal Control, Lecture 4: Linear Quadratic Regulator
verification_refs.locator: §LQR cost, CARE, and feedback solution
verification_refs.supports_claim: Derives the feedback gain from the cost-defined CARE solution, rather than from independently assigned pole targets.

facts.statement: The standard unconstrained LQR term uᵀRu penalizes control effort in the objective but does not impose hard actuator magnitude limits or state/input inequality constraints. Such bounds require a constrained formulation or separate implementation protections; saturation of an unconstrained LQR command changes the designed closed-loop law and must be analyzed separately.

verification_refs.citation: MIT, Underactuated Robotics, Chapter 8: Linear Quadratic Regulators
verification_refs.locator: §LQR with input and state constraints
verification_refs.supports_claim: Treats strict input/state constraints as an extension beyond the standard unconstrained closed-form LQR and describes solving a constrained trajectory optimization instead.

facts.statement: Continuous-time infinite-horizon LQR uses the CARE AᵀP+PA−PBR⁻¹BᵀP+Q=0 and gain K=R⁻¹BᵀP. Discrete-time infinite-horizon LQR for x[k+1]=A_dx[k]+B_du[k] uses the DARE P=A_dᵀPA_d−A_dᵀPB_d(R+B_dᵀPB_d)⁻¹B_dᵀPA_d+Q and gain K_d=(R+B_dᵀPB_d)⁻¹B_dᵀPA_d; the two equations are not interchangeable.

verification_refs.citation: MIT, Underactuated Robotics, Chapter 8: Linear Quadratic Regulators
verification_refs.locator: §Continuous-time Riccati equation and §Discrete-time Riccati equations
verification_refs.supports_claim: Derives continuous-time and discrete-time Riccati equations and the discrete-time optimal gain separately.

facts.statement: For standard continuous-time infinite-horizon LQR, detectability of (Q¹ᐟ²,A) is a condition on modes unpenalized or unobserved by the cost that supports the stabilizing CARE solution. If a separate Luenberger observer is needed because plant states are not measured, its estimation-error dynamics are A−LC and the pair (C,A) must be detectable for an observer gain to stabilize unobservable modes; cost detectability and measurement detectability are distinct checks.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare, 16.323 Principles of Optimal Control, Lecture 4: Linear Quadratic Regulator
verification_refs.locator: §LQR Observations, stabilizability and detectability of the performance output
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines the LQR detectability condition through modes seen in the cost performance output Cz, which need not be the physical output.

verification_refs.citation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, ECE 486 Control Systems, Lecture 22: State Estimation and Observer
verification_refs.locator: Observer error dynamics and detectability/observability condition
verification_refs.supports_claim: Derives observer estimation-error dynamics governed by A−LC and ties stability of observer poles to the measurement pair (A,C).

facts.statement: In the standard LQR objective, Q weights the quadratic state-deviation cost; increasing a selected diagonal weight therefore assigns greater cost to that state's deviation, with the optimal Riccati solution and feedback gain recomputed jointly. This does not prove that every state response, input demand, noise sensitivity, or robustness metric improves monotonically. Standard unconstrained LQR also does not enforce hard state or actuator limits, so those limits and implementation sensitivities must be checked separately.

verification_refs.citation: MIT Underactuated Robotics, Ch. 8: Linear Quadratic Regulators
verification_refs.locator: Infinite-horizon cost and Riccati/gain derivation; §LQR with input and state constraints
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines the objective xᵀQx+uᵀRu, derives the Riccati solution and gain jointly from Q, R, A, B, and treats state/input constraints as a separate constrained-LQR problem. This supports the cost-weight interpretation and shows that the standard unconstrained objective is not itself a hard-limit guarantee.

facts.statement: In standard LQR, R weights the quadratic control-effort cost: a larger relative R makes costly input use less attractive to the optimizer, while reducing R can permit more aggressive control and can produce faster response in particular plants. This is a cost tradeoff, not a universal monotonic response theorem; reduced R does not remove physical actuator limits, and saturation or neglected dynamics must be checked for the actual implementation.

verification_refs.citation: MIT Underactuated Robotics, Ch. 8: Linear Quadratic Regulators
verification_refs.locator: Infinite-horizon cost and Riccati/gain derivation; §LQR with input and state constraints
verification_refs.supports_claim: The objective explicitly penalizes uᵀRu and the optimal gain depends jointly on Q, R, and the plant. The notes treat hard state/input constraints separately from standard unconstrained LQR, so R must not be described as an actuator limit.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare 16.323, Principles of Optimal Control, Lecture 4
verification_refs.locator: Scalar LQR example and limiting Q/R discussion
verification_refs.supports_claim: The scalar example shows faster response for a particular limiting change in relative state/input weights. It is used only as an example of possible response change, not as a universal monotonic guarantee.

facts.statement: The standard regulator law u=−Kx minimizes a cost about the origin; tracking a nonzero constant operating point requires a feasible steady-state pair (x_r,u_r) and a shift to deviation coordinates (x−x_r,u−u_r). A static reference prefilter can provide nominal constant-reference scaling when the model and required steady-state inverse are valid, but model error can leave steady-state error. LQI instead augments the plant with an integral of tracking error and requires the augmented design problem to satisfy its stabilizability/Riccati conditions. Because actuator saturation can cause integrator windup, the implementation must include and validate suitable anti-windup or integral limiting behavior where saturation is possible.

verification_refs.citation: MIT Underactuated Robotics, Ch. 8: Linear Quadratic Regulators
verification_refs.locator: Standard regulator formulation and tracking cost in deviation from desired state/input
verification_refs.supports_claim: The standard infinite-horizon regulator cost is expressed in state and input, while its tracking formulation explicitly uses deviations (x−x_d) and (u−u_d). For a constant operating point, shifting to feasible equilibrium deviations yields the corresponding regulator coordinates.

verification_refs.citation: MIT 6.302, LQR and Integral Feedback
verification_refs.locator: Reference prefilter derivation and tracking-error-integral state augmentation
verification_refs.supports_claim: Derives a static reference scale for constant-reference tracking, states that model errors in the matrices can cause steady-state error, and constructs an augmented state by integrating tracking error.

verification_refs.locator: Description and Limitations for the plant with augmented integrator
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines the LQI feedback state as plant state plus integrator output, gives the tracking-error integrator update, and specifies stabilizability and Riccati data conditions for the augmented design.

verification_refs.locator: Back-calculation and clamping anti-windup descriptions
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that actuator saturation can leave an internal integrator wound up and describes back-calculation and clamping approaches. This supports the implementation warning, not a claim that every LQI design necessarily winds up.

facts.statement: After restoring a 4–20 mA loop, verify representative low, midpoint, and high output levels at the installed loop and receiving system, confirm the configured raw-to-engineering-unit scaling and applicable alarm/fault-current behavior, then document the returned-to-service state. The exact test points, alarm limits, trip logic, and acceptance tolerances are device- and application-specific; this is an end-to-end verification practice, not a universal trip-setting rule.

facts.statement: A thermistor measurement input should distinguish plausible in-range readings from open/short wiring faults and ADC rail or out-of-range conditions. The voltage/code associated with each fault depends on the thermistor divider, bias network, ADC input limits and component tolerances, so diagnostic thresholds must be derived and tested for that circuit. A detected fault should enter the application-defined safe fault state; the safe output or trip action is determined by the process hazard and system design, not by thermistor polarity alone.

verification_refs.citation: Texas Instruments, AM263Px MCU+ SDK: ADC Open Shorts Detection
verification_refs.locator: Example Description, OSD circuit configurations, and Qualification process
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes ADC pin open/short detection using switched bias resistors, identifies open and rail-short signatures, and lists required ADC configuration assumptions. It demonstrates topology-specific diagnostic behavior rather than universal fixed thresholds.

verification_refs.citation: Analog Devices, CN0545 Circuit Note: Thermistor Measurement
verification_refs.locator: Thermistor Measurements and Thermistor Design Considerations
verification_refs.supports_claim: Shows a specific NTC resistance range mapped through a divider to an ADC, requires optimizing for minimum/maximum sensor resistance and ADC range, and explains that thermistor resistance-to-temperature conversion is nonlinear. These circuit-dependent voltage ranges support deriving fault thresholds from the actual sensor/ADC topology.

facts.statement: A force-balance pressure transmitter operates by using feedback force to return its sensing linkage toward equilibrium; this constrains sensing-element motion and can reduce errors associated with spring-element fatigue while providing a substantially linear balance output. The mechanism can be bulky and susceptible to vibration-induced inertial output noise. Supply and power requirements depend on whether the design is pneumatic or electronic; for electronic designs, coil drive power and hazardous-area energy limits must be checked against the specific transmitter certification rather than assumed universally.

verification_refs.citation: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Industrial Instrumentation, Force-balance Pressure Transmitters
verification_refs.locator: Force-balance Pressure Transmitters, paragraphs on motion, linearity, fatigue, vibration, and power
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains pressure-to-force balancing, constrained sensing-element motion and linear output; states reduced susceptibility to spring fatigue, bulky mechanisms and vibration-induced output noise. It also notes that electronic force-balance drive power can affect intrinsic-safety energy limits; this is recorded as design-specific, not universal.

verification_refs.citation: Techniques de l'Ingénieur, Force balance sensors and transmitters
verification_refs.locator: §2 Force balance sensors and transmitters
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes the force-balance principle as keeping the sensing element near equilibrium and lists reduced fatigue, wear and hysteresis as benefits of the nearly static sensing element.

facts.statement: For a fixed plant and unity-feedback characteristic equation, changing scalar gain alone moves closed-loop poles only along that plant's root locus. If a desired pole location is not on the uncompensated locus, gain alone cannot realize it; adding controller poles/zeros changes the open-loop transfer function and therefore the root locus. Lead, lag, lead-lag, and PID structures are possible controller choices, but their realization and resulting stability/performance must be checked against the actual plant and implementation constraints.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare 16.06, Principles of Automatic Control, Lecture 13: Root Locus Rules (cont-d)
verification_refs.locator: pp. 3–4, Lead Compensator Example
verification_refs.supports_claim: Gives a specified desired closed-loop pole example where gain-only root locus does not pass through the target, then introduces lead compensation poles/zeros and recalculates the locus to meet the design point.

verification_refs.citation: MathWorks Control System Toolbox, Edit Compensator Dynamics in Control System Designer
verification_refs.locator: Compensator Dynamics; Lead and Lag Networks
verification_refs.supports_claim: Documents adding poles/zeros, integrator/differentiator dynamics, lead, lag and combined lead-lag networks and editing them in a Root Locus Editor. This supports the listed controller structures and that controller dynamics alter the root-locus design object.

facts.statement: Strain-gage and load-cell wiring must account for lead resistance and excitation drop, low-level signal susceptibility to electromagnetic coupling, and unwanted ground-current paths. Fault checks can include conductor continuity/insulation, bridge input/output and leg resistance, and no-load zero balance; open/short or bridge-imbalance interpretation must use the actual sensor data sheet or calibration baseline because resistance and zero limits are model-specific. Shielding, grounding, lead configuration, and the fault response are selected for the measurement topology and installation rather than by a universal wiring rule.

verification_refs.locator: Signal Conditioning for Strain Gages
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that long lead wires add bridge-arm resistance, cause offset and desensitize output; identifies remote sensing, filtering, bridge nulling and shunt calibration as relevant measurement-chain methods.

verification_refs.citation: OMEGA Engineering, The Strain Gage, Technical Data / Transactions, Vol. 3
verification_refs.locator: Application & Installation; Shielding; Guarding; Lead-Wire Effects
verification_refs.supports_claim: Identifies low-level signal susceptibility to capacitive/magnetic coupling, ground currents and parasitic contact/lead resistance; describes shielding, guarding, twisting, and lead-wire compensation while noting the actual scheme's limits.

facts.statement: For a specified negative-feedback loop, the Nyquist stability margin is assessed from the loop transfer around the -1 critical point; practical robustness review should linearize at relevant operating points and check gain, phase, and delay margins, while representing model uncertainty and sensor-noise tradeoffs explicitly. These linear margins do not certify behavior after actuator saturation: saturation is a nonlinear operating condition and must be assessed separately with actuator limits represented, including recovery or anti-windup behavior where applicable. Margin targets and the operating envelope are system-specific, not universal numeric rules.

verification_refs.locator: Open-loop response; DelayMargin; operating-point linearization tips
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines classical margins and delay margin for a specified negative-feedback open-loop model, and instructs linearizing a Simulink model at a particular operating point before computing margins.

verification_refs.supports_claim: Shows computing loop transfer functions by linearizing at a selected operating point, calculating classical and disk-based margins, and interpreting disk margins as gain/phase uncertainty tolerated without loss of closed-loop stability.

This supports treating saturation separately from a linear stability-margin calculation.

verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains margins as tolerable gain/phase changes, that robustness varies across frequency, and that tuning uses specified target margins; it gives examples rather than a universal required margin value.

facts.statement: Power-device control modes are not interchangeable: a power diode is an uncontrolled switch, an SCR is triggered on through its gate but latches and cannot be turned off through that gate, and its anode current must be commutated away for the recovery interval. Fully controlled MOSFET/IGBT switching is driven through the gate, but actual switching time and loss depend on operating current and voltage, junction temperature, gate resistance/drive, commutation path, and parasitic circuit layout; therefore device behavior is assessed in the converter's actual circuit conditions.

verification_refs.citation: Infineon, Power Diodes and Thyristors
verification_refs.locator: How Does a Thyristor Work?; Difference Between Power Diode and Thyristors
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes a power diode as an uncontrolled switch; explains gate-triggered SCR latching, inability to turn off using its gate, and the need to commutate anode current away for the recovery interval.

verification_refs.locator: §2.3 Dynamic characteristics; §2.4 Switching characteristics, pp. 13–17
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that IGBT switching performance depends on collector current/voltage, temperature, external gate resistance, board design and parasitics; recommends application tests and characterization. It explains that freewheel-diode recovery affects IGBT turn-on energy, demonstrating the role of commutation path.

verification_refs.supports_claim: Distinguishes insulated-gate MOSFET/IGBT voltage-driven switching from current-driven bipolar devices and describes gate voltage control of switching speed; it supports the gate-drive part of the claim, not a universal timing value.

facts.statement: An RTD channel verification and maintenance plan should address open/short or damaged connections, terminal and lead resistance, insulation leakage to the sheath, wiring configuration and lead imbalance, drift, moisture-related loop faults, and end-to-end loop operation as applicable to the sensor/transmitter installation. The mechanisms are not interchangeable: open/short and lead effects are checked against the selected input topology; insulation limits are sensor-specification dependent; drift alerts may require dual sensors; and water-ingress detection may be a transmitter loop-integrity diagnostic rather than direct RTD-element diagnosis. Do not assume every transmitter automates every check.

verification_refs.locator: §3.1.1 RTD Measurement Protection; §3.1.2 Thermocouple Degradation Diagnostic; §3.1.4 Sensor Drift Alert; §3.1.5 Loop Integrity; §2.6 Loop Test
verification_refs.supports_claim: RTD protection detects a broken, corroded, or loose wire in a 4-wire input; drift alert is a dual-input comparison; water in the wiring compartment is a loop-integrity fault; moisture intrusion is specifically listed for thermocouple degradation diagnostics, not generalized to the RTD element; and loop test verifies wiring, loop integrity, transmitter output, and connected recorders.

facts.statement: Converter and motor-drive selection should match the supply, motor/load duty, and required operating behavior, then assess application-relevant efficiency and thermal limits, input harmonics and power factor, protection, EMC and insulation/safety requirements, regenerative-energy handling, and product-specific maintenance needs. These are design-review categories, not a claim that every installation needs the same topology or mitigation: acceptable limits and required options depend on the supply, load, standards, duty cycle, environment, and selected product.

facts.statement: LOPA documents scenario causes/initiating frequencies, consequences, IPL assumptions, residual risk, and any required SIF risk reduction or target SIL; these results must remain traceable into SIF requirements development. The SRS then specifies the design-enabling functional and integrity requirements, including process measurements/trip points, safe state and output action, response time, proof-test interval, mode of operation, bypass/override, reset/restart, and operating modes as applicable. These detailed SRS fields are not all numerical outputs of the LOPA calculation and must be resolved by the safety lifecycle team from the hazard scenario and process design.

facts.statement: When more than one initiating scenario relies on the same SIF, assess the combined demand frequency and required risk reduction rather than treating each scenario as an isolated SIL assignment. Changes to process conditions, operating modes, initiating-event frequency assumptions, IPL availability/credit, or proof-test assumptions should be screened through the site's management-of-change and functional-safety lifecycle; where a change invalidates the hazard-analysis or SIF design basis, update the affected LOPA, SIL allocation, SRS, and verification evidence to the extent required by the reassessment. Replacement-in-kind and changes with no impact on the safety basis are handled according to the applicable site MOC procedure and jurisdiction.

verification_refs.supports_claim: States that LOPA scenarios are assessed individually but a shared SIF's combined demand frequency and RRF requirement need an additional aggregation step; failing to do so underestimates initiating frequency and required RRF.

verification_refs.locator: Management of Change; 29 CFR 1910.119(l)
verification_refs.supports_claim: For covered processes, describes written procedures for changes other than replacement-in-kind to process chemicals, technology, equipment, procedures and facilities, including technical basis, safety impact, authorization, procedure/PSI updates and training. Applicability is limited to the relevant U.S. PSM jurisdiction and covered processes.

verification_refs.citation: UK Health and Safety Executive, Control Systems: Safety-Related Systems and Instrumentation
verification_refs.locator: §Modification; §Proof testing
verification_refs.supports_claim: Requires a modification-control system to prevent unauthorized or ill-conceived changes and safety verification that required safety function and integrity are maintained; also links proof-test interval and failure detection to system risk/integrity.

verification_refs.citation: UK Health and Safety Executive, Plant Modification/Change Procedures
verification_refs.locator: Plant modification review and hazard assessment
verification_refs.supports_claim: Says process and plant modifications should receive safety, engineering and technical review and a risk assessment to identify hazards created by the change and determine necessary risk-reduction action.

facts.statement: 공정 제어에서 PI 형태가 흔히 사용되며, 측정 신호의 잡음은 미분 동작에서 주파수에 비례해 증폭될 수 있다. 미분동작을 추가하면 재튜닝 부담이 커질 수 있고, 잡음에 따른 과도한 최종제어요소 동작은 마모 또는 고장 위험을 높일 수 있으므로, PI 선택은 공정 동특성·측정 잡음·요구 성능을 고려한 실무적 선택이지 모든 공정에 대한 보편 규칙은 아니다.

verification_refs.citation: United Nations Industrial Development Organization, Training Course on Sustainable Industrial Development: Process Simulation and Optimization Techniques, PID control section
verification_refs.locator: PDF pp. 175–176, derivative-action pitfalls and controller-selection recommendations
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that a large proportion of typical plant feedback loops use PI when offset cannot be tolerated; derivative action may amplify measurement noise, causing abrupt manipulated-variable changes and potential wear on the final control element; recommends D when sluggishness warrants it and the signal is relatively noise-free.

verification_refs.citation: The Chemical Engineer, Practical Process Control Part 6: Derivative Action, Myke King CEng FIChemE
verification_refs.locator: Opening paragraphs and Noise problem section
verification_refs.supports_claim: Reports PI as the majority practice in process industry; explains that adding D requires retuning existing constants and is more difficult to search manually; derives frequency-proportional measurement-noise amplification and identifies potential rapid valve travel/failure. This supports practical tuning and final-element risk, not an unconditional claim that every D controller increases maintenance.

facts.statement: Control-valve characteristic selection should evaluate the installed relationship, not only the manufacturer's inherent curve: the installed curve depends on the system pressure conditions, including pump head and piping/equipment losses. An installed-flow/gain analysis can use minimum and maximum design-flow cases and the corresponding upstream/downstream pressures; include the normal operating case when it is part of the specified operating envelope. This is an engineering selection method, not a universal requirement for one particular calculation tool or acceptance threshold.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook—Refining, D103205X012
verification_refs.locator: §5.5 inherent and installed flow characteristic / installed valve gain terminology
verification_refs.supports_claim: Distinguishes manufacturer inherent characteristic under constant valve pressure drop from installed flow/gain under actual system conditions where pressure drop varies.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook—Oil and Gas, Chapter 3
verification_refs.locator: §3.1 sizing variables and §3.3 liquid maximum-flow calculation
verification_refs.supports_claim: Provides liquid-sizing inputs including flow, P1, P2, fluid temperature/properties, Pv, Pc, FL/FLP and fitting geometry; installed system pressure cases are therefore needed to evaluate the valve over its specified operating envelope.

facts.statement: Mechanical excitation near a structure's natural frequency can produce an enlarged response and, depending on excitation and structural design, fatigue or damage. In feedback loops, the loop dynamics and tuning can amplify some oscillations or pass measurement noise into controller output; resonance or instability is not an automatic consequence of every resonant response. Application review should therefore consider damping, loop bandwidth/tuning, and mechanical resonances together with the actual disturbance and equipment limits.

verification_refs.citation: National Instruments, Dynamic Structural Test Tutorial
verification_refs.locator: Modal Testing; Natural (or Resonant) Frequency; Damping Ratio
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines natural frequency as a frequency at which excitation can produce an exaggerated response and notes excitation near it can lead to fatigue, damage, or structural failure; identifies damping ratio as a modal parameter. The wording is conditional, not a guarantee of damage.

verification_refs.citation: Control Global, Controller Attenuation and Resonance Tips
verification_refs.locator: Controller amplification/resonance and tuning discussion
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that control-loop oscillations may be amplified by resonance depending on disturbance period and tuning, and describes reducing controller aggressiveness or judicious filtering as context-dependent responses; it does not claim every oscillation causes instability.

verification_refs.citation: Control Global, What Are Good Signal Filtering Tips?
verification_refs.locator: Noise amplification by proportional/derivative action; filter tradeoff
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes controller gain passing measurement noise into controller output and the tradeoff between reducing noise and slowing the loop; supports treating noise amplification as dependent on controller and filter dynamics.

facts.statement: Moving closed-loop poles farther into the stable half-plane generally targets faster nominal transients, but pole choices that demand large gains can make the closed-loop eigenstructure sensitive to model perturbations and may exceed actuator effort limits. For high-gain observers in particular, faster state reconstruction trades against measurement-noise sensitivity and transient peaking; these are not universal consequences of every faster pole choice. Discrete-time realization must also be checked against the selected sampling period. Therefore pole-placement results require implementation-level checks of control effort, saturation, noise, sampling and model uncertainty before field use.

verification_refs.citation: MathWorks, Pole Placement, Control System Toolbox documentation
verification_refs.locator: State-Feedback Gain Selection; Caution
verification_refs.supports_claim: Relates closed-loop pole locations to rise/settling/transient response and warns unrealistic pole choices can be badly conditioned; moving weakly controllable/observable poles may require high gain, making the closed-loop eigenstructure sensitive to perturbations.

verification_refs.citation: MathWorks, place: Pole placement design
verification_refs.locator: Pole-selection caution for high-order problems
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that some pole choices in high-order problems result in very large gains and that associated sensitivity problems call for caution.

verification_refs.citation: MathWorks, What Is LQR Optimal Control? State Space, Part 4
verification_refs.locator: Pole-placement response versus actuator effort and saturation demonstration
verification_refs.supports_claim: Demonstrates a pole-placement design with actuator saturation and shows reducing actuator use by changing the effort weight leads to a slower response; this is an example of the performance/effort tradeoff, not a universal quantitative rule.

verification_refs.citation: J. H. Ahrens and H. K. Khalil, High-gain observers in the presence of measurement noise: A switched-gain approach, Automatica 45(4), 2009
verification_refs.locator: Abstract and introduction: convergence speed, measurement noise and peaking tradeoff
verification_refs.supports_claim: For the studied class of high-gain observers, explains the tradeoff between faster state reconstruction and measurement-noise amplification and discusses transient peaking; the fact record therefore explicitly limits this claim to high-gain observer designs.

verification_refs.citation: MathWorks, Frequency Response Based PID Tuner documentation
verification_refs.locator: Target bandwidth and discrete controller sample-time constraint
verification_refs.supports_claim: Relates the target closed-loop bandwidth to the controller sampling period and imposes a sampling-dependent bandwidth bound for discrete-time tuning; this supports checking designed dynamics against actual sample time, not a universal pole-to-sample ratio.

facts.statement: A process historian is used to collect and retain time-series process data for historical retrieval and analysis; implementations may compress stored samples and retain value status/quality and timestamps. These capabilities and retention limits are product- and configuration-dependent. Timestamp semantics must be identified explicitly: a historian-assigned write/storage timestamp is not necessarily the original source/event time.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, DeltaV Continuous Historian FAQ
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes a process historian collecting process data in time-series form for storage/retrieval, configured historical data sets, compression, parameter value plus status collection, and the product's timestamp assignment at database write. This supports the functions while explicitly showing timestamp origin is implementation-specific.

verification_refs.citation: AVEVA Historian 2023 R2 documentation, System parameters
verification_refs.locator: QualityRule, TimeStampRule, and source/storage latency parameters
verification_refs.supports_claim: Documents configurable quality selection and timestamp rules, and distinguishes source-supplied timestamp latency from receipt and storage latency; this supports requiring documented semantics rather than assuming uniform behavior across historian products.

facts.statement: In the ISA-95/IEC 62264 model, manufacturing operations management (MOM) occupies Level 3 between control functions and Level 4 business planning. MES is one implementation class supporting Level 3 operations; the modeled activities include production operations such as scheduling/dispatching, execution, data collection and tracking, alongside quality, maintenance and inventory functions. Resource coordination and product/resource traceability can be represented through these models, but the exact functions and genealogy depth implemented by a particular MES vary by scope and configuration.

verification_refs.citation: International Society of Automation, ISA-95 Series of Standards overview
verification_refs.locator: Parts 2–5; ISA-95 model Levels 3 and 4
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines Part 3 as manufacturing operations management activity models, Part 4 as MOM objects/attributes, and describes Level 3 manufacturing operations management (including MES) separately from Level 4 business planning/ERP.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, OPC UA Common Object Model: ISA-95, §4.2.3
verification_refs.locator: Level 3 MOM functions and examples of supporting systems
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that MOM systems generally support Level 3 and ERP supports Level 4; lists production, quality, maintenance and inventory movement functions and examples including scheduling, work dispatching, work/product tracking, and historians.

verification_refs.citation: IEC 62264-3, Enterprise-control system integration—Activity models of manufacturing operations management
verification_refs.locator: Scope and operations tracking definition
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines the standard's Level 3 manufacturing operations management activity models, including production scheduling and tracking; tracking creates an organized record of resource and product use using tracking information.

facts.statement: In the ISA-95 functional hierarchy, ERP is associated with Level 4 business planning and logistics, while MES/MOM supports Level 3 manufacturing operations; their information interfaces are modeled separately. ERP products commonly integrate enterprise order, planning, materials/supply-chain, cost/finance and resource functions, but module scope varies. This distinction is about functional responsibility and integration, not a claim that ERP software can never exchange real-time data or participate in shop-floor workflows.

verification_refs.citation: International Society of Automation, ISA-95 Series of Standards overview
verification_refs.locator: ISA-95 Model: Level 3 and Level 4; Parts 2 and 5 interface scope
verification_refs.supports_claim: Places MES/manufacturing operations management at Level 3 and ERP/business planning and logistics at Level 4, and describes the information interface between these functional layers.

verification_refs.citation: SAP, What Is ERP? The Essential Guide
verification_refs.locator: ERP core business processes
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes ERP as supporting integrated enterprise processes including finance, manufacturing, supply chain, sales and procurement; it does not establish that every ERP deployment contains every module.

verification_refs.citation: Oracle, What Is ERP?
verification_refs.locator: ERP business activities and functional modules
verification_refs.supports_claim: Lists accounting, procurement, project management and supply-chain operations as ERP business activities and notes ERP suites can include inventory, manufacturing, order management, finance, planning and other modules.

facts.statement: When records from multiple equipment clocks are correlated by wall-clock timestamps, the clocks and timestamp conventions must be aligned to a common time basis and their offset, drift, uncertainty, timezone/UTC conversion and event-time semantics managed to the accuracy required by the use case. Clock synchronization improves timestamp comparability but by itself does not prove causal order when clock uncertainty, sampling, buffering or network delay can exceed the event separation; sequence numbers, source event relations or other ordering evidence may also be needed.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, OPC Unified Architecture Part 4: Services, §§7.11.3–7.11.4
verification_refs.locator: SourceTimestamp and ServerTimestamp definitions
verification_refs.supports_claim: Distinguishes source-applied time from server receive/known-accurate time, requires source timestamps in UTC, and says redundant source clocks should be synchronized.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, OPC Unified Architecture Part 3: Address Space Model, §8.37
verification_refs.locator: UtcTime and source/server timestamp clock note
verification_refs.supports_claim: States time values exchanged between OPC UA servers/clients are UTC and that SourceTimestamp and ServerTimestamp may originate from clocks that are not synchronized; clients perform UTC-to-local conversions.

verification_refs.citation: Network Time Foundation, Executive Summary: Computer Network Time Synchronization
verification_refs.locator: Clock offset, frequency offset and drift; periodic re-estimation
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines clock offset/frequency offset/drift and explains periodic offset and frequency re-estimation is needed because uncorrected errors accumulate.

verification_refs.citation: NIST, IEEE-1588 Standard for a Precision Clock Synchronization Protocol for Networked Measurement and Control Systems tutorial
verification_refs.locator: Ordering of data to/from multiple sources; synchronization accuracy and clock resolution
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that ordering information across multiple sources is limited by synchronization accuracy and clock resolution, supporting the caution that synchronized wall-clock timestamps alone do not always determine event causality.

facts.statement: Store-and-forward systems can persist messages locally while a destination is unavailable and forward them after reconnection, but loss prevention is bounded by the implementation's persistence, queue capacity, TTL/expiry and acknowledgment/retry behavior. Ordering guarantees, overflow handling and duplicate/redelivery behavior are transport- and product-specific; specify and test the required delivery semantics, expiry/overflow policy, idempotency or deduplication strategy, and recovery throughput for the application.

verification_refs.citation: Microsoft Learn, Operate Azure IoT Edge devices offline
verification_refs.locator: Reconnect and resync; restrictions and limits; TTL; host storage
verification_refs.supports_claim: Documents local storage of upstream messages during disconnection and delivery after reconnection in stored order; explicitly bounds retention by TTL and available disk space, and notes recovery delivery rate depends on connection speed and service latency. This is an implementation example, not a universal guarantee.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, OPC Unified Architecture Part 4: Services, §5.13.1.5 Queue parameters
verification_refs.locator: Queue size, discard policies, overflow indication and order
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines configured queue size, behavior when full, overflow indication for discarded notifications, and ordered return within a monitored item's queue; shows queue loss/order semantics must be understood rather than assumed globally.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, OPC Unified Architecture Part 11: Historical Access, §4.3
verification_refs.locator: Historians and interruption of data collection
verification_refs.supports_claim: Distinguishes interruptions that recover without loss from those creating gaps and requires historians to report data gaps as Bad_DataLost; inability to establish continuity is not to be treated as successful seamless recovery.

verification_refs.citation: Microsoft Learn, Send cloud-to-device messages from IoT Hub
verification_refs.locator: At-least-once delivery, acknowledgment, timeout and idempotent processing
verification_refs.supports_claim: Documents an at-least-once acknowledgment/retry contract in which timeout can cause redelivery and recommends idempotent processing; used only to support the conditional duplicate-handling requirement where the chosen transport has such retry semantics.

facts.statement: Historian compression can reduce the number of retained samples/storage required, while deadband filters suppress changes below a configured threshold; when applied to a signal needed for event detection or exact reconstruction, these lossy settings can omit small or brief changes and make the stored series differ from the raw input. The effect depends on the algorithm, thresholds, sampling, signal shape and whether compression is applied at source, transport or archive. Configure thresholds for the use case and preserve alarms, discrete state changes or other critical events through an appropriate separate event/status path when required; do not assume ordinary trend compression preserves them automatically.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, DeltaV Continuous Historian FAQ
verification_refs.locator: §3.8 Historian data compression; §§3.6–3.8 status and data collection
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes sloping-boxcar and horizontal-boxcar algorithms selected by configured display representation, a configurable compression deviation, and how stored collection rate depends on deviation and process variability. This supports implementation-dependent sample reduction, not lossless retention of every raw sample.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, OPC Unified Architecture Part 4: Services, §5.13.1.5 Queue parameters
verification_refs.locator: DataChangeFilter/deadband with bounded queues and overflow
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes deadband filtering and bounded notification queues; when queues overflow, values can be discarded and overflow is indicated, and deadband behavior can be unexpected when changes exceed queue capacity. Thus the output stream is not necessarily a full record of every input change.

verification_refs.citation: ISA InTech, Advanced Analytics Improve Predictive Models
verification_refs.locator: Historian archiving compression and offline/live data consistency
verification_refs.supports_claim: Warns that historian training data is often post-compression while live data may be pre-compression, and that inconsistent preprocessing/compression can reduce model fit and produce false positives/negatives; supports the analysis-fidelity consequence when exact signal characteristics matter.

facts.statement: An edge or gateway deployment can provide protocol translation, local buffering, offline/store-and-forward delivery, and local processing when those functions are implemented and configured; these device-level functions do not by themselves establish enterprise-wide data context, semantic consistency, or governance, which remain explicit integration responsibilities. Capabilities and limits vary by product and architecture.

verification_refs.citation: Microsoft Learn, Use Azure IoT Edge as a gateway for downstream devices; Operate Azure IoT Edge devices offline
verification_refs.locator: Gateway translation modules; offline store-and-forward; TTL and storage limits
verification_refs.supports_claim: Documents gateway-side protocol translation through modules, local store-and-forward, offline operation, and explicit TTL/disk constraints for this implementation. It supports conditional capabilities, not a claim that all gateways have identical behavior.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, Industrial Connectivity Solutions: OPC Foundation Cloud Reference Architecture
verification_refs.locator: Industrial connectivity architecture, semantic gaps, governance, edge/cloud context
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes gateway/connectivity architecture separately from semantic modeling and governance, warning that protocol connectivity alone does not supply semantic interoperability or governance. Supports treating enterprise context/governance as explicit architecture responsibilities.

facts.statement: A real-time system is judged by whether results or responses meet the timing constraints relevant to the application, not by zero latency or raw speed alone. The required deadline, latency/jitter bounds, and tolerance for a missed deadline depend on the controlled process and whether the timing requirement is hard or soft; determinism is a design property to establish where required, not an automatic guarantee of every real-time-labelled system.

verification_refs.citation: IEEE Technology Navigator, Real-time systems
verification_refs.locator: Definition and timing correctness discussion
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines real-time correctness as depending on both computation result and the time it is produced, and notes that latency/context-switch bounds must be characterized for deadline analysis.

verification_refs.citation: NIST Computer Security Resource Center Glossary, real time
verification_refs.locator: real time definition
verification_refs.supports_claim: Provides a standards-oriented glossary definition of real time, supporting the distinction between timing-constrained correctness and simply fast processing.

facts.statement: In OPC UA, namespace URIs distinguish naming authorities and help avoid identifier conflicts when information from sources is combined; NodeIds identify Nodes, while BrowseNames are not guaranteed to be globally unique and are used in browse paths. Therefore a human-readable tag name alone should not be treated as a complete globally unique semantic identity; the identifier and its namespace/model context must be preserved.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, OPC UA Part 3: Address Space Model, §§4.2, 4.4
verification_refs.locator: Namespace URIs, NodeIds, BrowseNames and AddressSpace
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines namespaces as URI-identified naming authorities, NodeIds as node identifiers, and BrowseNames as non-localized names that are not necessarily unique; the namespace index is a table index in the server/session context.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, Industrial Automation Basics, §9.2 Handling of OPC UA Namespaces
verification_refs.locator: NodeId versus BrowseName uniqueness
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that NodeId unambiguously identifies a Node, while different Nodes may share a BrowseName; namespaces distinguish identifiers from different naming authorities.

facts.statement: An OPC UA information model can represent domain concepts with typed Objects, Variables, DataTypes and References whose types define the semantics of relationships. Shared or companion information models can therefore give clients a common structured interpretation of assets and process data beyond transport connectivity; interoperability still depends on consistent model adoption, mappings, and implementation conformance.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, OPC UA Part 3: Address Space Model, §4.3
verification_refs.locator: Object Model
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines Objects in terms of Variables and Methods and allows relationships to other Objects to be expressed through the address-space model.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, UA Modelling Best Practices, §7
verification_refs.locator: Base modelling concepts
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes ObjectTypes and VariableTypes as defining semantics and structure, DataTypes defining value semantics, and ReferenceTypes defining relationship semantics.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, Industrial Connectivity Solutions: OPC Foundation Cloud Reference Architecture
verification_refs.locator: Semantic gaps and governance in industrial connectivity
verification_refs.supports_claim: Warns that protocol connectivity alone can leave semantic gaps and missing governance, supporting the caveat that transport connection does not itself establish semantic interoperability.

facts.statement: Industrial information models can associate process values with metadata and contextual objects rather than storing a bare value alone. OPC UA exposes typed Variables, Attributes and References, and the ISA-95 common object model covers equipment, physical assets, materials and personnel; this enables context such as units or asset/material relationships when the relevant model and fields are implemented. It does not guarantee every historian record contains every listed context field.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, OPC UA Part 3: Address Space Model, §§4.3–4.4
verification_refs.locator: Object Model; Node Attributes and References
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines typed Variables, Attributes and References as the structures used to represent values and relations in an OPC UA AddressSpace.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, OPC UA Common Object Model: ISA-95, overview and object model
verification_refs.locator: ISA-95 models for equipment, physical assets, material and personnel
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes ISA-95 information categories for material, equipment, physical assets and personnel and their exchange between manufacturing operations and enterprise systems.

facts.statement: Manufacturing genealogy can link consumed or produced material lots and sublots to equipment, batch/recipe and execution records, process conditions, and quality results so that product history can be traced for analysis or recall. ISA-95 models material lots and their assembly/trace relationships, while ISA-88 batch records may include recipe execution, equipment, alarms and other batch-relevant information. Complete genealogy is not automatic: the site must capture, identify, version, retain and correlate the required records across its systems.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, OPC UA Common Object Model: ISA-95, Material Information Model
verification_refs.locator: §8.4 Material Information Model; MaterialLot, MaterialSublot and assembly references
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines uniquely identified material lots/sublots, assembled-from relationships and material tracking; explains that traceability of materials used in a product supports quality analysis and recalls.

verification_refs.citation: ISA, ANSI/ISA-88.00.03-2003 preview, Batch Control—General and Site Recipe Models and Representation
verification_refs.locator: §3.2 batch production record definition
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines a batch production record as including execution information and identifies possible contents such as equipment information, batch-related alarms, control/master/site/general recipe, schedule and other batch-relevant records.

facts.statement: An event record represents an occurrence at a time, while a state value or snapshot describes a state at a point or over an interval; a current state snapshot alone may not reveal intermediate transitions. For sequence and troubleshooting analysis, retain relevant state-transition/event records with trustworthy time and ordering information. Such ordering supports reconstruction of chronology but does not by itself prove physical causality, and the available fields/history depend on server and application configuration.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, OPC UA Part 3: Address Space Model, §4.7.1
verification_refs.locator: Event Model—General
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines Events as specific transient occurrences and Event Notifications as reports of occurrences; a server need not produce Events while disconnected from the event source.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, OPC UA Part 9: Alarms & Conditions, §4.2
verification_refs.locator: Conditions and ConditionBranches
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines Conditions as representations of system/component state and distinguishes the current state branch from prior branches that may still need attention; history of prior branches is optional for servers.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, OPC UA Part 11: Historical Access, §§5.4, 6.5.2
verification_refs.locator: Historical Event read, time filtering and ordered results
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines historical Event retrieval by time and permits ordered event results; available historical fields depend on what the server stored, so sequence reconstruction is configuration dependent.

facts.statement: An IT/OT integration design should define functional ownership, interfaces/data semantics and security boundaries across control, manufacturing-operations and enterprise systems, while preserving OT performance, reliability and safety requirements. ISA-95 supplies a functional and information-exchange reference between manufacturing operations and enterprise functions; NIST OT guidance requires security recommendations to account for OT performance, reliability and safety. The exact component topology and protocols are implementation-specific, and segmentation alone does not guarantee control stability or security.

verification_refs.citation: ISA, ISA-95 Series of Standards: Enterprise-Control System Integration
verification_refs.locator: Purpose, functional levels and information exchange profiles
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes ISA-95 as an abstract model for information exchange between manufacturing-control and business functions and defines interfaces and information exchanged across levels.

verification_refs.citation: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology Security
verification_refs.locator: Abstract and OT security architecture recommendations
verification_refs.supports_claim: NIST states OT security guidance must address distinctive performance, reliability and safety requirements and presents typical OT topologies and risk-mitigating security countermeasures.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, Industrial Connectivity Solutions: OPC Foundation Cloud Reference Architecture
verification_refs.locator: Connectivity, semantics and governance across edge/cloud architecture
verification_refs.supports_claim: Warns that protocol connectivity without semantic alignment and governance creates integration gaps; supports defining data semantics and responsibility rather than treating transport as a complete integration contract.

facts.statement: Cross-system manufacturing records need stable entity identity or explicit alias mapping: ISA-95 materials and equipment are identified information objects, and ISA-95 Part 7 defines an alias service model for mapping identifiers across applications/namespaces. Where a production result depends on a recipe or controlled definition, retain the applicable version with the execution record so it can be interpreted and reproduced. Identifier schemes and version rules are enterprise-specific; the standards do not require every identifier to be globally identical across systems.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, OPC UA Common Object Model: ISA-95, §§8.2, 8.4
verification_refs.locator: Equipment identification and material class/definition/lot identifiers
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that equipment can have multiple IDs across vendor systems and applications and that material definitions/lots provide identifiers for production information exchange and traceability.

verification_refs.citation: ISA, ANSI/ISA-95.00.07-2017 preview, Enterprise-Control System Integration—Alias Service Model
verification_refs.locator: Alias directory and local/principal namespace mapping
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines an alias service for translating identifiers in information exchanges and mapping local namespace identifiers to a principal namespace and back.

verification_refs.citation: ISA, Selecting a batch solution just got simpler
verification_refs.locator: Batch recipe management and retrieving prior recipe versions
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes the practical need to recall how a product was made using a prior recipe version; this supports retaining the applicable recipe version for batch interpretation, not a universal schema mandate for all master data.

facts.statement: A data-governance framework should assign accountable owners and operational stewards for data domains, including responsibility for agreed definitions, quality monitoring and improvement, access policy, change approval, issue handling/remediation, and lifecycle controls. GOV.UK's data ownership model documents these responsibilities as one public-sector implementation; role names, separation of duties and exact workflow vary by organization and jurisdiction.

verification_refs.citation: UK Government, Data ownership model
verification_refs.locator: Data owners §§ responsibilities; data stewards §§ quality processes and standards; data custodians §§ access and audit
verification_refs.supports_claim: Assigns owners accountability for data meaning, content, quality and management; owners approve changes, maintain definitions, quality and access/retention policies; stewards monitor, investigate, triage, remediate and report quality issues and maintain data standards.

facts.statement: Data lifecycle governance should define appropriate retention periods and controlled archival, disposal or preservation in accordance with business purpose and applicable legal/regulatory obligations, with schedules reviewed as requirements change. In a historian or manufacturing data platform, data classes such as raw samples, compressed trends, events and audit records may need distinct schedules because their operational and evidentiary purposes differ; the required periods and categories are site-, sector- and jurisdiction-specific, not universal fixed durations.

verification_refs.citation: UK Government, Data ownership model
verification_refs.locator: Data owners: retention schedules, archival, disposal and preservation
verification_refs.supports_claim: Requires an appropriate retention schedule specifying storage periods, regular review, and compliance with legal requirements for archival, disposal and preservation.

verification_refs.citation: UK Government, Data ownership model
verification_refs.locator: Data steward responsibilities: data access, archival and deletion
verification_refs.supports_claim: Lists access, archival and deletion as governed processes facilitated by data stewards, supporting lifecycle-specific controls without prescribing a universal duration.

facts.statement: Successful protocol communication establishes data exchange, but semantic interoperability additionally requires systems to agree on the identity, structure and interpretation of exchanged values, including relevant units, status/quality, timestamp semantics and asset/process context. OPC UA provides fields and modelling constructs for some of these meanings, and ISA-95/companion models can standardize domain context; actual end-to-end interoperability still requires compatible models, mappings and conformant implementations.

verification_refs.locator: Semantic gaps, companion models and governance in connectivity
verification_refs.supports_claim: Warns that protocol connectivity without data semantics and governance can create semantic gaps and brittle integrations; recommends information models/context for richer interoperability.

verification_refs.locator: DataValue fields Value, StatusCode, SourceTimestamp and ServerTimestamp
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines value, status and source/server timestamp as distinct fields that may be present in a DataValue; applications must interpret these semantics rather than treating payload value alone as the whole record.

verification_refs.locator: ISA-95 domain objects and information exchange
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines domain object models for equipment, physical assets, personnel and material to support common manufacturing-operations information exchange.

facts.statement: Acquisition configuration is more than choosing a scan rate: the source update model, sampling and publication/reporting intervals, change filters/deadbands, queue behavior, scaling, engineering units and value quality jointly determine which values are observed and how consumers interpret them. For OPC UA specifically, a negotiated sampling interval is a best-effort rate, can differ from the underlying source update cycle, and may be revised by server capability; the required choices depend on the process dynamics and consumer use case.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, OPC UA Part 4: Services, §5.13.1.2 Sampling interval
verification_refs.locator: Sampling interval, best-effort rate and source update behavior
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines sampling interval as the fastest requested sampling rate, characterizes it as best effort, notes supported rates may be revised, and explains that underlying source update rates may be slower or exception-based.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, OPC UA Part 4: Services, §5.13 Monitored Item Service Set
verification_refs.locator: Sampling, filters, reporting and queue semantics
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines sampled monitored values, notification filters and queue behavior; data-change filters and bounded queues affect which values are reported and retained.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, OPC UA Part 6: Mappings, §5.2.2.17 DataValue
verification_refs.locator: Value, StatusCode and timestamps
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines status and source/server timestamps as separate DataValue fields associated with the value.

verification_refs.locator: EUInformation and engineering unit metadata
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines engineering-unit metadata used with analog values, supporting the need to preserve units and scaling context for interpretation.

facts.statement: Data provenance/traceability records can link the relevant source entities, transformations or processing activities, responsible systems/agents, resulting records and subsequent revisions or audited changes. These links support assessment of data quality/reliability and reconstruction of how a result was produced; they do not guarantee reproducibility unless the required inputs, versions, configuration, time/quality semantics and change records are actually captured and retained. The appropriate lineage depth depends on use and compliance requirements.

verification_refs.edition_or_version: W3C Working Group Note, 30 April 2013; accessed 2026-10-10
verification_refs.locator: §1 Introduction; entities, activities, agents, derivation and revision
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines provenance records over entities and activities that produce/deliver or influence an object and identifies uses including assessing trust, verifying process requirements and reproducing how a result was generated; models entities, activities, agents, derivation and revision.

verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes tracking historical corrections by recording original values and who made changes and generating audit events; also notes requirements vary for initial bulk insertion and event identity.

verification_refs.supports_claim: States not all servers support auditing and specifies audit event behavior when that capability is supported, supporting the condition that auditability depends on implementation.

facts.statement: Within this repository's study taxonomy, SW-07 owns industrial communication protocols, device integration and interoperability; SW-11 owns industrial data collection, quality, context, historian/MES/ERP integration and traceability; SW-12 owns the use of those data for model features, training, inference and lifecycle. This is a local topic-routing/ownership contract, not a universal industry taxonomy; adjacent topics may mention another lane's concepts as context without transferring ownership.
