facts.statement: When RTD calibration or range characterization is required, compare the assembled sensor/measurement chain with a traceable reference thermometer in a sufficiently stable, well-characterized temperature source at points spanning the intended range. The uncertainty budget should include relevant reference/source/readout contributions and RTD/application effects such as self-heating, immersion/thermal contact, lead resistance and repeatability or stability. Exact points, corrections and uncertainty terms depend on range, wiring, sensor design and calibration method; a blanket requirement for the same number of points in every application is not implied.

verification_refs.citation: NIST, Industrial Thermometer Calibrations
verification_refs.locator: Industrial platinum resistance thermometer comparison calibrations and uncertainty statements
verification_refs.supports_claim: NIST calibrates industrial platinum resistance thermometers by comparison with an ITS-90 calibrated standard platinum resistance thermometer in stirred liquid baths over specified ranges and publishes calibration uncertainty; uncertainty may exclude the digital readout, demonstrating the need to account for the complete measurement chain.

verification_refs.citation: NIST, Guide on Secondary Thermometry: Industrial Platinum Resistance Thermometers
verification_refs.locator: §4 Limitations in performance; self-heating and immersion/lead resistance effects
verification_refs.supports_claim: Identifies self-heating, immersion, response time, lead resistance, insulation, hysteresis and stability/reproducibility among IPRT performance limits; self-heating depends on sensor construction and application thermal contact.

verification_refs.citation: NIST SP 250-22, Platinum Resistance Thermometer Calibrations
verification_refs.locator: Calibration procedure, thermal equilibrium and self-heating
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes allowing thermal equilibrium before measurements and assessing self-heating using different currents/zero-current extrapolation, illustrating that excitation and equilibration can contribute to calibration uncertainty.

facts.statement: Loop-shaping a lead/lag or PID compensator involves application-specific choices of crossover/bandwidth, stability margins, low-frequency gain for tracking/disturbance rejection, and high-frequency roll-off for noise and model uncertainty. Before deployment, check whether the linear design remains acceptable over relevant operating points and nonidealities such as process delay, actuator saturation/rate limits, valve deadband and model error; linear Bode margins alone do not represent all nonlinear implementation behavior. The target values and validation tests depend on the loop's operating envelope and risk/performance requirements.

verification_refs.citation: MathWorks, Bode Diagram Design
verification_refs.locator: Loop shaping to bandwidth and gain/phase-margin specifications
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes Bode loop shaping by adjusting open-loop bandwidth and designing to gain/phase-margin requirements.

verification_refs.citation: MathWorks, Loop Shaping for Performance and Robustness
verification_refs.locator: Low-frequency gain, high-frequency rolloff, model uncertainty, crossover and bandwidth limits
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that low-frequency gain improves offset/disturbance rejection, high-frequency rolloff protects robustness where model phase is uncertain, and crossover/bandwidth are limited by plant uncertainty and unstable poles/zeros.

verification_refs.citation: MathWorks, Analyze Control Systems with Delays
verification_refs.locator: Dead-time phase lag and bandwidth/stability impact
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that process delays add phase lag and constrain bandwidth and closed-loop stability; models delay uncertainty for controller analysis.

verification_refs.citation: MathWorks, Control of a Linear Electric Actuator Using Control System Tuner
verification_refs.locator: Controller tuning with actuator saturation limits and nonlinear simulation
verification_refs.supports_claim: Demonstrates tuning a controller with saturation limits and checking performance in nonlinear simulation rather than relying only on a linear design.

verification_refs.citation: ISA InTech, Automation Basics: Closed-loop control troubleshooting
verification_refs.locator: Valve deadband, measurement filtering, tuning and stability margin
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that valve mechanical deadband can mimic sluggish controller tuning and cannot be corrected merely by controller retuning; recommends diagnosing loop elements and keeping a healthy margin from the stability limit.

facts.statement: For a stable unity-negative-feedback loop with a finite nonzero plant DC gain, an unsaturated actuator, and a controller containing nonzero integral action, the loop has an uncancelled integrator (unless it is cancelled elsewhere); under these conditions the standard final-value/error-constant result gives zero steady-state error to a step input. This conclusion does not apply if closed-loop stability, non-cancellation, actuator linearity, or the final-value theorem conditions fail.

verification_refs.citation: Unity-feedback error-constant and final-value theorem derivation
verification_refs.locator: L(s)=C(s)G(s), C(s) contains Ki/s; stable unsaturated unity-feedback step error
verification_refs.supports_claim: With finite nonzero G(0), nonzero integral gain contributes an uncancelled pole at the origin to L(s). For a stable closed loop and unit step, E(s)=1/[s(1+L(s))], so lim(s→0)sE(s)=0, provided the final-value theorem conditions hold.

verification_refs.citation: MathWorks, Anti-Windup Control Using PID Controller Block
verification_refs.locator: Actuator saturation, integration windup and anti-windup methods
verification_refs.supports_claim: Documents that actuator saturation can place the controller in a nonlinear region and cause integral windup, so the ideal unsaturated linear-loop error conclusion must not be extended to saturated operation.

facts.statement: For the standard continuous lead network C(s)=K(1+Ts)/(1+αTs) with K,T>0 and 0<α<1, the high-frequency gain relative to its DC gain is 1/α. Lead networks can increase stability margins, crossover/bandwidth and speed, but the raised high-frequency controller gain can increase response to high-frequency measurement noise and sensitivity to neglected high-frequency plant dynamics. It does not mean saturation or unacceptable noise must occur; those depend on signal levels, actuator limits and the plant.

verification_refs.citation: MathWorks, Edit Compensator Dynamics in Control System Designer
verification_refs.locator: Lead networks: stability margins, bandwidth and rise time; pole/zero description
verification_refs.supports_claim: States lead networks can increase stability margins and system bandwidth and reduce rise time, with the lead zero at lower natural frequency than its pole.

verification_refs.citation: University of Michigan, Control Tutorials for MATLAB and Simulink, Designing Lead and Lag Compensators
verification_refs.locator: Lead compensation high-frequency gain and noise discussion
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that a lead compensator raises high-frequency gain, which can increase crossover and speed but may amplify high-frequency noise.

verification_refs.citation: Standard lead-network transfer-function asymptotes
verification_refs.locator: C(0)=K and lim(ω→∞)|C(jω)|=K/α
verification_refs.supports_claim: For C(s)=K(1+Ts)/(1+αTs), the DC gain is K and high-frequency gain tends to K/α; their ratio is 1/α. As a controller, that gain multiplies high-frequency error/noise components in the control signal, while actual saturation depends on signal magnitude and actuator limits.

facts.statement: A documented manual-tuning approach for some process loops is to first disable integral and derivative action and tune proportional gain to a stable response, then add a small integral contribution to reduce residual error; derivative action may be added when the application benefits from its damping, but is not required for every loop. This is an example procedure, not a universal or mandatory PID tuning sequence; process dynamics and operating constraints govern the chosen method.

verification_refs.citation: ISA InTech, Optimizing to the Tune of a PID Equation
verification_refs.locator: § P, PI, then PID manual tuning; PI example and optional derivative action
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes a manual sequence that first tunes proportional action with integral and derivative cancelled, adds integral once the PV response is stable, and uses derivative only as appropriate; it also explicitly notes many applications need only PI or P, not all three modes.

facts.statement: Field PID tuning should be based on measured or otherwise justified process dynamics, including dead time and relevant time constants, and should check whether the instrument and final control element can support the desired response. Depending on the loop, relevant constraints include measurement noise and filter lag, valve deadband/stiction and associated wear, output limits and actuator saturation with anti-windup, execution/sample timing, derivative filtering, and manual/automatic tracking for bumpless transfer. These are application-dependent checks, not a universal requirement to enable every feature or use one fixed tuning recipe.

verification_refs.citation: ISA InTech, Loop Tuning Basics: Self-Regulating Processes
verification_refs.locator: Challenges; process understanding, instrumentation/final-control-element performance, deadband, resolution, response time, interactions and output movement
verification_refs.supports_claim: Recommends understanding process response and verifying instrumentation and final control element before tuning, including valve deadband/resolution, flow gain and appropriate response time; tuning aggressiveness depends on loop interaction and consequences of output movement.

verification_refs.citation: ISA InTech, Loop Tuning Basics: Complex Process Responses
verification_refs.locator: Step tests and identified dead time, process time constants, operating-range variation, and stability checks
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes identifying process gain, dead time and primary/secondary time constants using repeated step tests, using dynamics in tuning calculations, checking changes over the operating range, and validating stability/resonance.

verification_refs.citation: ISA InTech, Automation Basics: Closed-loop Control Troubleshooting
verification_refs.locator: Valve stiction, valve deadband, PV noise/filter and stability-limit margin
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that stiction and deadband can cause oscillation or apparent sluggishness and need valve-side diagnosis/maintenance rather than retuning alone; a noise filter changes loop dynamics and requires retuning; recommends margin from the stability limit.

verification_refs.citation: ISA InTech, Optimizing the Future by Leveraging the Past
verification_refs.locator: Stiction behavior and recurring final-control-element action
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes stiction requiring excess force, creating recurring final-element action that can accelerate wear of associated process equipment.

verification_refs.citation: ISA, PID Tuning Appendices
verification_refs.locator: Appendix checklist: bumpless transfer, setpoint/output limits, anti-reset windup, module scan time, filtering, rate time and process constraints
verification_refs.supports_claim: Provides an implementation checklist covering output limits matched to process/equipment/valve constraints, anti-reset-windup limits, scan rate, signal filter, derivative/rate versus dead time and bumpless transfer; states settings must be verified as applicable.

verification_refs.citation: MathWorks, PID Controller
verification_refs.locator: Derivative filter, output saturation/anti-windup and tracking for bumpless transfer
verification_refs.supports_claim: Documents a first-order derivative filter, configurable output limits and anti-windup methods, and signal tracking for bumpless transfer; these are implementation options, not mandatory features for every PID loop.

facts.statement: For the continuous LTI model x_dot=Ax+Bu, y=Cx with D=0, measured-state law u=-Kx+N_r r gives x_dot=(A-BK)x+B N_r r. Thus K determines the homogeneous closed-loop matrix A-BK, while N_r scales the reference-driven equilibrium; they serve different roles.

verification_refs.citation: State-space substitution of the state-feedback reference law
verification_refs.locator: Substitute u=-Kx+N_r r into x_dot=Ax+Bu
verification_refs.supports_claim: Direct substitution yields x_dot=(A-BK)x+B N_r r; K appears in the homogeneous state matrix and N_r multiplies the reference input.

verification_refs.citation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, ECE 486 Control Systems, Lecture 21: Pole Placement
verification_refs.locator: State feedback with reference: x_dot=(A-BK)x+Br and closed-loop poles
verification_refs.supports_claim: Derives the closed-loop state equation and relates closed-loop poles to eigenvalues of A-BK for reference-driven state feedback.

facts.statement: For a controllable pair (A,B), full-state feedback can assign the eigenvalues of A-BK, but that pole-placement result alone does not impose unit DC gain from the reference to the measured output. The reference-to-output transfer is C(sI-A+BK)^(-1)B N_r for D=0, and its value at s=0 depends on C, A, B and K as well as the reference scaling.

verification_refs.citation: Closed-loop state-space transfer derivation
verification_refs.locator: Y/R=C(sI-A+BK)^(-1)B N_r; evaluate at s=0 when defined
verification_refs.supports_claim: The reference transfer contains the resolvent and output map in addition to the pole locations; assigning eigenvalues does not algebraically set the DC transfer value to one.

verification_refs.citation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, ECE 486 Control Systems, Lecture 21: Pole Placement
verification_refs.locator: Closed-loop poles and reference-to-output transfer under state feedback
verification_refs.supports_claim: Derives the reference-to-output transfer matrix and identifies closed-loop poles as eigenvalues of A-BK, distinguishing pole locations from the transfer numerator/DC gain.

facts.statement: For a continuous SISO model with D=0, stable A-BK and a finite nonzero closed-loop DC gain, the constant prefilter N_r=-[C(A-BK)^(-1)B]^(-1) makes the nominal steady-state output equal a constant reference. The inverse is scalar; this formula is not directly valid when the DC gain is zero, undefined, or the inverse does not exist.

verification_refs.citation: Steady-state solution of the closed-loop state equation
verification_refs.locator: 0=(A-BK)x_ss+B N_r r; y_ss=Cx_ss; solve y_ss/r=1
verification_refs.supports_claim: Solving the steady-state equation gives x_ss=-(A-BK)^(-1)B N_r r and y_ss/r=-C(A-BK)^(-1)B N_r; setting this scalar gain to unity yields the stated N_r, subject to invertibility and stability.

verification_refs.citation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, ECE 486 Control Systems, Lecture 21: Pole Placement
verification_refs.locator: Reference-to-output state-feedback transfer; steady-state obtained from s=0 when stable
verification_refs.supports_claim: Provides the closed-loop reference transfer from which the DC gain and its prefilter scaling follow.

facts.statement: A constant reference prefilter scales the command using the nominal plant and feedback design; it does not use measured tracking error and therefore does not automatically remove model error or an independent unmeasured disturbance. Exact tracking from this feedforward scaling depends on the assumed model and the existence of the required DC-gain inverse.

verification_refs.citation: Closed-loop signal-path derivation with reference feedforward and independent disturbance input
verification_refs.locator: Separate transfer paths from reference prefilter and disturbance injection point
verification_refs.supports_claim: The prefilter multiplies the reference path only; an independent disturbance has a separate transfer path and is not cancelled by a constant scaling of the reference. Plant/model mismatch changes the nominal DC scaling.

verification_refs.citation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, ECE 486 Control Systems, Lecture 1: Feedback Control for the Impatient
verification_refs.locator: Separate reference, plant-input disturbance and output-disturbance transfer paths
verification_refs.supports_claim: Derives distinct closed-loop paths for reference tracking and disturbances injected at different locations, supporting that a reference-only feedforward scaling does not cancel an independent disturbance path.

facts.statement: For a feasible continuous-time tracking problem, augmenting the controller with the integral of constant-reference output error supplies an integrator internal model. If the augmented closed loop is asymptotically stable, the plant has no blocking invariant zero at the origin for the selected input-output channel, and the actuator does not remain saturated, the error to a constant reference can converge to zero. Constant-disturbance rejection likewise depends on disturbance injection location and closed-loop feasibility; it is not unconditional.

verification_refs.citation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, ECE 486 Control Systems, Lecture 9: PID Control
verification_refs.locator: Integral control, constant reference tracking, constant disturbance rejection, system type and saturation
verification_refs.supports_claim: Derives that integral action gives perfect constant-reference tracking and rejects a constant disturbance in the illustrated stable closed-loop case, and explicitly discusses saturation/windup and stability conditions.

verification_refs.citation: Final-value theorem for a stable integral-augmented servo loop
verification_refs.locator: xi_dot=r-y; bounded xi at steady state implies r-y=0, if closed-loop convergence and feasibility hold
verification_refs.supports_claim: At an equilibrium with a finite integral state, xi_dot=0 requires r-y=0. The derivation requires a feasible equilibrium and stable augmented dynamics; invariant zeros, actuator limits or infeasibility can prevent the stated result.

facts.statement: For a continuous LTI plant x_dot=Ax+Bu, y=Cx with D=0 and xi_dot=r-y, the augmented state x_a=[x^T,xi^T]^T obeys x_a_dot=[[A,0],[-C,0]]x_a+[[B],[0]]u+[[0],[I]]r. Under u=-K_x x+K_i xi, the closed-loop state matrix is [[A-BK_x,BK_i],[-C,0]]; the sign convention must remain consistent.

verification_refs.citation: Block-matrix construction from plant and output-error integrator equations
verification_refs.locator: Stack x_dot=Ax+Bu and xi_dot=r-Cx
verification_refs.supports_claim: Stacking the plant state and error-integral state gives the stated A_a and input matrices; substituting the stated feedback law yields the corresponding signed closed-loop blocks.

facts.statement: Controllability of the original pair (A,B) alone does not guarantee controllability or stabilizability after adding an output-error integrator. For arbitrary pole assignment, the augmented pair must be controllable; for asymptotic stabilization, it must at least be stabilizable. An invariant zero at s=0 in the selected plant input-output channel can obstruct the integrator mode and prevent the required augmentation property.

verification_refs.citation: PBH controllability/stabilizability test applied to the integral-augmented pair
verification_refs.locator: Augmented closed-loop mode at s=0 and rank of [sI-A_a, B_a]
verification_refs.supports_claim: Controllability or stabilizability must be evaluated for the augmented pair. The PBH rank test at the added integrator eigenvalue s=0 exposes loss of controllability associated with an invariant zero at the origin; original-pair controllability alone does not establish the augmented rank condition.

verification_refs.citation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, ECE 486 Control Systems, Lecture 21: Pole Placement
verification_refs.locator: Arbitrary pole placement requires a completely controllable pair
verification_refs.supports_claim: States arbitrary full-state-feedback pole assignment under complete controllability, supporting the distinction between arbitrary placement and merely stabilizing feedback.

facts.statement: A constant state-feedback prefilter is nominal reference-path feedforward scaling, whereas integral action feeds measured output error back through a controller state. The former can correct nominal DC scaling but is model dependent; the latter can reject feasible constant errors/disturbances under stability and actuator assumptions, while adding dynamics and possible windup. They are not interchangeable guarantees.

verification_refs.citation: Comparison of reference-feedforward and error-integral signal paths
verification_refs.locator: Reference scaling path versus xi_dot=r-y error feedback path
verification_refs.supports_claim: The prefilter multiplies the command path while the integral state is driven by output error; their disturbance, model-error and saturation behavior therefore differs.

verification_refs.citation: MathWorks, Anti-Windup Control Using PID Controller Block
verification_refs.locator: Integral windup under actuator saturation and anti-windup approaches
verification_refs.supports_claim: Documents that integral action can wind up under actuator saturation and describes anti-windup methods; it does not make a nominal reference prefilter equivalent to feedback.

facts.statement: Reference tracking and disturbance rejection must be derived from the disturbance injection location. A reference prefilter that only scales r cannot by itself cancel an independent plant-input or output disturbance; those disturbance paths require feedback rejection, a measured-disturbance feedforward path, or another modeled control mechanism.

verification_refs.citation: Closed-loop superposition for reference, plant-input disturbance and output disturbance
verification_refs.locator: Separate transfer functions by disturbance injection point
verification_refs.supports_claim: In a linear model, reference scaling changes the transfer multiplying r, while an independent disturbance has its own transfer path; scaling r cannot cancel an arbitrary independent disturbance signal.

verification_refs.citation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, ECE 486 Control Systems, Lecture 1: Feedback Control for the Impatient
verification_refs.locator: Distinct closed-loop transfer paths from reference and disturbances
verification_refs.supports_claim: Derives independent transfer paths from reference, plant-input disturbance and output disturbance, which depend on disturbance injection point.

facts.statement: If an actuator saturates while an integral-error state continues accumulating, the controller can wind up and show delayed recovery when the requested output returns within actuator limits. Conditional integration/clamping, back-calculation, or a tracking-based scheme can mitigate this behavior, but the method must match where saturation occurs and the implementation architecture; saturated responses require separate validation.

verification_refs.citation: MathWorks, Anti-Windup Control Using PID Controller Block
verification_refs.locator: Saturation, integrator windup, back-calculation, clamping and tracking mode
verification_refs.supports_claim: Shows that saturation with continued integration creates windup and delayed recovery, and documents back-calculation, clamping and tracking approaches with architecture-dependent conditions.

verification_refs.citation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, ECE 486 Control Systems, Lecture 9: PID Control
verification_refs.locator: Figure 6 and discussion of integral control with saturation
verification_refs.supports_claim: Illustrates integrator accumulation under actuator saturation and the need to distinguish ideal linear tracking from saturated operation.

facts.statement: For a finite-dimensional LTI plant with observer-based state feedback, the nominal closed-loop characteristic polynomial factors into the state-feedback and observer-error factors, so their gains can be designed separately. Arbitrary pole assignment requires controllability of (A,B) and observability of (A,C); asymptotic stabilization requires (A,B) stabilizable and (A,C) detectable. Detectability alone does not guarantee that a stabilizing state-feedback gain exists.

verification_refs.citation: Observer-based feedback transformed into plant state and estimation-error coordinates
verification_refs.locator: e=x-x_hat; triangular closed-loop matrix with diagonal blocks A-BK and A-LC
verification_refs.supports_claim: Using u=-K x_hat and observer correction L(y-C x_hat), the coordinates (x,e) produce a block-triangular closed-loop matrix whose diagonal blocks are A-BK and A-LC. Stabilizability of (A,B) and detectability of (A,C) permit choices making both blocks Hurwitz; arbitrary eigenvalue placement requires controllability and observability.

verification_refs.citation: Richard M. Murray, Control and Dynamical Systems, Chapter 7: Output Feedback
verification_refs.locator: Theorem 7.3, eigenvalue assignment by output feedback
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that the output-feedback characteristic polynomial factors into state-feedback and observer factors, that the two gains depend on separate model pairs, and that arbitrary roots can be assigned when the system is reachable and observable.

facts.statement: An inherent valve flow characteristic is the relationship between valve travel and flow coefficient measured or defined at constant pressure drop across the valve; under the corresponding non-choked liquid conditions, flow is proportional to Cv.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §2.4.1 Inherent flow characteristic
verification_refs.locator: §2.4.1; constant valve differential pressure and simplified flow relation
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines inherent characteristic at constant valve differential pressure and says flow is proportional to Cv under that condition.

facts.statement: An installed flow characteristic is the actual flow-versus-travel relationship with the valve operating in its process pipeline; it depends on both the valve's inherent characteristic and the pipeline pressure-loss behavior.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §2.4.2 Installed flow characteristic
verification_refs.locator: §2.4.2; installed flow characteristic
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that installed flow versus travel is a function of the process pipeline and the valve's inherent characteristic.

facts.statement: Inherent and installed characteristics are distinct: the former is defined at constant valve pressure drop, whereas the latter reflects actual process-pipeline conditions; they may approach one another when valve differential pressure remains nearly constant.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §2.4 Control valve flow characteristics
verification_refs.supports_claim: Separates the constant-pressure-drop inherent curve from installed behavior and notes equality when valve pressure drop remains constant.

facts.statement: A normalized inherent-characteristic plot may use relative valve travel on the horizontal axis and relative flow coefficient (Cv/Cv-rated) on the vertical axis; the exact rated-travel and capacity conventions should be stated.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Control Valve Handbook, Chapter 1: Introduction to Control Valves, Figure 1.19
verification_refs.locator: Figure 1.19; rated travel and rated flow coefficient axes
verification_refs.supports_claim: Plots rated travel against rated flow coefficient for inherent valve characteristics.

facts.statement: For turbulent, non-choked liquid flow with negligible viscosity correction, the basic valve relation is Q proportional to Cv times the square root of valve pressure drop divided by specific gravity; it is not a universal equation for compressible or choked flow.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook—Oil and Gas, §6 Liquid Flow; Liquid Sizing Equation
verification_refs.locator: §6, equation Q = Cv√(ΔP/G); discussion of choking limitation
verification_refs.supports_claim: Gives the basic liquid relation and explains its breakdown as liquid flow approaches choking.

facts.statement: An ideal linear inherent characteristic has a constant slope of relative flow coefficient versus relative travel; equal increments of travel therefore produce equal absolute increments of Cv under the characteristic's reference conditions.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §2.4.1.B Linear inherent flow characteristic
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines a linear characteristic as relative opening directly correlating with percentage flow at constant valve pressure drop.

facts.statement: An ideal equal-percentage inherent characteristic gives the same percentage increase in flow coefficient for each equal increment of travel, at constant valve pressure drop.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §2.4.1.C Equal percentage inherent flow characteristic
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines equal-percentage behavior as a constant percentage increase for equal opening increments at constant differential pressure.

facts.statement: With normalized travel x from 0 to 1 and range parameter R defined as Cv(1)/Cv(0), the ideal equal-percentage law y=Cv(x)/Cv(1)=R^(x−1) follows from a constant relative increase per equal travel increment.

verification_refs.citation: Derivation from constant relative increment definition
verification_refs.locator: dCv/Cv = k dx; boundary conditions y(0)=1/R and y(1)=1
verification_refs.supports_claim: Integrating dCv/Cv=k dx gives an exponential; applying the stated normalization and endpoint ratio gives y=R^(x−1). This defines R here and does not make a rangeability claim.

facts.statement: Because equal-percentage behavior has a constant relative increment, its absolute Cv increment per equal travel increment is smaller at low Cv and larger at high Cv along the ideal inherent curve.

verification_refs.citation: Derivative of ideal equal-percentage curve
verification_refs.locator: dCv/dx = k Cv for k=ln(R)>0
verification_refs.supports_claim: The absolute slope is proportional to current Cv, hence is smaller at lower Cv and larger at higher Cv for a positive range parameter R>1.

facts.statement: A quick-opening inherent characteristic develops a large fraction of its capacity at small travel, with progressively smaller additional capacity gain as travel increases; it is commonly used for on-off service, but service suitability remains application-dependent.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §2.4.1.A Quick opening inherent flow characteristic
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines near-maximum flow at very small opening and identifies on-off service as a common use.

facts.statement: At fixed valve differential pressure and fixed liquid properties in non-choked conditions, liquid flow follows the valve Cv curve proportionally; this is the reference basis for comparing inherent characteristics.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook—Oil and Gas, §6 Liquid Flow
verification_refs.locator: §6, basic liquid flow equation
verification_refs.supports_claim: At fixed differential pressure and specific gravity, the basic non-choked liquid relation makes Q proportional to Cv.

facts.statement: In an installed process pipeline, flow-dependent pressure losses can change the pressure differential available across the valve; consequently the installed flow curve can differ from the inherent curve even when source and receiver pressures are fixed.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §2.4.2 Installed flow characteristic
verification_refs.locator: §2.4.2; dynamic pressure losses and changing valve differential pressure
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that pipeline dynamic losses cause valve pressure drop to vary with flow and installed behavior depends on the process pipeline.

facts.statement: For a fixed-geometry system with approximately constant loss coefficient in a sufficiently turbulent regime, frictional head/pressure loss scales approximately with flow squared; this approximation does not include static head and can fail when the loss coefficient changes materially.

verification_refs.citation: KSB Centrifugal Pump Lexicon, System characteristic curve
verification_refs.locator: Head-loss equation and H_L ~ Q² under constant loss coefficient and sufficiently high Reynolds number
verification_refs.supports_claim: Derives quadratic loss scaling from velocity proportional to Q with constant loss coefficient and sufficiently high Reynolds number; separates static/geodetic head.

facts.statement: For a fixed-speed centrifugal pump operating on a stable, continuously negative-slope H–Q characteristic, developed head decreases as flow increases; the actual pump curve depends on pump design and operating conditions, so this is not universal for every centrifugal-pump curve.

verification_refs.citation: KSB Centrifugal Pump Lexicon, Characteristic curve
verification_refs.locator: H/Q curves; stable curve defined by continuously negative slope
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines a stable centrifugal-pump H/Q curve by its continuously negative slope and notes that curve shape depends on pump design.

facts.statement: For fixed reservoir pressures and elevations, static/geodetic head is independent of flow rate; it contributes a nonzero flow-independent term to system head, in addition to flow-dependent friction losses.

verification_refs.citation: KSB Centrifugal Pump Lexicon, System characteristic curve
verification_refs.locator: Static pressure/elevation terms and system curve intercept
verification_refs.supports_claim: Identifies pressure and elevation terms independent of Q and explains that static head shifts the system curve vertically.

facts.statement: A linear inherent trim does not guarantee a linear installed flow-versus-travel curve: if valve differential pressure varies with flow, the liquid-flow relation combines Cv(travel) with the changing pressure drop.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §§2.4.1–2.4.2
verification_refs.locator: Linear inherent characteristic and installed flow characteristic definitions
verification_refs.supports_claim: Says linear inherent equals installed only if valve pressure drop remains constant; otherwise installed curve depends on pipeline and inherent curve.

facts.statement: An equal-percentage inherent characteristic is often selected to help produce a more nearly linear installed response when valve pressure drop decreases as flow rises, but it does not guarantee a linear installed curve; process-specific sizing/modeling is required.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §2.4.1.C and §2.4.2
verification_refs.locator: Equal-percentage purpose and installed performance conditions
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes equal percentage as intended to linearize installed response in normal applications where available valve DP decreases with opening due to other system losses; also says actual conditions and modeling are needed.

facts.statement: Control-valve characteristic and size selection must use the actual process operating conditions and the target installed behavior; a trim label alone is insufficient to establish suitability across an operating range.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §§2.2–2.4.3
verification_refs.locator: Operating conditions, installed performance and installed gain
verification_refs.supports_claim: States successful sizing/selection depends on actual process conditions and that installed performance/gain should guide characteristic and size selection.

facts.statement: Typical application mappings for linear, equal-percentage, and quick-opening trims are guidance rather than universal rules: actual suitability depends on the process pressure distribution, operating range, valve sizing, and control objective.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §§2.2–2.4.6
verification_refs.locator: Actual process conditions; characteristic selection; installed performance and characterization
verification_refs.supports_claim: Requires actual process conditions for selection and explains that desired installed characteristics depend on the pipeline/process and may need specific valve sizing or characterization.

facts.statement: Valve authority is a dimensionless measure of the valve's share of a defined system pressure-drop budget at a stated operating condition. Because conventions differ (for example, valve drop relative to total variable circuit drop versus a valve drop normalized to a closed-valve condition), the formula and system boundary must be declared before comparing values.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Control valve authority—Ask the flow control expert
verification_refs.locator: Definition and note that authority is not internationally standardized
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines a valve-authority factor using valve differential pressure at a stated flow relative to closed-valve differential pressure, explains high/low interpretations, and explicitly notes that the term is not internationally standardized; therefore convention and condition must be identified.

facts.statement: Under the explicitly defined simple-series convention at one operating point, authority may be written a=ΔPv/(ΔPv+ΔPrest), where ΔPv is valve pressure drop and ΔPrest is the remaining variable pressure loss in the defined circuit; this is not interchangeable with every vendor's authority convention.

verification_refs.citation: Pressure-drop balance for a defined series circuit
verification_refs.locator: ΔPtotal,variable=ΔPv+ΔPrest and ratio definition
verification_refs.supports_claim: For a series path with static terms excluded from the variable-drop budget, pressure-drop additivity gives the stated ratio. The condition prevents applying it to parallel paths or a different authority convention.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Control valve authority—Ask the flow control expert
verification_refs.locator: Authority definition and non-standardization caveat
verification_refs.supports_claim: Confirms authority conventions require care and are not standardized internationally.

facts.statement: An authority calculation is meaningful only after defining the hydraulic boundary and pressure-drop convention; pumps, static head, bypasses, and parallel branches can change which pressure drops belong in the denominator and may invalidate a simple series-circuit formula.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §§2.2–2.4.4
verification_refs.locator: Actual process conditions, process pressure model, pump curve and pipeline boundary conditions
verification_refs.supports_claim: Says actual process conditions determine selection and the valve pressure model depends on piping losses, pump curve and boundary conditions; calculations assume specific process-model conditions.

facts.statement: As flow changes in an installed circuit, flow-dependent piping and equipment losses change and redistribute the pressure drop available across the valve; the direction and amount depend on the pressure source, system topology, and operating point.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §2.4.2 Installed flow characteristic
verification_refs.locator: Lines/section describing dynamic losses and changing valve Δp with flow
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that pipe/equipment dynamic losses change with flow and cause valve inlet/outlet pressure and valve differential pressure to vary.

facts.statement: When the valve takes a small share of the relevant system pressure drop, changes in other system losses can strongly affect its available Δp and installed flow curve; low authority can therefore increase distortion from the inherent curve, but magnitude and shape depend on trim and system conditions.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Control valve authority—Ask the flow control expert
verification_refs.locator: Interpretation of high and low authority
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that low authority means pipeline pressure loss is significant compared with valve loss and that authority can be used to study installed characteristic; the statement is accordingly conditional rather than a universal shape claim.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §2.4.2
verification_refs.locator: Installed curve is a function of pipeline and inherent characteristic
verification_refs.supports_claim: Supports dependence on both system and trim, not a fixed distortion shape.

facts.statement: There is no single authority value that is a universal pass/fail criterion for all control-valve systems; acceptable allocation depends on the declared authority convention, operating range, controllability target, energy cost, pump/system limits, and process requirements.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Control valve authority—Ask the flow control expert
verification_refs.locator: Authority is not internationally standardized; use for installed characteristic and rules of thumb
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explicitly notes lack of international standardization, undermining any universal numerical acceptance threshold; Valmet presents authority as a study/selection factor.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §§2.2–2.4.3
verification_refs.locator: Process-specific selection and gain guidance
verification_refs.supports_claim: Selection depends on actual process conditions and installed gain; its numeric recommendations are framed as rules of thumb, not universal acceptance criteria.

facts.statement: A valve selected with excess capacity may meet required flow at a relatively low travel; whether it is oversized must be judged against the actual minimum, normal, and maximum process cases, not nominal line size alone.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §2.4.3 Installed gain
verification_refs.locator: Figures 19–20 and discussion of oversized valve at small flows
verification_refs.supports_claim: Shows that oversized valves can have high installed gain at small flows and contrasts proper sizing; the claim is limited to process capacity versus required case.

facts.statement: For the same non-choked liquid flow and fluid properties, the basic sizing relation implies that a larger effective Cv requires a smaller valve pressure drop; this can reduce the valve's share of circuit pressure loss, subject to the actual system boundary and operating point.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook—Oil and Gas, §6 Liquid Flow
verification_refs.locator: Q=Cv√(ΔP/G), rearranged at fixed Q and G
verification_refs.supports_claim: Rearranging the basic liquid equation gives ΔP=G(Q/Cv)^2, so increasing Cv lowers required valve ΔP for fixed Q and G within the equation's domain.

facts.statement: An oversized valve can exhibit high installed gain at small process flows, making small position changes produce relatively large flow changes and potentially worsening accuracy or promoting hunting; this is a possible outcome, not an inevitable result for every valve and loop.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §2.4.3 Installed gain
verification_refs.locator: Figures 19–20; oversized-valve gain and possible hunting
verification_refs.supports_claim: States oversized valves cause high gain with small flows, poor control accuracy and possible hunting, and shows the gain curve; 'can' preserves that the outcome depends on application.

facts.statement: Inherent valve gain is the local slope of the inherent flow or relative-Cv characteristic with respect to valve travel under its constant-pressure-drop reference condition; normalization determines its numerical value.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §§2.4.1 and 2.4.3
verification_refs.locator: Inherent curve definition; installed gain as flow/travel slope
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines inherent characteristic at constant Δp and gain as a relative-flow change divided by relative-travel change; applying the same slope definition to the inherent curve yields inherent gain.

facts.statement: Installed valve gain is the local change in actual relative flow divided by the corresponding change in relative travel along the installed characteristic; its value depends on the chosen flow and travel normalization.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §2.4.3 Installed gain
verification_refs.locator: Equation (11) definition and finite-difference implementation
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines installed gain as change in relative flow divided by relative travel, and notes a finite-difference calculation in software.

facts.statement: Installed valve gain is generally a function of operating point and can vary with flow and travel because both the inherent curve and pressure-drop distribution contribute to the installed curve; it should not be assumed constant without evaluation.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §2.4.3 Installed gain
verification_refs.locator: Gain curve varies over valve travel and required flow range
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes gain curves across travel and says variation in gain over the required flow range changes relative flow response to the same signal change.

facts.statement: Installed gain need not equal inherent gain: the installed curve includes process-pipeline pressure behavior in addition to the valve's constant-Δp inherent characteristic.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §§2.4.1–2.4.3
verification_refs.locator: Inherent/installed curve definitions and installed gain
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines the curves under different conditions and shows installed gain as the slope of the installed curve, which depends on process pipeline and trim.

facts.statement: An equal-percentage inherent characteristic can help compensate for a changing process/valve pressure relationship in some applications, but it does not guarantee constant process or loop gain; the installed process model and control objective determine suitability.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §§2.4.1.C, 2.4.3, 2.4.6
verification_refs.locator: Equal-percentage design intent, installed gain selection, and nonlinear process compensation
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes equal percentage as designed to linearize installed characteristic in normal pressure-redistribution cases, but recommends actual installed-gain/process analysis and notes nonlinear process compensation is application-dependent.

facts.statement: If installed valve gain changes substantially across the required operating range, the same controller output change can cause different relative flow changes at different operating points; this can make a fixed controller tuning feel more or less aggressive, subject to the other loop dynamics.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §2.4.3 Installed gain
verification_refs.locator: Gain variation and flow change per signal change
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that gain variation causes different relative flow changes for the same relative signal change and is usually undesirable for controllability; the statement limits extension to the full-loop tuning behavior.

facts.statement: Inherent rangeability is commonly expressed as the ratio of largest to smallest Cv over which the deviation from a specified inherent characteristic remains within stated controllability limits; the limit definition and test conditions must accompany the ratio.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Control Valve Handbook, Chapter 1: Introduction to Control Valves
verification_refs.locator: Rangeability definition
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines rangeability as the largest/smallest flow coefficient ratio within which deviation from specified flow characteristic remains within stated limits; also relates it to max/min controllable flow.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Rangeability—Ask the flow control expert
verification_refs.locator: Inherent rangeability and stated controllable limits
verification_refs.supports_claim: Notes rangeability definitions vary and inherent rangeability depends on controllability limits, with practical ratio based on maximum and minimum controllable Cv.

facts.statement: Rangeability is not the ratio of maximum to minimum valve travel; it concerns the controllable flow coefficient or flow range under specified characteristic-deviation/controllability limits.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Control Valve Handbook, Chapter 1: Introduction to Control Valves
verification_refs.locator: Rangeability definition
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines the ratio by Cv or controllable flow rates and deviation limits, not travel endpoints.

facts.statement: Installed rangeability is commonly expressed as maximum-to-minimum controllable flow in the installed system, with endpoints determined by stated installed-characteristic/gain tolerance and controllability requirements; it is not a universal intrinsic valve-only number.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Rangeability—Ask the flow control expert
verification_refs.locator: Installed rangeability definition and vendor-dependent controllability limits
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines installed rangeability through max/min flow within a stated deviation tolerance and explains limits depend on gain tolerance, friction, response and application.

facts.statement: Installed rangeability can be lower than or otherwise differ from rated/inherent catalog rangeability because process pressure distribution, selected valve sizing, mechanical friction, and installed controllability limits affect the usable flow endpoints.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Rangeability—Ask the flow control expert
verification_refs.locator: Inherent versus installed rangeability; response and friction effects
verification_refs.supports_claim: Separates inherent from installed rangeability and says installed limits depend on controllability, gain criteria, friction, and system conditions; comparison requires matching the stated limits.

facts.statement: Process turndown describes the ratio of the process's required maximum to minimum operating flow, whereas valve rangeability describes the valve's controllable range under defined conditions and tolerances; the two ratios need not be equal.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Control Valve Handbook, Chapter 1: Introduction to Control Valves
verification_refs.locator: Rangeability definition as valve controllability range
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines valve rangeability using controllability of the valve; comparing this with a process's independently specified required flow ratio shows they are different requirements, not an identity.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Rangeability—Ask the flow control expert
verification_refs.locator: Inherent and installed rangeability definitions
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines valve rangeability in terms of controllable flow/Cv and tolerance, distinct from the process's required operating span.

facts.statement: Installed performance should be evaluated over the required process flow range, including minimum, normal, and maximum cases where applicable, because travel, valve Δp, and installed gain vary with operating condition.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §§2.2, 2.4.2–2.4.4
verification_refs.locator: Actual operating conditions, multiple flow conditions, installed curves and gain over required range
verification_refs.supports_claim: Requires actual process conditions, uses multiple flow conditions to model pressure behavior, and evaluates installed flow/gain across the required range; minimum/normal/maximum are a practical case set when applicable.

facts.statement: A final control-valve selection check should examine predicted installed flow and gain over the required process range together with the actual process conditions; inherent/catalog characteristic alone does not establish installed controllability.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual, §§2.2–2.4.4
verification_refs.locator: Actual process conditions, installed characteristic and gain curves, and limitations of static selection calculations
verification_refs.supports_claim: Recommends modeling installed flow and gain from actual process conditions and notes a full dynamic analysis is needed to guarantee an optimum valve for a nonlinear complete loop.

facts.statement: For a canonical underdamped second-order response, damping ratio affects overshoot and rise-time behavior, so a design target is selected against required transient specifications rather than from a universal optimum. A real control design must also account for disturbance-response objectives and physical constraints such as actuator limits or safety-related output limits; the canonical second-order formulas alone do not prove those real-system requirements are satisfied.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare, 2.004 Dynamics and Control II, Lecture 21
verification_refs.locator: §1.1 second-order step response; damping-ratio compromise between overshoot and rise time
verification_refs.supports_claim: Derives the underdamped second-order overshoot and settling response from ζ and ωn, and describes ζ≈0.707 as a compromise between overshoot and rise time rather than a universal optimum.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare, 6.241J Dynamic Systems and Control, course text
verification_refs.locator: Feedback-system performance specifications: disturbance rejection, command following, noise rejection
verification_refs.supports_claim: Identifies disturbance rejection as an explicit feedback-system performance specification, distinct from nominal step-response metrics.

verification_refs.citation: Engineering LibreTexts, Introduction to Control Systems, §4.2 Transient Response Improvement
verification_refs.locator: Step-response specifications and desired pole locations
verification_refs.supports_claim: Relates rise time, peak time, overshoot, and settling time to second-order poles and damping ratio; design specifications determine desired pole locations.

verification_refs.citation: Engineering LibreTexts, Measurements, Instrumentation and Controls, Chapter 10: System
verification_refs.locator: Discussion of performance, actuator saturation/overheating, and practical constraints
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that control design must balance performance with practical constraints and that control effort can exceed actuator limits (saturation/overheating); these plant constraints are not captured by the ideal second-order damping-ratio formulas.

facts.statement: A gain interval that makes a nominal characteristic polynomial stable establishes nominal mathematical stability only for the modeled plant and assumptions; it does not establish adequate field robustness or feasibility. Before choosing an operating gain, the design should check stability margins against delay/model variation and verify disturbance/noise performance and bounded actuator effort over relevant operating conditions.

verification_refs.citation: Lund University, Engineering Program, Control Theory textbook, §8.5 Stability Margins
verification_refs.edition_or_version: 2016 edition hosted by Lund University; accessed 2026-10-10
verification_refs.locator: §8.5; gain, phase, and delay margins as robustness distance from instability
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that stability alone is not enough in practice and introduces gain, phase, and delay margins as measures of robustness/how far the system is from instability; Nyquist analysis also accommodates modeled delay.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare, 2.017J Design of Electromechanical Robotic Systems, Control Systems—Loop Shaping
verification_refs.locator: Pole placement requirements: stability, speed, robustness; actuator saturation and hardware stress
verification_refs.supports_claim: Lists stability, speed and robustness as pole-placement requirements, says larger gains demand larger control input, and calls for avoiding actuator saturation and hardware stress.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare, 6.241J Dynamic Systems and Control, course text
verification_refs.locator: Performance specifications: disturbance rejection and noise rejection
verification_refs.supports_claim: Treats disturbance rejection and noise rejection as performance specifications separate from nominal closed-loop stability.

facts.statement: 형상관리는 프로젝트에서 통제 대상으로 선정·식별한 구성항목과 그 기술문서·모델·하드웨어·소프트웨어 등의 변경 및 상태를 관리한다. 어떤 세부 자산을 CI로 지정할지는 시스템 경계와 형상관리 계획에서 정해야 하며, 나열된 모든 자산 유형을 모든 시스템에서 반드시 CI로 취급한다는 뜻은 아니다.

verification_refs.citation: NASA, Systems Engineering Handbook, §6.5 Configuration Management
verification_refs.locator: §6.5.1.2.2 Identify Baseline to be Under Configuration Control; lines 297–298, 362–365
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes selecting CIs, associating configuration documentation, assigning unique identifiers, establishing baselines, and maintaining controlled lists that can include documents, hardware, software, and models.

verification_refs.citation: NASA NPR 7123.1B, Appendix C, configuration management requirements
verification_refs.locator: C.3.5.4(a)–(b), configuration plan and baseline identification
verification_refs.supports_claim: Requires the project to identify controlled items, identifiers, owners, and baseline configurations as part of its configuration-management strategy.

facts.statement: 형상변경 절차는 CI의 중요도와 변경의 영향·범위에 비례하는 검토·승인 수준을 정하고, 승인권한과 변경 실행 책임을 문서화해야 한다. 위험이 크거나 여러 시스템·현장 제품에 파급되는 변경에는 더 높은 수준 또는 다학제 검토를 적용할 수 있으며, 소규모 변경에도 동일한 위원회 구조를 강제하는 보편 규칙은 아니다.

verification_refs.citation: NASA Software Engineering Handbook, SWE-082: Authorizing Changes
verification_refs.locator: Requirements 4.1.4; §§2, 3, especially levels of control and change authority
verification_refs.supports_claim: Requires procedures to designate control levels and the persons/groups authorized to approve and make changes. Its rationale says control levels depend on criticality and impact range, and its guidance ties authority to complexity, cost, risk, or effect; lower-risk changes may use lower authority while critical or far-reaching changes may need formal review.

verification_refs.citation: NASA, Systems Engineering Handbook, §6.5 Configuration Management
verification_refs.locator: §6.5.1.2.3 Manage Configuration Change Control
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes systematic proposal, evaluation, approval, incorporation, and implementation verification, with a change-control board and change authority suited to project objectives and stakeholder responsibilities.

facts.statement: CI 식별정보는 해당 시스템과 형상관리 계획에 맞춰 CI를 명확히 참조하고 재구성·영향분석할 수 있도록 유지한다. 필요한 속성에는 고유 식별자, 구성요소와 버전, 물리·논리 위치, 소유자·관리정보, 운영 상태, 다른 CI/시스템과의 관계·의존성이 포함될 수 있으며, 승인·적용 상태는 별도 형상상태기록과 연결한다.

verification_refs.citation: NIST SP 800-128, Guide for Security-Focused Configuration Management of Information Systems
verification_refs.locator: §3.1.2, pp. 25–27 (component inventory and CI attributes); §3.1.3, pp. 27–28 (CI identification and data elements)
verification_refs.supports_claim: Lists typical inventory attributes including unique identifier, system association, software version/license, physical/logical location, owner, operational status, and additional relationships/dependencies; says CI records may include system placement, ownership, components, versions, dependencies on other CIs, and information needed to rebuild the CI. The guide presents these as system-specific selected data elements, not a universal mandatory field list.

verification_refs.citation: NASA NPR 7123.1B, Appendix C, configuration management requirements
verification_refs.locator: C.3.5.4(b)–(d), CI identifier/owner, approval, implementation status and baseline differences
verification_refs.supports_claim: Requires unique identifiers and owners for controlled CIs; change control records approval and monitors implementation, while configuration records track change disposition, status and differences between baselines.

facts.statement: NASA SWE-113 software change/problem reports include the affected software item and current configuration, problem/change description and justification, originator and priority/severity, impact or analysis, disposition, implementation/release verification, status, and safety impacts. Additional fields such as expected benefits or explicit acceptance criteria may be added by project procedure; they are not asserted here as universal mandatory fields for every change system.

verification_refs.citation: NASA Software Engineering Handbook, SWE-113: SW Change Request/Problem Report
verification_refs.locator: Requirement 5.2.5.1(a)–(l); §§1–3
verification_refs.supports_claim: Specifies software item identity; problem/change description and justification; originator and priority/severity; impact analysis including changed CI, schedules, cost, products or tests; approval/disapproval; implementation/release verification; status; safety aspects; current configuration; and workarounds. facts.statement: In the NASA software-release process described by SWE-085, a release package is prepared and delivered under documented approval and release procedures; its scope identifies included configuration items, versions, revisions, and dependencies, while package records may include version description, release notes, installation and test/rollback material, and a checked master copy. The exact artifact set depends on the project's applicable requirements; this source does not establish that every listed item is universally mandatory for every plant or software release.
