facts.statement: If an incremental encoder produces f counted pulses per second and the configured decoding yields N_eff counted pulses per mechanical revolution, rotational speed is n=60f/N_eff rpm. N_eff must use the receiver's actual x1/x2/x4 edge-count definition; interpreting catalog PPR without the decoder convention can introduce a factor error.

verification_refs.citation: Dimensional derivation from pulse count and rotational frequency
verification_refs.locator: revolutions/second = (pulses/second)/(pulses/revolution); multiply by 60 seconds/minute
verification_refs.supports_claim: Since f has units pulses/s and N_eff has units pulses/rev, f/N_eff is rev/s; multiplying by 60 s/min gives rpm. The pulse/revolution count must match the decoding convention.

facts.statement: If m decoded encoder edges are counted during a gate interval Δt seconds and N_eff is the decoded edge count per mechanical revolution, the gate-average speed estimate is n=60m/(N_eff·Δt) rpm. A finite gate quantizes the result in increments of 60/(N_eff·Δt) rpm per count; this is resolution/quantization, not a universal bound on all measurement error.

verification_refs.citation: Dimensional derivation from edge count over a fixed time gate
verification_refs.locator: m/N_eff = revolutions in Δt; divide by Δt for rev/s and multiply by 60 for rpm
verification_refs.supports_claim: The measured edge count divided by edges per revolution gives revolutions during the gate. Dividing by the gate duration gives rev/s; multiplication by 60 gives rpm. One-count quantization is one speed step of 60/(N_eff·Δt) rpm under the stated gate method.

facts.statement: An incremental encoder represents shaft movement as pulses/count transitions relative to a reference; an external counter/controller accumulates those transitions to obtain relative position and can derive speed from pulse timing. Unless the accumulated count is retained through power loss or re-established by a reference/homing procedure, an incremental output alone does not identify the shaft's absolute position after restart.

verification_refs.citation: Danaher/Dynapar, Encoder Handbook, Absolute vs. Incremental Coding
verification_refs.locator: Absolute vs. Incremental Coding; incremental count retention and homing discussion
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes incremental encoders as providing pulses relative to motion; position requires external electronics to accumulate counts; counts can be lost on power interruption/transients, so equipment may need to be driven to a reference/home position. The statement preserves the exception where a controller separately retains or re-establishes position.

facts.statement: A quadrature incremental encoder provides A and B channels in nominally quadrature phase (90 electrical degrees); the channel lead/lag sequence indicates direction. The effective counts per revolution depend on which edges and channels the receiving counter decodes, so x1/x2/x4 mode must be reflected in N_eff.

verification_refs.citation: Danaher/Dynapar, Encoder Handbook, Absolute vs. Incremental Coding
verification_refs.locator: Incremental Coding; quadrature and x1/x2/x4 decoding
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes A/B channels 90 electrical degrees out of phase, direction determined by phase relationship, and ×2/×4 edge decoding increasing counts per revolution.

verification_refs.citation: Rockwell Automation, ControlLogix High-speed Counter Module Installation Instructions, 1756-UM007E-EN-P
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 2, Encoder x4 mode and A/B timing diagrams
verification_refs.supports_claim: Specifies the module's x4 mode counts rising and falling edges of A and B; the timing diagrams distinguish direction by which channel leads, and the module assumes 90-degree A/B phase difference.

facts.statement: An incremental encoder's index/marker/Z output is typically a once-per-revolution reference pulse used for homing, locating a reference, or checking accumulated A/B counts. It is a reference mark, not by itself a code for the shaft's absolute multi-turn position; turn counting and retention require other system logic.

verification_refs.citation: Dynapar, Incremental Encoder Technology: Benefits and Application Uses
verification_refs.locator: Optional signals: Index or Z channel
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes an optional index/Z channel as a one-pulse-per-revolution signal used for homing and verification of A/B pulse count. The once-per-revolution reference does not itself encode the accumulated number of revolutions.

facts.statement: An absolute encoder outputs a digital code/word associated with its absolute angular position (single-turn or multi-turn capability depends on the model). Speed can be estimated from successive position samples divided by their time interval; achievable dynamic response also depends on sampling/update rate and communication latency, not resolution alone.

verification_refs.citation: Danaher/Dynapar, Encoder Handbook, Absolute vs. Incremental Coding
verification_refs.locator: Absolute Coding
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes absolute encoders as generating a unique digital word corresponding to position and retaining a valid position output across power interruption, in contrast with incremental accumulated counts.

verification_refs.citation: Dynapar, How to Calculate Encoder Resolution
verification_refs.locator: Absolute encoder resolution and serial communication/data rate discussion
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that absolute encoders provide discrete position words when interrogated and that usable information per sampling period depends on communication/data rate; the speed-from-position-difference equation is the standard finite-difference derivation under known sample intervals.

facts.statement: Encoder resolution terminology must be interpreted using the specific manufacturer's and receiving device's definitions: incremental encoder PPR may describe output cycles/pulses per revolution, while decoded count per revolution can be multiplied by x1/x2/x4 edge processing; CPR/counts may be used for discrete positions or accumulated counts. Therefore N_eff must be derived from the encoder specification and actual decoder mode rather than inferred from an acronym alone.

verification_refs.citation: Dynapar, How to Calculate Encoder Resolution
verification_refs.locator: Encoder resolution definition; incremental PPR and quadrature edge decoding
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines incremental resolution in PPR and explains x4 edge decoding multiplies the counted pulses; this shows that catalog PPR and decoded counts/revolution are distinct quantities.

verification_refs.citation: OMRON Industrial Automation, Rotary Encoder Explanation of Terms
verification_refs.locator: Incremental Encoder output signal count; phase-Z origin signal
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines resolution/output count as the number of incremental signal outputs in one shaft revolution and distinguishes the once-per-revolution origin signal; supports checking the manufacturer's own terminology rather than assuming an acronym universally determines decoded counts.

facts.statement: For an incremental encoder with N_eff decoded counts per revolution at n rpm, the count-event rate is f=n·N_eff/60 counts/s. Encoder output electronics and the receiving counter/input each have finite frequency or pulse-width limits; the selected maximum speed and decode mode must remain within both applicable limits. Increasing decoded counts/revolution increases event rate at the same shaft speed.

verification_refs.citation: Dynapar, How to Calculate Encoder Resolution
verification_refs.locator: Incremental Encoder Resolution Calculation
verification_refs.supports_claim: Gives maximum supported PPR as operating frequency × 60 / maximum RPM, algebraically equivalent to the event-rate relation; explains encoder operating frequency limits.

verification_refs.citation: Rockwell Automation, ControlLogix High-speed Counter Module Installation Instructions, 1756-UM007E-EN-P
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 2, Encoder x1/x4 frequency and minimum pulse width
verification_refs.supports_claim: Specifies a receiving counter's maximum encoder mode frequency and minimum pulse width, demonstrating that the receiver has its own input limits in addition to encoder output limits.

facts.statement: A common high-frequency-oscillator inductive proximity sensor generates an alternating electromagnetic field at its sensing face; a conductive metal target entering that field induces eddy-current losses that damp the oscillator, and the sensor electronics switch the output when the change crosses its threshold. Repeated gear-tooth or flag passages can create pulses whose frequency is related to target passage rate; conversion to shaft speed requires the target count per revolution and correct pulse interpretation.

verification_refs.citation: Balluff, The basic operating principle of an inductive proximity sensor
verification_refs.locator: Oscillator, electromagnetic field, eddy-current losses and output switching
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes the LC oscillator and sensing field; conductive metal induces eddy currents which absorb energy and reduce oscillator amplitude until a Schmitt-trigger threshold switches the output.

verification_refs.citation: Danaher/Dynapar, Encoder Handbook, Incremental Coding
verification_refs.locator: Incremental pulse counting and speed/position measurement
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that a controller counts periodic motion pulses and uses their rate for speed; the target-events-per-revolution factor is required to convert pulse rate to shaft revolutions.

facts.statement: A permanent-magnet DC tachogenerator generates an output voltage whose magnitude is approximately proportional to shaft speed over its specified operating range; the output polarity can indicate direction for a bipolar measurement circuit. The proportionality constant, linearity, ripple, loading error and temperature behavior are device-specific and require the manufacturer's specification/calibration.

verification_refs.citation: NEMA MG 1-2016, Motors and Generators, DC Permanent-Magnet Tachometer Generators for Control Systems
verification_refs.locator: Part 16, DC permanent-magnet control tachometer generator definition
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines a DC permanent-magnet control tachometer generator as a DC generator designed to have output voltage proportional to rotor speed for control-system use.

verification_refs.citation: Nidec Leroy-Somer, Engineering Guide to Position and Speed Feedback Devices for Variable Speed Drives and Servos
verification_refs.locator: DC tacho-generators
verification_refs.supports_claim: States DC tachogenerator output amplitude is directly proportional to shaft speed and polarity is determined by direction; a device-specific calibration constant and operating limitations remain applicable.

facts.statement: A passive variable-reluctance magnetic pickup commonly places a permanent magnet and coil near a rotating ferromagnetic tooth/target; target passage changes magnetic reluctance/flux and induces an AC voltage in the coil. Pulse frequency follows target passage rate, while raw signal amplitude is speed-dependent and also varies with air gap and target geometry/material, so a low-speed signal may fall below an interface's detection threshold. Exact sensitivity and minimum usable speed depend on the pickup and signal conditioner.

verification_refs.citation: Analog Devices, Fail-Safe, Low-Speed, Variable-Reluctance Sensors
verification_refs.locator: Abstract and construction/operation, lines 21–24 and 35–37
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes a magnet and coil near a steel rotating target; target passage changes reluctance and flux and induces current/voltage in the coil. It explicitly states unprocessed signal amplitude is proportional to target speed and can become too small for high-speed-designed conditioning at low speed.

verification_refs.citation: National Instruments, NI-9752 User Manual and Specifications
verification_refs.locator: VR Input, minimum threshold and constant-gap amplitude/speed behavior
verification_refs.supports_claim: Specifies a minimum signal amplitude required by its VR input to produce a digital output and states pulse amplitude is directly proportional to target speed at constant gap; its interface-specific threshold supports qualifying minimum-speed detectability.

verification_refs.citation: Magnetic Sensors Corporation, Variable Reluctance (VR) Sensors
verification_refs.locator: FAQ: target material, air gap and output amplitude
verification_refs.supports_claim: States standard VR pickups require a ferrous target and that signal amplitude depends on target speed, air gap, and target magnetic/geometric properties; larger gap can reduce amplitude and risk signal loss.

facts.statement: A digital tachometer is an RPM-measuring instrument, not necessarily a tachogenerator: some instruments accept external pulse inputs from an encoder or other detector and calculate/display rotational speed using a configured pulse-per-revolution value; other handheld tachometers derive RPM optically or by contact. The instrument's input type and sensing method must be identified from its manual rather than inferred from the word 'tachometer'.

verification_refs.citation: Tsuruga Electric, 4961 Tachometer Instruction Manual
verification_refs.locator: Digital Tachometer Mode, P1 pulse count/revolution for rotary encoder or similar
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes a digital tachometer mode with an external pulse input and a configurable pulse count per revolution, explicitly including a rotary encoder as an input source.

verification_refs.citation: Fluke, 931 Tachometer Users Manual
verification_refs.locator: Optical (non-contact) and contact RPM measurement procedures
verification_refs.supports_claim: Documents one handheld tachometer instrument that measures RPM either optically using a reflective strip or by contact adapter, showing that 'tachometer' names the measuring instrument and does not imply a DC tachogenerator sensing principle.

facts.statement: For the Rosemount 3051 three-valve manifold configuration documented by Emerson, normal differential-pressure measurement has the high- and low-side isolation valves open and the equalizing valve(s) closed, so each process pressure reaches its corresponding transmitter port. A separate drain/vent fitting or valve is configuration-dependent and must be identified on the actual manifold; it is not the central equalizing valve.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Rosemount, 3051 Reference Manual, Integral Manifold Operation
verification_refs.edition_or_version: Reference Manual 00809-0100-4051 Rev AA, January 2007; accessed 2026-10-10
verification_refs.locator: §2, Integral Manifold Operation, three-valve configuration, pp. 2-20–2-21
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manual depicts the three-valve arrangement with both isolate valves open and equalize closed during normal operation. Its diagram separately labels drain/vent valves, supporting the distinction between an equalizing valve and a separate drain/vent provision.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 3051S Series Scalable Pressure, Flow, and Level Solution Reference Manual, 00809-0100-4801
verification_refs.locator: Hardware Installation, § Performing zero trim at static line pressure with 3-valve and 5-valve manifolds, p. 70
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that in normal operation the two isolate (block) valves between process ports and transmitter are open and the equalize valve is closed.

facts.statement: A DP transmitter span/calibration test must apply a known differential pressure between its H and L ports with the test arrangement specified by the transmitter/manifold procedure. If an equalizing passage remains open between the two sides, it shunts the differential and tends to equalize port pressures; that condition cannot establish a nonzero span input. Process isolation and reference-side configuration are test-setup dependent and must follow the actual device's approved procedure.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Rosemount, 3051 Reference Manual, Integral Manifold Operation
verification_refs.edition_or_version: Reference Manual 00809-0100-4051 Rev AA, January 2007; accessed 2026-10-10
verification_refs.locator: §2, pp. 2-20–2-21, equalizing valve operation
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes opening the center equalizing valve to equalize pressure on both transmitter sides; this shunts a differential between the ports and is the equalized zero condition, not a nonzero span stimulus.

verification_refs.citation: Differential-pressure definition at the transmitter ports
verification_refs.locator: ΔP=P_H−P_L; a nonzero span stimulus requires independently maintained unequal port pressures
verification_refs.supports_claim: By definition, if an open equalizing path makes P_H=P_L, then ΔP=0; it cannot provide a nonzero differential pressure span input. This derivation does not prescribe a particular hazardous-process valve sequence.

facts.statement: For a material in a uniaxial linear-elastic regime, Young's modulus E is the proportionality between axial stress and axial strain (σ=Eε). At the same uniaxial stress, a material with larger E has smaller axial strain. This does not by itself determine a component's total displacement without its geometry, boundary conditions, and loading distribution.

verification_refs.citation: NIST Special Publication 960-11, Recommended Practice Guide: Data Evaluation Theory and Practice for Materials Properties
verification_refs.locator: §2, Hooke's law and elastic modulus definition
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines Hooke's law σ=Eε for linear response at sufficiently low stress and identifies E as Young's modulus; discusses generalized tensor form for anisotropic crystals, which supports restricting the scalar statement to the stated uniaxial condition.

verification_refs.citation: NISTIR 7847, Mechanical Properties of Materials: Young's Modulus and Stress-Strain Behavior
verification_refs.locator: p. 7, stress proportional to strain at low stress; nonlinear and plastic cases
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that for many metals at low tensile stress, stress is proportional to strain and the proportionality constant is Young's modulus; distinguishes nonlinear initial elastic behavior and plastic deformation, supporting the explicit linear-elastic condition.

verification_refs.citation: Algebraic consequence of the uniaxial Hooke's law relation
verification_refs.locator: ε=σ/E for fixed σ; therefore increasing E reduces ε, within the same linear-elastic assumptions
verification_refs.supports_claim: Rearranging σ=Eε gives ε=σ/E. For fixed positive stress magnitude in the stated regime, axial strain magnitude is inversely proportional to E. Total component displacement additionally requires length/geometry and boundary conditions.

facts.statement: In a variable-reluctance inductive sensor with a ferromagnetic core and a simple unsaturated magnetic path, changing the air gap changes magnetic-circuit reluctance and therefore coil inductance (approximately L=N²/ℜ); increasing the gap generally increases reluctance and lowers inductance under that model. In an AC eddy-current probe near a conductive target, target conductivity, magnetic permeability, thickness/geometry, excitation frequency, and lift-off can affect induced currents and the probe-coil impedance. These dependencies are coupled and model/calibration dependent; their direction and magnitude are not universal for every sensor geometry.

verification_refs.citation: Rose-Hulman Institute of Technology, Sensors and Transducers instructional text, Example 8.9 Variable Reluctance Displacement Sensor
verification_refs.locator: Example 8.9, variable-reluctance sensor and air-gap magnetic circuit equation
verification_refs.supports_claim: States inductance varies inversely with magnetic-circuit reluctance, reluctance increases as air gap increases, and gives an air-gap-dominated L≈μ0N²A/(2g) approximation when core permeability is large. This supports the direction only under the stated simplified magnetic-circuit assumptions.

verification_refs.citation: ASTM E2884-22, Standard Guide for Eddy Current Testing of Electrically Conducting Materials Using Conformable Sensor Arrays
verification_refs.supports_claim: States eddy-current array responses can be converted to lift-off, conductivity, permeability, and thickness-related properties; penetration depends on excitation frequency, conductivity, permeability, and geometry; sensitivity generally decreases as coating/lift-off increases. It also cautions that property separation depends on frequency and material conditions.

verification_refs.citation: Federal Highway Administration, Tunnel—Eddy Current Testing (ECT)
verification_refs.locator: Physical Principle; depth dependence of frequency, conductivity and permeability; lift-off effect
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that AC-excited probe coils induce eddy currents in conductive material; their secondary field affects coil impedance. Penetration depends on frequency, conductivity and permeability, and coil-to-target distance affects signal strength through lift-off.

facts.statement: With flux linkage λ=L(i,x)i for a variable-inductance element, the passive-sign-convention terminal voltage is v=dλ/dt=L·di/dt+i·dL/dt when L is represented as the applicable differential/linear inductance and varies with the measured state x. Under sinusoidal small-signal excitation with L approximately fixed during a carrier cycle, the ideal coil impedance is R+jωL; a sensor circuit can infer the measurand through changes in voltage/current magnitude or phase, impedance, a bridge differential output, or an LC resonance frequency when that specific circuit topology is used. These are alternative readout architectures, not simultaneous requirements for every inductive sensor.

verification_refs.citation: Flux-linkage definition and chain-rule derivation for a variable inductance
verification_refs.locator: λ=L(i,x)i; passive-sign-convention v=dλ/dt; for L=L(x(t)) and linear λ=Li, v=L·di/dt+i·dL/dt
verification_refs.supports_claim: Differentiating flux linkage λ=Li by the product/chain rule gives the two terms. The equation is conditional on the stated flux-linkage model and voltage polarity convention; nonlinear magnetic devices require the appropriate differential flux-linkage relation.

verification_refs.citation: Rice University ECE 435 course text, Chapter 12: Sensors and Transducers
verification_refs.locator: Variable-inductance sensor and AC bridge discussion
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes variable-inductance transducers and AC bridge conversion of inductance change to output voltage, including differential sensor arrangements.

verification_refs.citation: Ramón Pallás-Areny and John G. Webster, Sensors and Signal Conditioning, 2nd ed., §5.2 AC Bridges
verification_refs.locator: §5.2, AC bridge with reactive sensor and differential inductive sensor
verification_refs.supports_claim: Shows an AC bridge with an inductive sensor impedance and explains conversion of sensor impedance change into a bridge output voltage; the differential configuration increases sensitivity while affecting linearity.

facts.statement: In a parametric resistive, capacitive, or inductive sensing arrangement, the measurand changes an electrical parameter (R, C, or L); an excitation/readout circuit converts that parameter change into an observable electrical signal. Voltage, current, bridge imbalance, impedance, phase, or frequency are topology-dependent alternatives, not outputs required simultaneously or by every sensor.

verification_refs.citation: National Instruments, PXIe-6368 User Manual, Signal Conditioning
verification_refs.locator: Signal Conditioning and Sensors and Transducers sections
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that sensors/transducers commonly require signal conditioning to be accurately acquired, and that many require excitation, bridge completion, linearization, or amplification; names filtering, isolation and amplification as front-end functions. It does not imply every sensor uses every function.

verification_refs.citation: Analog Devices, AN-830: Using the AD7142 Capacitance-to-Digital Converter
verification_refs.locator: pp. 1-2, capacitance-sensing block diagram and excitation/readout description
verification_refs.supports_claim: Shows a dedicated excitation driving a capacitive sensor and a capacitance-to-digital readout, supporting the parametric-sensor/readout chain for this circuit example.

verification_refs.citation: Rice University ECE 435 course text, Chapter 12: Sensors and Transducers
verification_refs.locator: Variable-resistance, variable-capacitance, variable-inductance transducer and bridge/readout discussions
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes parameter-changing transducers and circuit readout, including bridge conversion for variable-impedance sensors; the registry claim deliberately treats output forms as circuit-specific alternatives.

facts.statement: For the idealized component models used here, uniform-conductor resistance is R=ρl/A=l/(κA), parallel-plate capacitance is C=εA/d (neglecting fringing and with the relevant dielectric permittivity), and a linear lumped magnetic circuit has reluctance ℜ≈l_m/(μA) and inductance L≈N²/ℜ. Thus R, C, and L depend on material parameters and geometry. Young's modulus is a separate mechanical constitutive property relating stress and strain in the linear-elastic regime; it is not electrical conductivity, permittivity, or permeability.

verification_refs.citation: OpenStax, University Physics Volume 2, §9.3 Resistivity and Resistance
verification_refs.locator: Eq. 9.9 and accompanying derivation
verification_refs.supports_claim: Derives R=ρL/A for a uniform conductor and distinguishes material resistivity from the geometry-dependent resistance.

verification_refs.citation: OpenStax, University Physics Volume 2, §8.1 Capacitors and Capacitance
verification_refs.locator: Parallel-Plate Capacitor derivation and dielectric discussion
verification_refs.supports_claim: Derives the plate-capacitance dependence on plate area and separation and explains that the intervening dielectric changes capacitance; ideal parallel-plate assumptions are stated.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare, Electromagnetic Field Theory: A Problem-Solving Approach, Part 2
verification_refs.locator: Magnetic-circuit reluctance and inductance equations (8), (11)-(12)
verification_refs.supports_claim: Gives magnetic reluctance as path length divided by permeability and area and derives L=N²/ℜ for the lumped magnetic-circuit model.

verification_refs.citation: NISTIR 7847, Mechanical Properties of Materials
verification_refs.locator: Elastic modulus and stress-strain discussion
verification_refs.supports_claim: Treats elastic modulus as a mechanical stress-strain material property, distinct in kind from electrical conductivity, permittivity and magnetic permeability.

facts.statement: Encoder selection should distinguish whether the application needs speed/count only, directional information, incremental position relative to a reference, or absolute position. Quadrature incremental signals can encode direction and, with compatible decoding, provide up to four counts per cycle; absolute encoders report position codes. Resolution must match the application and remain within the encoder and receiver frequency capabilities, and output type must match the controller interface.

verification_refs.citation: Encoder Products Company, WP-2002: Applying Encoders
verification_refs.locator: Executive Summary and Common Interfacing Issues
verification_refs.supports_claim: Distinguishes absolute and incremental feedback, unique absolute position and incremental reference counting; states quadrature provides directional information and can increase resolution up to four times with compatible receiving devices. Also warns that too-high resolution can exceed encoder/receiver frequency capability, while too-low resolution can limit speed or position control.

verification_refs.citation: Encoder Products Company, TB-109: Specifying Output Types for Encoders
verification_refs.locator: Determining What Output Type Your Application Needs
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that output channel/type selection depends on the receiving device and controller requirements; differential output should be paired with a compatible differential receiver.

facts.statement: Reliable encoder pulse acquisition depends on matching encoder output type and voltage/supply range to the receiver, and on cable length, routing, shielding, grounding, termination, and receiver input compatibility. Cable or conducted/radiated noise can distort edges or cause false/missed counts. Differential line-driver output reduces common-mode noise only when paired with a compatible differential receiver, and any termination, shielding, or grounding practice must follow the applicable encoder, cable, and controller instructions.

verification_refs.citation: Encoder Products Company, WP-2004: Noise & Signal Considerations
verification_refs.locator: Electrical Noise, Differential Signals, Cable Lengths, Cable Termination, Cable Connection
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains radiated and conducted noise including ground loops and power supplies; cable length/capacitance can distort edges and cause counts errors; differential noise immunity requires both line-driver output and differential receiver; termination and grounding/shield connection affect signal quality.

verification_refs.citation: Encoder Products Company, TB-109: Specifying Output Types for Encoders
verification_refs.locator: NPN open-collector, push-pull, and differential line-driver sections
verification_refs.supports_claim: Documents distinct output types, level shifting and supply-dependent behavior, and the need to match the output to controller input type and voltage capability.

verification_refs.citation: Encoder Products Company, General Installation & Wiring Guide
verification_refs.locator: § Electrical Connection and Cable Routing
verification_refs.supports_claim: Instructs installers to match wiring to the receiving device, minimize cable length, route away from noisy power wiring, maintain continuity and use line-driver complementary signals for reduced noise where applicable.

facts.statement: In a representative cage-guided balanced sliding-stem globe trim, the plug-to-seat-ring seating interface is the primary closed-seat boundary, while a separate piston/seal ring between the plug's upper outside diameter and cage bore restricts internal high-to-low pressure leakage across the balancing interface. The body, cage, plug, stem, seat and balance chamber therefore serve distinct mechanical or pressure-boundary roles; the exact pressure areas and sealing interfaces are construction-specific and must be taken from the selected valve drawing/manual.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Fisher Control Valve Handbook, 5th ed., Chapter 3: Valve and Actuator Types
verification_refs.locator: §3.1.1.3, cage-style trim / balanced valve plug discussion
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes the seal between the upper plug outside diameter and cage bore as limiting leakage from upstream high pressure to downstream low pressure in balanced designs, and distinguishes that path from the seat/flow path.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Fisher HP and HPA Valves Instruction Manual, D101634X012
verification_refs.locator: §3.6 and Figures 9-10, balanced trim; plug seal/cage and plug/seat interfaces
verification_refs.supports_claim: Shows balanced plug and cage, separate plug-to-seat and upper seal-to-cage seating surfaces, and product-specific seal installation orientation.

facts.statement: The signed axial pressure force on a sliding-stem control-valve plug is the resultant of pressure acting on the construction's effective projected surfaces, resolved along a declared positive stem axis. Its direction cannot be inferred from the words flow-up/flow-down alone: pressure-tends-to-open/close equations differ with plug balance construction, flow orientation, upstream/downstream pressure locations, port area, and stem area. Use the actual valve geometry and manufacturer's force convention.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Fisher HP and HPA Control Valves Product Bulletin, D103428X012
verification_refs.locator: Actuator sizing force method; balanced/unbalanced and flow-up/flow-down force equations
verification_refs.supports_claim: Provides separate force equations for balanced/unbalanced plugs and flow-up/flow-down pressure-tends-to-open/close constructions, including port and stem areas; its sign note interprets negative force as pressure assisting closure.

verification_refs.citation: Resultant pressure force on a wetted surface
verification_refs.locator: F_p = -∫_S p n dA; axial component is the projection onto the declared positive stem axis
verification_refs.supports_claim: Pressure traction integrated over the actual wetted surfaces gives the resultant; its signed axial component depends on pressure distribution, projected areas, surface normals and the selected axis convention.

facts.statement: For the documented Fisher cage-guided balanced trim, the plug seal/piston ring at the plug-to-cage interface restricts internal leakage across the balancing path between higher-pressure and lower-pressure regions. This is distinct from leakage across the closed plug-to-seat-ring interface; their acceptance ratings and leakage classes must not be assumed identical and are product/rating-specific.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Fisher Control Valve Handbook, 5th ed., Chapter 3
verification_refs.locator: §3.1.1.3, balanced-plug cage-style valves
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that a piston-ring type seal between the plug upper portion and cage bore limits upstream high-pressure leakage into the downstream low-pressure system, distinct from the seat flow path.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Fisher HP and HPA Valves Instruction Manual, D101634X012
verification_refs.locator: Figures 9-10 and §3.6 balanced TSO trim
verification_refs.supports_claim: Identifies a lower plug-to-seat-ring seating surface and a distinct upper plug-seal-to-cage seating surface; installation and seal type vary by trim.

facts.statement: In the Fisher sliding-stem actuator-sizing force method, required operating force is composed of static plug-unbalance force, seat load, packing friction, and additional forces required by particular applications or constructions. These are separate force contributors; the selected valve's manufacturer method and operating cases determine their values and any required sizing margin.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Fisher HP and HPA Control Valves Product Bulletin, D103428X012
verification_refs.locator: Actuator sizing for sliding-stem valves, force method, pp. B-1–B-2
verification_refs.supports_claim: Lists static plug unbalance, seat load, packing friction, and application/construction-specific forces, with total force as their sum; the method separately accounts for pressure tending to open or close.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Fisher Control Valve Handbook, 5th ed., Chapter 5: Control Valve Sizing
verification_refs.locator: §5.11.1 Globe Valves, actuator sizing
verification_refs.supports_claim: Lists unbalance force, seat load, packing friction and application-specific forces as separate contributions to required operating force.

facts.statement: In Apache Flink event-time stream processing, watermarks signal progress in event time; an event arriving after the watermark has passed its timestamp is late, and the application must define how such late events affect its window results. This documents Flink's event-time model, not a universal requirement or capability of every historian or streaming product.

verification_refs.citation: Apache Flink, Timely Stream Processing
verification_refs.locator: Event Time and Watermarks; Lateness
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines watermarks as event-time progress indicators and late elements as records arriving after the event-time clock indicated by watermarks has passed their timestamp; explains out-of-order data and application handling of late elements.

facts.statement: OPC UA DataChangeFilter defines a STATUS trigger that reports a notification when the StatusCode changes, independently of a numeric value-change threshold. This is a protocol-level option; whether an application configures it and how downstream historian storage treats the notification are separate implementation choices.

verification_refs.citation: OPC Foundation, OPC UA Part 4: Services, §7.22.2.2 DataChangeFilter
verification_refs.locator: DataChangeTrigger STATUS and STATUS_VALUE
verification_refs.supports_claim: Specifies STATUS as a trigger when the StatusCode changes; separately specifies STATUS_VALUE for StatusCode or value changes and describes deadband filtering for value changes.

facts.statement: For liquid-in-glass thermometers, calibration corrections are conditional on the specified immersion and emergent-stem temperature. Using a thermometer under a different immersion/stem-temperature condition can require a stem correction; this does not imply that the same correction model applies to thermocouples, RTDs, or every industrial temperature assembly.

verification_refs.citation: NIST, Precision Measurement and Calibration: Selected NBS Papers on Temperature, Special Publication 300, Vol. 2
verification_refs.locator: §5.4 Corrections for Emergent Stem
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that scale corrections for partial-immersion thermometers apply only at the indicated immersion and a particular stem temperature, and that a correction is required when the use condition differs.

verification_refs.citation: NIST, Thermometer Calibration: A Model for State Calibration Laboratories, NBS Monograph 174
verification_refs.locator: §3.2.3 ASTM thermometers and §3.3.10 stem temperature correction
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes partial-immersion thermometers as used to a specified immersion line/depth and the emergent stem as being at a different ambient temperature, for which stem-temperature correction is addressed.

facts.statement: An OT backup/recovery plan should identify, for each prioritized asset, the files, applications, tools, licenses, and supporting components needed to restore it. NIST examples include control/logic and configuration files, I/O lists, firmware, HMI graphics, license keys, vendor tools, support documentation, OS/VM images, and redeployment software; the exact set depends on the asset and recovery scenario.

verification_refs.citation: NIST, SP 1339, OT Backup Quick Start Guide
verification_refs.locator: Identify assets critical to operations; identify files, applications, and spare parts required to restore
verification_refs.supports_claim: Calls for identifying files, software applications, and spare parts needed to restore the environment and gives examples including program/logic/configuration files, I/O lists, firmware, HMI graphics, license keys, vendor tools, support documentation, OS/VM images, and redeployment software.

facts.statement: Process gain is the ratio of a process-variable change to a corresponding change in controller output. In a nonlinear installed system, this is a local/operating-condition-dependent relationship and can vary as flow, load, pressure drop, or other process conditions change; it should not be assumed constant solely from a valve's inherent characteristic.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Fisher Control Valve Sourcebook—Refining, D103205X012
verification_refs.locator: §5.5 Control Valve Functions and Characteristics Terminology, Process Gain
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines process gain as the change in controlled process variable divided by a corresponding change in controller output.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook—Refining, D103205X012
verification_refs.locator: §5.5 installed valve gain terminology
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines installed valve gain as the slope of the installed characteristic for a specific system with pressure drop changing naturally; therefore it is a function of valve travel and the installed operating conditions, not solely the inherent trim curve.

facts.statement: For a single-loop negative-feedback model linearized about a fixed operating point, with controller, actuator/positioner, installed valve, process, and measurement blocks connected in series around the loop, the open-loop (loop) gain is the product of those block gains (or transfer functions). The product model is local to the operating point and the stated block structure; nonlinear, interacting, or multiloop systems require the corresponding model rather than a universal scalar product.

verification_refs.citation: MIT OpenCourseWare, 2.017J Design of Electromechanical Robotic Systems, Control System Design
verification_refs.locator: Closed-Loop Transfer Function / single-loop feedback-system gain
verification_refs.supports_claim: Presents the standard single-loop feedback block model and its loop/open-loop gain relationship.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Fisher Control Valve Handbook, 5th ed., Chapter 2: Control Valve Performance
verification_refs.locator: §2.1 Process Control Terminology; process gain and control-loop component gains
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines process gain through the valve assembly, process, and measurement devices and describes the product of their gains as process gain, distinct from controller gain.

facts.statement: In a locally linearized loop, if installed-valve gain changes with operating point in the opposite direction to process gain such that their product varies less, the combined loop/process gain can vary less over that range, with other gains held fixed. This is a conditional algebraic relationship, not a claim that a particular trim automatically achieves compensation in every plant.

verification_refs.citation: Algebraic derivation from the local cascade gain identity
verification_refs.locator: For G_total = G_fixed × Gv(x) × Gp(x), inverse co-variation of Gv and Gp reduces variation in their product when the product is approximately constant.
verification_refs.supports_claim: Directly follows by multiplying the local gains of the serial linearized blocks; it is conditional on consistent definitions and other factors held fixed.

facts.statement: Seat leakage is flow through a valve in its fully closed position under specified test differential pressure and temperature; minimum controllable flow is the lowest throttled flow that remains controllable under the applicable valve/system conditions. They are different operating conditions and metrics, so very low or zero specified seat leakage does not imply a zero minimum controllable throttling flow.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Fisher Control Valve Sourcebook—Refining, D103205X012
verification_refs.locator: §5.5 terminology: Rangeability and Seat Leakage
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines rangeability using maximum/minimum controllable flow and separately defines seat leakage as flow when the valve is fully closed under specified differential pressure and temperature.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Fisher Control Valve Sourcebook—Oil and Gas
verification_refs.locator: §1.5 Rangeability
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines rangeability as the ratio of maximum and minimum controllable flow rates.

facts.statement: Liquid control-valve choking calculations use upstream and downstream absolute pressures (P1, P2), liquid vapor pressure (Pv), liquid critical pressure ratio factor (FF), and the valve liquid pressure-recovery factor (FL); FF depends on the liquid critical pressure Pc in the cited IEC-based sizing relation. The local vena-contracta pressure (Pvc) is used to explain vapor formation and pressure recovery. This variable set is for the stated liquid-sizing model, not a claim that every vendor interface uses identical labels or workflows.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Product Bulletin 59.1:095, Choked Flow, D104173X012
verification_refs.locator: Liquid choked-flow equation and definitions of FL, FF, Pv, Pc
verification_refs.supports_claim: Gives ΔPchoked = FL²[P1 − FF·Pv], defines FL and FF, and gives FF = 0.96 − 0.28(Pv/Pc)^0.5; text explains liquid vapor formation at the vena contracta.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook—Oil and Gas, Chapter 3
verification_refs.locator: §3.1 terminology and §3.3 maximum liquid flow/choked-flow calculations
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines P1, P2, Pc, Pv, FF, FL, and ΔP and describes liquid maximum-flow calculations using the pressure-recovery and critical-pressure factors.

facts.statement: For the compared Fisher valve constructions, a smaller FL corresponds to higher pressure recovery and can produce a lower vena-contracta pressure, increasing cavitation susceptibility under the same process conditions. This is a construction- and condition-dependent comparison, not a universal ranking of all valve products.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Product Bulletin 59.1:095, Choked Flow, D104173X012
verification_refs.locator: Comparison of globe and rotary valves by FL and pressure recovery
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that compared rotary products generally have smaller FL and higher recovery than globe valves, and explains this can allow damaging cavitation before choking because of FL and flow geometry.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 4th ed., Chapter 4: Cavitating Applications
verification_refs.locator: §4.7 backpressure and vena-contracta pressure
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that increasing downstream pressure increases vena-contracta pressure and can prevent it from falling below vapor pressure; describes high recovery as a factor in cavitation susceptibility.

facts.statement: For a fixed liquid, valve construction, inlet pressure, and operating case, reducing the valve pressure drop by raising downstream pressure raises vena-contracta pressure in the described Fisher model; if the pressure remains above the liquid vapor pressure, cavitation is avoided for that case. The conclusion is conditional and does not mean every pressure-drop reduction or operating change guarantees cavitation-free service.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 4th ed., Chapter 4: Cavitating Applications
verification_refs.locator: §4.7 backpressure device and vena-contracta pressure
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that raising downstream pressure reduces valve differential pressure, raises vena-contracta pressure, and—if correctly sized—can keep vena-contracta pressure above vapor pressure and prevent cavitation.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Product Bulletin 59.1:095, Choked Flow, D104173X012
verification_refs.locator: ΔPchoked = FL²[P1 − FF·Pv]
verification_refs.supports_claim: For fixed valve and liquid conditions, defines the liquid choked pressure-drop threshold; reducing actual valve ΔP by raising P2 moves the operating pressure drop away from that threshold, subject to the sizing model.

facts.statement: Fisher's cited selection method distinguishes an incipient-cavitation coefficient (Ki) for initial vapor-bubble generation/collapse from a cavitation coefficient (Kc) for the beginning of cavitation-related damage and vibration. These coefficients depend on valve style/trim, and the handbook notes that specific Ki values are generally unavailable and its selection guidelines have application restrictions. Thus cavitation onset/damage criteria are model- and service-dependent; they are not a single universal threshold applicable to every valve and fluid.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 4th ed., Chapter 4: Cavitating Applications
verification_refs.locator: §4.8 terminology (Ki, Kc) and application-guideline restrictions
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines Ki as the incipient cavitation coefficient for initial bubble generation/collapse, states its specific values are generally unavailable, defines Kc as valve-style/trim-dependent and predictive of beginning cavitation damage/vibration, and restricts example selection guidance to water and stated customer/application conditions.

facts.statement: For a Rosemount remote-seal system, response time depends on transmitter sensor range, capillary length and inside diameter, and fill-fluid viscosity (which is affected by process and ambient temperature). Emerson also specifies selecting fill fluid within the process/ambient temperature range and considering application-specific fluid requirements; the exact response and compatibility limits are assembly-specific, not universal values.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Rosemount, Differential Pressure (DP) Level Transmitters and Diaphragm Seal Systems Reference Manual 00809-0100-4002
verification_refs.supports_claim: Lists transmitter sensor range, capillary length/ID and fill-fluid viscosity (affected by process and ambient temperature) as response-time factors; states fluid selection depends on application, temperature limits, and process needs, with cold fluid potentially slowing response.

facts.statement: For the Emerson Anderson Greenwood Series 200/400 non-flowing pilot option described in its product data sheet, a gas-service pressure-spike snubber uses fixed orifices and small volume chambers to damp transient pressure rises while leaving average static system pressure unaffected. This product-specific evidence supports transient damping by a snubber, but does not establish a universal damping-versus-measurement-response trade-off for all snubbers or dampers.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Anderson Greenwood Series 200/400/500/700/800 Pilot Operated Relief Valves Product Data Sheet VCTDS-00543-EN
verification_refs.locator: § Accessories and Options, Pressure Spike Snubber (Gas Service), p. 58
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes this option for specified gas-service pilot applications; fixed orifices and small volume chambers damp transient pressure rises, while average static system pressure is unaffected.

facts.statement: AVEVA Historian is documented as an operations-control process database providing process, alarm, and event history, time-series storage/compression, query and retrieval functions, and trend analysis with alarm details shown in context. This product-specific evidence establishes historian capabilities beyond simple backup storage, but does not imply that every historian product provides every listed function or that a historian replaces a backup system.

verification_refs.citation: AVEVA, AVEVA Historian product documentation
verification_refs.locator: Overview; Advanced data storage and compression; Trend application; Query application
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes AVEVA Historian as an operations-control process database for process/alarm/event history with storage/compression and query interface; the Historian Client provides historical trend analysis and overlays alarm details in trend context.

facts.statement: Control range may be expressed as the valve-travel interval over which installed valve gain remains within stated acceptance limits. Emerson/Fisher's Control Valve Sourcebook defines it using normalized installed gain from 0.5 to 2.0; that is the sourcebook's criterion and must not be treated as a universal acceptance band for every process or project.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook: Refining
verification_refs.locator: §5.2, Process Control Terminology, p. 5-112
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines control range as valve travel range where installed valve gain stays between normalized values 0.5 and 2.0; this registry preserves that as the cited source's criterion rather than universalizing it.

facts.statement: For control valves, minimum controllable flow is distinct from seat leakage: Emerson/Fisher defines clearance flow as flow below the minimum controllable flow while the closure member is not seated, and defines rangeability using the maximum and minimum controllable flow (or Cv) within stated characteristic-deviation limits. Siemens' variable-flow hydronic guidance further relates minimum controllable load to valve rangeability and authority in that application. These sources do not verify every factor in the Pack's compound list (including Reynolds effects and measurement noise) as universal determinants.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook: Refining
verification_refs.locator: §5.5, Control Valve Functions and Characteristics Terminology, pp. 5-117–5-118
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines clearance flow as flow below minimum controllable flow with the member not seated; defines rangeability by max/min Cv within stated deviation limits and allows the max/min controllable-flow interpretation; separately defines seat leakage at fully closed position.

verification_refs.citation: Siemens Building Technologies, Balancing and Control Valve Sizing for Direct-Return, Variable-Flow Hydronic Systems, Document 149-990
verification_refs.locator: Valve Rangeability, pp. 13–14, Eqs. (4)–(5)
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines rangeability as maximum/minimum controllable flow and gives a hydronic application estimate for minimum controllable load based on rangeability and authority; the registry explicitly limits this relation to that context.

facts.statement: Functional safety for process-industry SIS follows a lifecycle: risk assessment informs risk-reduction requirements and allocation; the required function and integrity are specified; SIS is designed, implemented, installed, commissioned and validated; it is operated, maintained and periodically proof-tested; modifications are managed; and the system is eventually decommissioned. HSE identifies these as the key lifecycle principles of BS EN 61511. The exact SRS field list remains governed by the applicable project standard and requirements, not inferred from this lifecycle summary.

verification_refs.citation: UK Health and Safety Executive, Functional safety
verification_refs.locator: Functional Safety; lifecycle principles, lines 59-68
verification_refs.supports_claim: HSE lists risk assessment, allocation, specification, design/implementation, installation/commissioning/validation, operation/maintenance/periodic proof testing, modification management, decommissioning, and lifecycle management processes as key principles of BS EN 61511.

facts.statement: For a process-industry SIS, the operator should be able to demonstrate routine maintenance, the basis for proof-test frequency, SIS-specific maintenance arrangements, and a procedure for modifying the SIS; operation and maintenance are intended to maintain the designed functional safety. HSE's COMAH assessment guidance asks for these records and evidence. It does not by itself establish that every listed trend field in the Pack is a universal mandatory log item.

verification_refs.citation: UK Health and Safety Executive, Discipline guidance for assessment of C&I issues in COMAH reports
verification_refs.locator: Full assessment and criteria 5.2.4.3/5.2.4.4, lines 108-128, 201-215
verification_refs.supports_claim: Requires evidence of SIS routine maintenance, SIS-specific maintenance, proof-test frequency and its derivation, and SIS modification procedure; states maintenance objective is preserving designed functional safety. Registry explicitly does not universalize the full Pack log-field list.

facts.statement: A practical feedback-loop design review can include measurement noise and filtering, sampling and delay, actuator limits/saturation and anti-windup, setpoint prefilter/feedforward choices, stability margins, time- and disturbance-response checks, and nonlinear saturation validation. These are context-dependent review dimensions rather than mandatory identical tests for every loop. MathWorks control-design guidance documents these as available analysis/design concerns and demonstrates their interactions.

verification_refs.citation: MathWorks, Validate Tuned Control System
verification_refs.locator: Extract and Plot System Responses; Validate Design in Simulink Model
verification_refs.supports_claim: Recommends evaluating reference tracking/time responses and stability margins, extracting sensitivity responses, and validating a tuned linearized design in the full nonlinear model.

verification_refs.citation: MathWorks, Anti-Windup Control Using PID Controller Block
verification_refs.locator: Performance Without Using Anti-Windup; Configure Back-Calculation; feedforward scenario
verification_refs.supports_claim: Demonstrates saturation with dead time, integrator windup, anti-windup recovery, cascaded actuator dynamics, and feedforward interactions; applicability depends on the actual configuration.

verification_refs.citation: MathWorks, Frequency-Domain Specifications
verification_refs.locator: Gain Limit and frequency-domain tuning requirements
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes frequency-domain design goals for disturbance rejection, roll-off, sensitivity, control effort, and avoiding saturation.

verification_refs.citation: MathWorks, Control System Designer Tuning Methods
verification_refs.locator: Graphical Tuning Methods table
verification_refs.supports_claim: Identifies Bode tuning for bandwidth and gain/phase margins, closed-loop tuning for reference tracking/disturbance/noise rejection, and root-locus design for time-domain constraints.

facts.statement: Takt time is available production time divided by customer demand for the same planning interval, expressing the demand-driven production pace. Cycle time is the time actually measured to produce a part or complete a process; effective/machine/operator cycle-time variants may include different work elements. They are related for capacity comparison but are not interchangeable definitions.

verification_refs.citation: Lean Enterprise Institute, Takt Time
verification_refs.locator: Definition and calculation example
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines takt time as available production time divided by customer demand and explains its purpose is matching production with demand.

verification_refs.citation: Lean Enterprise Institute, Cycle Time
verification_refs.locator: Definition; Machine, Effective Machine, and Operator Cycle Time
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines cycle time as actual measured time to produce a part or complete a process and distinguishes specific machine/operator/effective variants.

facts.statement: In a serial production line, the throughput bottleneck is the resource whose capacity/performance most constrains system output under the operating conditions; blocking and starvation caused in part by finite-buffer states also affect line throughput. Therefore a local efficiency increase at a non-bottleneck resource does not by itself imply an equal increase in total line output; the constraint can shift as conditions change.

verification_refs.citation: NIST, A Framework for Manufacturing System Design and Analysis
verification_refs.locator: Manufacturing system design analysis; bottleneck and throughput discussion
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that addressing a throughput bottleneck can increase line throughput and that bottleneck analysis identifies a machine impeding overall production-line throughput.

verification_refs.citation: C.-T. Kuo, J.-T. Lim, S. M. Meerkov, Bottlenecks in serial production lines: A system-theoretic approach, Mathematical Problems in Engineering 2 (1996), 853949
verification_refs.locator: Abstract and bottleneck definition
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines bottleneck via its effect on system performance and analyzes serial-line bottleneck identification using manufacturing blocking and starvation relationships.

facts.statement: OEE is commonly expressed as Availability × Performance × Quality. The factor definitions must share a declared equipment/process and planned-production scope: availability compares run time with planned production time, performance compares actual output rate with ideal rate, and quality compares good output with total output. OEE is a productivity/equipment-effectiveness KPI, not a sufficient standalone measure of delivery, cost, safety, or demand responsiveness; KPI scope and thresholds need to fit the business and operating context.

verification_refs.citation: Lean Enterprise Institute, Overall Equipment Effectiveness
verification_refs.locator: OEE definition and factor equation
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines OEE as availability rate × performance rate × quality rate and explains the factors as downtime, speed and scrap/rework losses.

verification_refs.citation: ISO 22400-2:2014, Automation systems and integration — KPIs for manufacturing operations management — Part 2
verification_refs.locator: Introduction; Scope, lines 82-146
verification_refs.supports_claim: States manufacturing KPIs are specified by formula and elements; KPI values alone are not sufficient for management/execution, company-specific thresholds may be needed, and manufacturing productivity feedback is contextual.

verification_refs.citation: NIST, Methods and Tools for Performance Assurance of Smart Manufacturing Systems
verification_refs.edition_or_version: Journal of Research of NIST 121 (2016), accessed 2026-10-10
verification_refs.locator: §4.3 Targeted Performance Objective for Smart Manufacturing — Productivity, pp. 303-304
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes OEE as a quantitative productivity measure and notes that different strategic objectives and operating situations may require different performance measures.

facts.statement: A common production-planning architecture separates long-term demand/capacity simulation, a master production schedule for finished products or important assemblies, and resource-constrained detailed scheduling of orders and operations. MPS items may be planned separately before dependent BOM levels are planned, while detailed scheduling considers resource/component availability and order dates. These are planning layers, not a universally fixed duration or calendar horizon; the actual horizon and freeze rules are organization- and system-specific.

verification_refs.citation: SAP Help Portal, Long-Term Planning (PP-MP-LTP)
verification_refs.locator: Purpose and long-term/rolling planning example
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes long-term production planning and short-/medium-term simulations, including annual or rolling-quarter planning and checking demand plans against available capacity.

verification_refs.citation: SAP Help Portal, Master Production Scheduling Procedure
verification_refs.locator: Process Flow
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes MPS as separately planning master schedule items; the MPS run plans that level, with dependent BOM requirements addressed in subsequent planning.

verification_refs.citation: SAP Help Portal, Production Planning and Detailed Scheduling (PP/DS)
verification_refs.locator: Use and functions
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes detailed optimization/scheduling of resource schedules and order dates/times while considering resource and component availability.

verification_refs.citation: NIST IR 6232, Manufacturing Planning and Execution Objects Foundation Interfaces
verification_refs.locator: A41 Develop Operation Sequence & Detailed Schedule
verification_refs.supports_claim: Distinguishes production plan/master schedule from local detailed operation sequencing and scheduling with setup, queue, throughput and resource considerations. Does not impose a universal time horizon.

facts.statement: A production unit-cost measure is meaningful only after its cost boundary and output denominator are defined consistently. Product-cost-per-unit methods allocate the relevant direct-material, direct-labor, and manufacturing-overhead costs to units; process-costing may use equivalent units for partially completed production. For an operational cost-per-good-unit measure, the chosen good-output denominator and treatment of scrap, rework, and yield must be stated. This is a measure-definition choice, not a universal accounting denominator or a claim that unit cost changes in a fixed proportion with volume.

verification_refs.citation: OpenStax, Principles of Accounting, Volume 2: Managerial Accounting, §6.3 Calculate Activity-Based Product Costs
verification_refs.locator: Unit-level, batch-level and product-level costs; overhead per unit; cost per unit
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains unit-level, batch-level and product-level cost pools and calculates overhead per unit by dividing overhead by product units, then combines material, labor and overhead into product cost per unit.

verification_refs.citation: OpenStax, Principles of Accounting, Volume 2: Managerial Accounting, §2.2 Identify and Apply Basic Cost Behavior Patterns
verification_refs.locator: Fixed and variable cost behavior; average variable cost
verification_refs.supports_claim: Distinguishes fixed and variable cost behavior and describes average variable cost as total variable cost divided by units produced; this supports rejecting a universal proportional unit-cost/volume rule.

verification_refs.citation: OpenStax, Principles of Accounting, Volume 2: Managerial Accounting, §5.3 Explain and Compute Equivalent Units and Total Cost of Production in an Initial Processing Stage
verification_refs.locator: Equivalent-unit calculation and reconciliation
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains equivalent-unit computations for partially completed production and reconciliation of costs and units in process costing.

facts.statement: In common MRP implementations, net material requirements are calculated by comparing planned or exact demand with available stock and scheduled receipts; procurement proposals are sized and dated using configured lot-sizing and lead-time parameters. For in-house production, dependent component requirements can be derived by BOM explosion. An MRP material plan does not by itself prove supplier reliability, physical line-side availability, alternate-part qualification, or finite-capacity feasibility; those require their own data and checks.

facts.statement: First-pass yield (FPY) counts units that complete the defined process and meet quality requirements without scrap, rework, retest, or diversion; it is distinct from a final yield measure that may count repaired/reworked units as good. Scrap and rework ratios use explicitly defined quantity bases, and their formulas can differ by KPI framework and process boundary. Therefore FPY, total/final yield, scrap, and rework metrics must state the entry/output population, inspection stage, and rework inclusion rule before comparison; the labels alone do not guarantee interchangeable denominators.

facts.statement: In classical assembly-line balancing, work elements are assigned to ordered workstations while respecting task-precedence constraints and station cycle-time limits; the balance seeks to reduce workload imbalance or station count/cycle time according to the selected problem formulation. Takt time expresses the production pace required by customer demand and can inform standardized work and operator workload design. Worker eligibility, equipment capability, ergonomics, model mix, and setup constraints are additional problem-specific restrictions rather than assumptions guaranteed by every basic balancing model.

facts.statement: Throughput is an output rate, WIP is the quantity of work within a declared process boundary, and flow/cycle/lead time is a time measure; these are dimensionally and operationally different KPIs and must not be used as synonyms. For a consistently bounded, stable production system using matching long-run averages, Little's Law relates average WIP = average throughput rate × average flow time. The terms 'cycle time' and 'lead time' can be defined differently across contexts, so measurement start/end events, included buffers, product mix, and time basis must be stated before comparisons or use of the relationship.

These sources support capability and qualification as planning considerations, but do not define a universal headcount, shift pattern, leave/absence formula, or skill-matrix format; those remain demand-, process-, site-, and jurisdiction-specific.

facts.statement: A process-capacity estimate should compare declared available operating time with the work content and cycle time of the relevant process or resource. A manufacturing process-capacity sheet can account for manual time, machine time, tool-change time, and per-shift operating time; operator loading can then be compared with takt, the customer-demand pace. The resulting capacity is conditional on its shift calendar, product mix, resource assumptions, and process definition; a theoretical rate is not proof of achieved plant output, and no universal efficiency multiplier follows from this method.

facts.statement: Production lot-size decisions trade setup frequency against inventory and flow. Larger lots can reduce setup frequency, while smaller lots can reduce average cycle stock. Yet where extra setups consume constrained capacity, smaller lots can increase utilization, queue time and lead time. The direction and optimum are conditional on setup time, demand and capacity, not universal.

facts.statement: Standard-cost variance analysis compares actual results with an appropriate standard/budget for the actual production level, then separates cost effects using declared accounting drivers. Common manufacturing analyses distinguish direct-material price and quantity variances, direct-labor rate and efficiency variances, and variable-overhead spending and efficiency variances. Scrap/rework, energy, or downtime can be investigated as operational causes or cost categories when data and accounting policy support them, but they are not one universal set of formal variance accounts. Variance signals require investigation of causes; they do not by themselves identify a corrective action.

facts.statement: Manufacturing product cost is commonly organized into direct materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead; overhead can include indirect materials/labor, utilities, and production-equipment depreciation. Whether an individual item is direct or indirect depends on whether it can be economically traced to the product and on the selected costing method. Scrap, rework, energy, and consumables may be tracked or allocated for operational or managerial cost analysis, but their treatment in a unit-cost measure is purpose- and policy-dependent rather than a universal fixed list.

facts.statement: A remote diaphragm-seal system isolates the transmitter sensor from the process with a process-facing diaphragm and a liquid fill system. In a capillary configuration, diaphragm displacement/pressure is transmitted through the fill fluid in the capillary to the transmitter sensor. Such systems are used to isolate instruments from process media or temperature conditions that are unsuitable for direct connection; fill-fluid selection, temperature exposure, capillary length, and elevation/static head affect measurement performance and response. The fill liquid is not literally incompressible; treating it as incompressible is an engineering approximation, not a material property.

facts.statement: For two pressure taps separated vertically by a known distance x in the same continuous, homogeneous, static liquid of density rho, the pressure difference is ΔP = rho g x after correcting transmitter/reference and installation head offsets. Therefore rho = ΔP/(g x). This inference is invalid if the taps do not share the same liquid column, density is stratified between taps, or the pressure datum/head offsets are uncorrected.

verification_refs.citation: Hydrostatic equation derivation from dP/dz = -rho g for a homogeneous static liquid

verification_refs.supports_claim: Integration of the hydrostatic pressure gradient for constant density gives ΔP = rho g x; algebraic rearrangement gives rho = ΔP/(g x), with units (Pa)/(m/s²·m)=kg/m³.

facts.statement: For a liquid of known, representative density rho, hydrostatic pressure difference between a bottom tap and a pressure reference at the gas space is ΔP = rho g h after correcting static fill-fluid and installation-head offsets; thus h = ΔP/(rho g). One differential-pressure measurement cannot independently determine both unknown liquid density and unknown level without an additional independent constraint or measurement.

verification_refs.citation: Hydrostatic equation derivation for a liquid column
verification_refs.locator: Integrate dP/dz = -rho g across liquid height h: P_bottom - P_surface = rho g h
verification_refs.supports_claim: For known uniform representative density, pressure difference is rho g h and rearranges to h=ΔP/(rho g); units reduce to metres. Without density or level known, one scalar pressure-difference equation cannot uniquely determine both unknowns.

facts.statement: For liquid service with downstream pressure below vapor pressure (P2 < Pv), flashing vapor persists downstream and cannot be eliminated by the control valve alone. Damage mitigation is application-specific: suitable valve outlet/body geometry can reduce flow turning, droplet impingement or erosive velocity, and downstream piping and material selection should be considered. Damage severity is not determined by a universal fixed formula or geometry checklist.

It explicitly notes no industry standard or scientific method for predicting flashing-damage intensity.
