verification_refs.supports_claim: The range values are endpoint evaluations of the signed sensor input. Wet-leg, process-column, remote-seal fill-fluid, and mounting-elevation terms enter only if present in the actual pressure paths; the method does not require all such terms or a zero LRV.

facts.statement: Rosemount 3051SHP의 차압 측정에서 Maximum Working Pressure는 정상 운전 중 허용되는 static line pressure이며, 한쪽 포트에 full static pressure가 걸리도록 잘못 밸브 조작하면 출력 이동이 생겨 재영점 조정이 필요하다. 허용 정압과 과압 한계는 해당 모델 번호의 사양으로 확인한다.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Rosemount, 3051S High Pressure Manual Supplement 00809-0100-4851
verification_refs.locator: §§8.2.13–8.2.15: Overpressure limits, Maximum Working Pressure limits, Static pressure limits
verification_refs.supports_claim: The supplement distinguishes model-specific overpressure limits from maximum working pressure, defines MWP as maximum pressure allowed in normal operation and static line pressure for a DP transmitter, and states that mis-valving which exposes one side to full static pressure causes output shift and requires re-zeroing. It lists the 3051SHP product limits; these are not generalized to other models.

facts.statement: 차압식 액면은 액주 정수압에서 높이를 환산하므로 유체 비중/밀도 변화가 정확도에 영향을 주며 보상이 필요할 수 있다. 비접촉 radar는 표면 echo를 이용하고 제조사 자료는 매질 밀도변화가 정확도에 영향을 주지 않는다고 설명하지만, echo와 설치조건은 별도 검토한다. GWR은 probe를 따라 진행한 펄스가 유전율 경계에서 반사되는 원리이므로 매질의 유전율과 probe/application 조건을 확인한다. 이 원리 차이만으로 보편적 우열을 단정하지 않는다.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Differential Pressure Level Transmitter / Rosemount 3051S DP Level Measurement
verification_refs.locator: How DP level works; density compensation FAQ
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that DP level uses the pressure difference due to liquid head and specific gravity and that density change may require compensation for accurate level measurement.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Non-Contacting Radar Transmitters
verification_refs.locator: Measurement principle and changing media density feature statement
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes non-contact radar echo measurement and states that changing media density does not affect accuracy for the cited Rosemount product family; this is not generalized to every instrument or installation.

verification_refs.citation: Endress+Hauser, Guided radar level measurement
verification_refs.locator: Guided pulse propagation along probe and reflection at dielectric discontinuity
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that guided radar pulses travel along the probe and part of the pulse is reflected at the medium surface because of a change in relative dielectric constant.

facts.statement: Endress+Hauser Micropilot FMR56/FMR57 pulsed time-of-flight radar emits radar pulses from the antenna, receives them after reflection at the product surface, and uses the round-trip time of flight to determine the distance from the reference point to the surface.

verification_refs.citation: Endress+Hauser, Micropilot FMR56/FMR57 Technical Information TI01042F/00/EN/11.25-0
verification_refs.locator: §Function and system design—Measuring principle, p. 7
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manual says the ToF device measures from its process-connection reference point to the product surface; radar pulses are emitted by the antenna, reflected at the surface, and received again; distance is proportional to pulse time of flight.

facts.statement: For Endress+Hauser Micropilot FMR56/FMR57, measured distance D is referenced to the configured measurement reference point and level is calculated as L=E−D, where E is the entered empty calibration distance. The reference point and tank datum must therefore be consistently defined in calibration.

verification_refs.citation: Endress+Hauser, Micropilot FMR56/FMR57 Technical Information TI01042F/00/EN/11.25-0
verification_refs.locator: §Function and system design—Measuring principle, p. 7; setup parameters p. 7
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manual defines reference point R, empty calibration E, measured distance D and level L, and explicitly gives L=E−D. The same configured reference point is used for the measured distance and empty calibration.

facts.statement: Non-contact radar level measurement transmits microwave signals from an antenna toward a liquid or bulk-solid surface and receives the reflected signal; microwave radar is electromagnetic-wave sensing, not acoustic-wave sensing.

verification_refs.citation: VEGA, Non-contact radar level measurement
verification_refs.locator: How does non-contact radar level measurement work?
verification_refs.supports_claim: VEGA states that the radar antenna transmits microwaves toward the measured product, the product surface reflects them, and the antenna receives them; application covers liquids and solids. Microwave radiation is electromagnetic radiation, distinguishing it from acoustic ultrasonic sensing.

facts.statement: For FMCW radar, the transmitted continuous-wave frequency is swept over time; for a linear sweep over bandwidth Δf during sweep time T_s, the sweep slope is S=Δf/T_s.

verification_refs.citation: Endress+Hauser, Micropilot NMR81 Technical Information TI01252G/00/EN/07.23-0
verification_refs.locator: §Function and system design—Measuring principle, p. 5
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manual describes FMCW as a continuously varying frequency wave, modulated as a sawtooth between f1 and f2, and identifies the known slope k of the frequency modulation. For a linear segment, slope equals frequency span divided by elapsed sweep time.

facts.statement: At normal incidence from air into a lossless, nonmagnetic dielectric with relative permittivity ε_r, the electric-field amplitude reflection coefficient is Γ=(1−√ε_r)/(1+√ε_r), and its magnitude is |Γ|=(√ε_r−1)/(√ε_r+1). This ideal boundary coefficient is not by itself a complete field echo-strength prediction.

verification_refs.citation: Normal-incidence Fresnel reflection derived from tangential E/H boundary conditions
verification_refs.locator: Γ=(η₂−η₁)/(η₂+η₁); η₁≈η₀, η₂=η₀/√ε_r
verification_refs.supports_claim: Tangential-field continuity at a planar normal-incidence boundary gives Γ_E=(η₂−η₁)/(η₂+η₁). For air η₁≈η₀ and a lossless nonmagnetic dielectric η₂=η₀/√ε_r, so Γ_E=(1−√ε_r)/(1+√ε_r); taking absolute value gives (√ε_r−1)/(√ε_r+1). The derivation applies only to the stated ideal boundary conditions and does not alone predict installed radar echo strength.

facts.statement: For a stationary reflector and an ideal linear FMCW sweep with slope S=B/T_s, the transmit/echo frequency difference is f_b=Sτ; combining this with the round-trip propagation delay gives D=v_g f_b/(2S)=v_g f_b T_s/(2B). Real measurement depends on chirp linearity, signal processing and propagation speed along the gas path.

verification_refs.citation: Endress+Hauser, Micropilot NMR81 Technical Information TI01252G/00/EN/07.23-0
verification_refs.locator: §Function and system design—Measuring principle, p. 5
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manual gives Δf=kΔt, states Δt is round-trip transit time and D=cΔt/2, and identifies c as wave propagation speed; combining these with k=B/T_s yields the stated ideal stationary-target distance formula.

verification_refs.citation: Texas Instruments, AWR1243 Sensor: Highly Integrated 76–81-GHz Radar Front-End for Emerging ADAS Applications
verification_refs.locator: §Highly linear chirp generation, precise and repeatable, pp. 5–6
verification_refs.supports_claim: TI states FMCW chirp linearity impacts estimated range accuracy, nonlinear chirps smear the FFT peak and cause range inaccuracy, and signal processing is used to estimate range. This corroborates the stated need to account for real-device chirp and processing effects; the E+H manual supplies propagation-speed dependence.

facts.statement: Industrial guided-wave radar (GWR) uses TDR: low-power, nanosecond-scale high-frequency pulses propagate along a conductive probe (rod, cable or coaxial form), reflect at the product-surface dielectric/impedance discontinuity, and the instrument uses round-trip time of flight to determine distance. This probe-guided arrangement is distinct from free-space FMCW transmission and beat-frequency processing.

verification_refs.citation: Endress+Hauser, Levelflex M FMP40 Operating Instructions BA243F/00/en
verification_refs.locator: §11.3.1 Measuring principle, p. 116
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manual identifies the measurement as ToF/TDR, describes high-frequency pulses injected into and led along a probe, reflection at the product surface, electronic evaluation, and distance proportional to impulse round-trip time.

verification_refs.citation: Endress+Hauser, Relative Thickness I—White Paper on measuring emulsions in dehydration processes WP01077F/00/EN/01.18
verification_refs.locator: Guided radar technology section
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes guided radar as TDR using low-power nanosecond pulses guided along a probe, surface reflection and conversion of the pulse time difference to distance; notes propagation speed changes in fluid according to relative permittivity.

verification_refs.citation: VEGA, VEGAFLEX 81 TDR sensor for continuous level and interface measurement of liquids
verification_refs.locator: Application area
verification_refs.supports_claim: VEGA lists cable, rod and coaxial sensor variants for its guided-wave TDR instrument.

verification_refs.citation: Endress+Hauser, Micropilot NMR81 Technical Information TI01252G/00/EN/07.23-0
verification_refs.locator: §Function and system design—Measuring principle, p. 5
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes the separate Micropilot FMCW method as continuous-wave emission with frequency sweep and frequency-difference processing, supporting the stated distinction from probe-guided TDR.

facts.statement: Radar commissioning should compare the displayed reference distance and calculated level with known actual values, inspect the echo/envelope curve and signal quality, and use model-supported false-echo mapping or threshold/range settings to suppress vessel interference without masking the true level. Tracking and diagnostics are model-specific and should be configured for the process; they are not interchangeable across products.

verification_refs.citation: Endress+Hauser, Micropilot M FMR245 FOUNDATION Fieldbus Operating Instructions BA00253F/EN/13.11
verification_refs.locator: Commissioning functions 008 and 051–052, p. 54
verification_refs.supports_claim: Function 008 displays measured distance from the reference point and calculated level for comparison with actual values; function 051 triggers interference-echo mapping based on comparison with actual distance and maps only up to the selected endpoint.

verification_refs.citation: Endress+Hauser, Micropilot S FMR531 HART/4–20 mA Operating Instructions BA207F/EN/04.09
verification_refs.locator: §6.6.1 Envelope curve with FieldCare, p. 65
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manual recommends evaluating the envelope curve after basic setup, displays signal and quality-related curves, and explains that weak level echoes or strong interference echoes can be addressed by sensor orientation.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 5408 Non-Contacting Radar Level Transmitter product documentation
verification_refs.locator: Smart Echo Supervision and Signal Quality Metrics feature descriptions
verification_refs.supports_claim: For the 5408 product specifically, Emerson says echo supervision tracks echoes and distinguishes obstruction echoes from the product surface, and signal-quality diagnostics alert operators to antenna coating or buildup. This is not generalized to every model.

verification_refs.citation: Endress+Hauser, Micropilot FMR67 Technical Information FY01056F/EN/01.21
verification_refs.locator: Commissioning settings: envelope curve, mapping threshold/window and echo fine adjustment
verification_refs.supports_claim: Lists model-specific envelope-curve, mapping threshold/window and echo fine-adjustment parameters, supporting that these settings are product-specific rather than universal constants.

facts.statement: For a given antenna beam angle, the illuminated footprint grows with distance according to beam geometry; a larger aperture generally produces a narrower radar beam and can reduce interception by tank internals. Objects such as nozzles, walls, agitators or other structures within/near the beam can produce disturbing echoes, so mounting and the actual beam path must be checked for the selected device.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 5408 and 5408:SIS Reference Manual 00809-0100-4408
verification_refs.locator: §3.3.3 Antenna size and §3.3.5 Non-metallic tanks
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manual states that a larger antenna concentrates the beam, increases antenna gain and weak-echo margin, produces a smaller beam angle and reduces interference from tank internals; nearby objects outside a tank may also cause disturbing echoes and should be kept outside the beam where possible.

verification_refs.citation: Conical beam geometry
verification_refs.locator: Circular footprint diameter d=2R tan(θ/2) for beam angle θ and range R
verification_refs.supports_claim: For a conical beam with fixed full angle θ, a plane perpendicular to the beam at distance R is intersected by a circle of diameter d=2R tan(θ/2); therefore the illuminated footprint increases with range for fixed beam angle.

verification_refs.citation: Endress+Hauser, Micropilot M FMR245 FOUNDATION Fieldbus Operating Instructions BA00253F/EN/13.11
verification_refs.locator: Commissioning function 051, p. 54
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manual describes interference echoes and false-echo mapping in the tank installation and directs the installer to compare measured distance with the actual product-surface distance before suppressing echoes.

facts.statement: For a free-space pulse radar, one-way distance is D=v_gτ/2, where τ is the round-trip echo delay and v_g is propagation speed along the gas/vapor path; in ordinary air v_g is close to c₀. High-pressure or dense polar vapor can change propagation speed, so the correction need is process-gas-specific rather than universally zero.

verification_refs.citation: Endress+Hauser, Micropilot FMR56/FMR57 Technical Information TI01042F/00/EN/11.25-0
verification_refs.locator: §Function and system design—Measuring principle, p. 7
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manufacturer defines distance from reference point to product surface from radar-pulse time of flight and uses the round-trip factor one half (D=c·t/2) for the cited pulse radar.

verification_refs.citation: Endress+Hauser, Radar level measurement in high temperature and pressure applications
verification_refs.locator: Speed of radar signals; change in speed in steam
verification_refs.supports_claim: The technical note states radar propagation speed is affected by the gas phase's pressure and temperature depending on dielectric polarization; hydrocarbon vapors may have little effect while polar steam can produce substantial speed change. This supports evaluating the actual gas/vapor rather than assuming every process gas behaves like ordinary air.

verification_refs.citation: Round-trip time-of-flight distance calculation
verification_refs.locator: D=(v_g τ)/2 for a pulse traversing the path to the reflector and back
verification_refs.supports_claim: If a pulse travels at path speed v_g for round-trip elapsed time τ over a stationary one-way distance D, total path length is 2D=v_gτ; solving gives D=v_gτ/2. The path speed must match the actual gas/vapor path.

facts.statement: For an ideal linear FMCW sweep of bandwidth B, the conventional two-target range resolution is approximately ΔR=v_g/(2B). This physical ability to separate nearby reflectors is distinct from single-target measurement error/accuracy and repeatability, and should not be equated with an FFT display/bin interval (which can change with observation and FFT settings without changing transmitted bandwidth). Range-estimation accuracy is affected by SNR, frequency/phase estimation, chirp linearity and the measurement setup/calibration.

verification_refs.citation: Texas Instruments, Intro to mmWave Sensing: FMCW Radars—Module 1: Range Estimation
verification_refs.locator: Range estimation and range-resolution summary
verification_refs.supports_claim: TI derives the separation condition for two distinct range peaks and concludes that range resolution is c/(2B), depending on swept chirp bandwidth; it distinguishes RF sweep bandwidth from IF sampling bandwidth.

verification_refs.citation: JCGM 200:2012 International Vocabulary of Metrology (VIM), entries 2.13 and 2.21
verification_refs.locator: 2.13 Measurement accuracy; 2.21 Measurement repeatability
verification_refs.supports_claim: VIM defines accuracy as closeness of agreement with a true quantity value and repeatability as precision under repeatability conditions; neither is the two-reflector resolving capability defined for radar range resolution.

verification_refs.citation: Infineon, FMCW Radar Digital Signal Processing—Training Handout
verification_refs.locator: Range-frequency estimation and FFT spectral resolution
verification_refs.supports_claim: The handout derives FFT spectral-bin spacing from sampling and NFFT, then derives radar range resolution from the minimum resolvable IF-frequency difference and transmitted sweep bandwidth. Thus numerical FFT-bin spacing and physical two-target resolving capability are related but not generally interchangeable; FFT padding can alter displayed bin interval without altering the transmitted waveform bandwidth.

verification_refs.citation: The Role of Millimeter-Waves in the Distance Measurement Accuracy of an FMCW Radar Sensor, Sensors 2019
verification_refs.locator: Frequency/phase estimation method and SNR/linearity discussion
verification_refs.supports_claim: The study reports that frequency- and phase-estimation methods improve distance accuracy, estimator variance depends on SNR and sample count, and FMCW ramp linearity critically influences range accuracy.

verification_refs.citation: Endress+Hauser, Micropilot NMR81 Technical Information TI01252G/00/EN/07.23-0
verification_refs.locator: Measuring reference point and calibration/configuration description
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manufacturer defines the measurement reference point and configured distance/empty calibration; commissioning must use consistent installation reference geometry, so setup/calibration affects reported level distance.

facts.statement: Low-permittivity or poorly reflecting products can yield weak radar surface echoes and reduce usable range. Application assessment should consider range, actual surface/solids condition, antenna gain and orientation, interference/noise level and the remaining echo margin; a single dielectric threshold alone does not guarantee success or failure.

verification_refs.citation: Endress+Hauser, Micropilot FMR57 free-space radar product information
verification_refs.locator: Application limits
verification_refs.supports_claim: For the cited FMR57, Endress+Hauser lists reduced maximum range for low dielectric constant, poor reflection properties, angle of repose, extremely loose low-bulk-weight solids, and buildup. This supports checking actual media and surface condition rather than applying one universal range.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 5408 and 5408:SIS Reference Manual 00809-0100-4408
verification_refs.locator: §3.3.3 Antenna size; §3.3.4 Antenna inclination
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manual states higher antenna gain improves margin for weak surface echoes, a larger aperture reduces beam angle/interference, and slight inclination toward a solids surface slope may improve a weak echo.

verification_refs.citation: Endress+Hauser, Micropilot S FMR531 HART/4–20 mA Operating Instructions BA207F/EN/04.09
verification_refs.locator: §6.6.1 Envelope curve with FieldCare, p. 65; §9.4 orientation and echo quality
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manufacturer recommends reviewing the envelope curve after setup, reports echo quality as indication of whether a sufficiently large measuring signal is obtained, and describes orientation adjustment to increase useful echo or reduce interference.

verification_refs.citation: Received echo-to-noise margin definition
verification_refs.locator: Echo margin is received useful-echo level relative to receiver noise/interference threshold
verification_refs.supports_claim: Detection reliability depends on the useful echo exceeding the receiver's noise and interference floor by a sufficient margin. Therefore range and signal/noise conditions must be considered with reflectivity and antenna gain; this is a link-budget condition, not a universal dielectric cutoff.

facts.statement: Radar installation geometry must follow the selected antenna's minimum nozzle diameter and maximum nozzle height/recess guidance; long or narrow nozzles, a recessed antenna, and objects in the beam can introduce interference or reduce the usable upper range. Emerson's cited 5408 guidance aligns liquid-service antennas perpendicular to the product surface and permits a slight parabolic-antenna tilt toward a sloped solids surface when the echo is weak. These are model/application instructions, not universal dimensions or a single alignment rule for every radar.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 5408 and 5408:SIS Reference Manual 00809-0100-4408
verification_refs.locator: §3.3.3–3.3.4 Antenna size/inclination; nozzle requirement tables, pp. 20–23
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manual gives model/antenna-specific minimum nozzle diameters and maximum heights, identifies the accuracy limitation near recessed nozzles, says objects inside a process-seal nozzle may affect measurement, directs perpendicular alignment for liquid surface, and allows slight parabolic-antenna inclination toward a weak-echo solids slope.

verification_refs.citation: Endress+Hauser, Micropilot FMR51/FMR52 Technical Information TI01040F/EN/10.20
verification_refs.locator: Mounting in nozzles, p. 44
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manual tabulates antenna-specific maximum nozzle heights and diameter limits, notes restrictions for longer nozzles, requires a smooth burr-free end and mapping if the antenna is recessed, and states antenna extensions can create near-range interference echoes and reduce maximum measurable level.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 5408 Reference Manual 00809-0100-4408
verification_refs.locator: §7.5.2 Handling disturbances at top of tank, p. 137
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manual identifies disturbing echoes from tank nozzles and prescribes review of the echo curve and model-specific amplitude threshold endpoints to manage them.

facts.statement: Product buildup on a non-contact radar antenna can create disturbing echoes and impair level tracking. Manufacturer guidance recommends checking the echo curve and cleaning the antenna; air purge is an option on compatible models. For heavy condensation or aggressive service, select an antenna/process-seal design rated for that application; insulation and heat tracing are documented countermeasures for sulfur-vapor service, not universal requirements. Signal-quality diagnostics can support condition-based preventive maintenance.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 5408 and 5408:SIS Reference Manual 00809-0100-4408
verification_refs.locator: §7.5.2 and troubleshooting, pp. 107–108
verification_refs.supports_claim: For the cited transmitter, product buildup on the antenna is listed as a cause of level stuck high; the manual recommends using the false-echo suppression function where appropriate, analyzing the echo curve/thresholds, cleaning the antenna, or using a model with an air-purging connection.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 5408 Non-Contacting Radar Level Transmitter product information
verification_refs.locator: Key features and application description
verification_refs.supports_claim: Emerson specifies a process-seal antenna for heavy-condensation/aggressive-media applications and Signal Quality Metrics that alert to possible antenna coating or buildup so preventive maintenance can be scheduled.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Level Measurement Solutions for Sulfur Pits
verification_refs.locator: Accurate Level Measurement in Heavy Vapors
verification_refs.supports_claim: For sulfur-vapor service, Emerson recommends insulating and heat-tracing the nozzle to reduce sulfur condensation/buildup, avoiding tall nozzles where possible, and using signal-quality metrics to determine when cleaning is needed.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 5400 Level Transmitter Product Data Sheet 00813-0100-4026
verification_refs.locator: Solids applications—Air purging
verification_refs.supports_claim: The datasheet describes an air-purge connection to prevent antenna clogging in extremely dusty applications and gives model-specific air supply guidance; it does not establish purge as a universal radar requirement.

facts.statement: Radar level measurements can contain interference echoes from tank internals such as pipes, filling nozzles, agitator blades, and other reflectors. In some geometries, a signal reflected from the product surface can reflect again from the tank roof or another strong reflector and return as a multiple-reflection echo; wall-reflected multipath can also broaden the received response. These effects can interfere with the surface echo or reduce measurement accuracy, but their occurrence and magnitude are geometry- and device-dependent.

verification_refs.citation: KROHNE, Fundamentals of Radar Technology for Level Gauging, 4th edition (revised and expanded), by Dr.-Ing. Detlef Brumbi
verification_refs.locator: §8.4 Interference, pp. 46–47
verification_refs.supports_claim: KROHNE identifies pipes, filling nozzles, agitator blades and other internals as possible interference reflectors; describes surface-to-tank-cover/strong-reflector multiple reflections and wall-reflected multipath; and explains their potential to distort the echo pattern or reduce measurement accuracy.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Rosemount 5408 and 5408:SIS Reference Manual 00809-0100-4408
verification_refs.locator: §7.5.2 Suppressing false echoes, p. 134
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manual states that stationary objects with horizontal surfaces can generate strong false echoes and that echoes can interfere with the product-surface echo; it advises identifying objects against tank drawings/inspection before suppressing them.

facts.statement: Microwave radar propagation is generally less dependent on the carrier gas than ultrasonic sound velocity is on gas composition and temperature. For ordinary air in typical tank heights, propagation and attenuation corrections are often small; however, propagation velocity depends on gas, pressure, and temperature, while dense pressurized vapor such as ammonia can strongly attenuate some radar bands. Condensation or deposits on the antenna can also produce interference reflections. The effect must therefore be assessed for the actual gas, pressure, temperature, frequency band, and antenna condition rather than treated as universally zero.

verification_refs.citation: KROHNE, Fundamentals of Radar Technology for Level Gauging, 4th edition (revised and expanded), by Dr.-Ing. Detlef Brumbi
verification_refs.supports_claim: The handbook contrasts ultrasonic sound-velocity dependence on gas composition/temperature with radar microwave’s near-independence from carrier medium; quantifies small ordinary-air effects for typical tanks; states propagation rate depends on gas, pressure, and temperature and can require correction at high pressure; identifies pressure-dependent dense ammonia vapor as a severe attenuation case for X-band; and lists condensation/deposits as possible interference reflectors.

verification_refs.citation: Endress+Hauser, Radar measurement in the presence of pressure and gas layers (EHtalkline 82)
verification_refs.locator: Pressure and gas-layer effects
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manufacturer explains that gas pressure/temperature and dielectric properties can affect propagation, with polar steam potentially more significant than common hydrocarbon vapor; effects depend on gas and operating conditions.

facts.statement: The received-power distance dependence is not the same for every radar reflector. KROHNE's level-radar treatment distinguishes a reflector large enough to fill the beam, for which received power in a large-area tank is approximated as decreasing with distance squared, from a reflector smaller than the beam, for which its effective radar cross-section produces the fourth-power distance dependence. Therefore a point/small-target monostatic radar equation is a link-budget model for limited reflectors, not a universal law for a broad liquid or solids surface; reflector area, antenna gain, propagation loss, and surface reflection properties matter.

verification_refs.citation: KROHNE, Fundamentals of Radar Technology for Level Gauging, 4th edition (revised and expanded), by Dr.-Ing. Detlef Brumbi
verification_refs.locator: §6.5 Modified radar equation, pp. 34–35; §7.5, p. 44
verification_refs.supports_claim: KROHNE separates a large reflecting area that fully intersects the beam from a target smaller than the beam cross-section. It states the large-area tank approximation decreases with distance squared, whereas very tall tanks or interference from small internals use the fourth-power case and effective radar cross-section. Antenna gain, atmospheric attenuation, and surface reflection factor are included.

facts.statement: For a fixed aperture, a shorter wavelength (higher carrier frequency) generally permits higher antenna gain and a narrower beam; a specified beam width may therefore be achieved with a smaller antenna at higher frequency, subject to the actual antenna design. This does not make FMCW range resolution proportional to carrier frequency: ideal two-target range resolution is governed primarily by swept bandwidth, with implementation and signal processing also relevant. Frequency selection is application-specific and should compare range, dielectric/echo conditions, foam and condensation/buildup, nozzle/installation constraints, process limits, integration, and project-specific cost; there is no universally superior carrier frequency.

verification_refs.citation: KROHNE, Fundamentals of Radar Technology for Level Gauging, 4th edition (revised and expanded), by Dr.-Ing. Detlef Brumbi
verification_refs.locator: §5.2 Antenna gain and §5.3 Radiation angle, pp. 24–25
verification_refs.supports_claim: The handbook relates antenna gain to aperture area and wavelength, and beam width to aperture relative to wavelength; smaller wavelength with comparable aperture gives higher gain/narrower beam, while actual antenna geometry remains relevant.

verification_refs.citation: Texas Instruments, Intro to mmWave Sensing: FMCW Radars—Module 1: Range Estimation
verification_refs.locator: Range estimation and range-resolution summary
verification_refs.supports_claim: TI derives ideal two-target range resolution as c/(2B), where B is swept bandwidth, distinguishing the transmitted sweep bandwidth from carrier frequency and IF bandwidth.

verification_refs.citation: Endress+Hauser, Solutions for Continuous Level Measurement in Liquids
verification_refs.locator: §1.1 Frequency overview and §1.3 Radar selection aid, pp. 5–8
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manufacturer compares 6, 26, and 80 GHz families for beam angle/antenna size, turbulence, foam, condensation/buildup, dielectric range, process connections, and pressure/temperature conditions, demonstrating application-dependent tradeoffs rather than universal frequency superiority.

facts.statement: Foam thickness, density, and variability can attenuate or split the apparent level echo, and turbulent or sloped surfaces can change echo strength and the fraction returned toward the antenna. Antenna alignment, frequency/model, and surface geometry therefore matter; for cited solids applications a slight inclination toward a weak-echo slope may help, while liquid-service alignment is normally toward the surface normal. Filtering/tracking can improve echo evaluation, but settings must preserve response to genuine level changes; no single damping or averaging setting is suitable for all processes.

verification_refs.citation: Endress+Hauser, Solutions for Continuous Level Measurement in Liquids
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manufacturer explains that foam type/thickness affects attenuation and echo amplitude, variable foam can cause jumps between foam top and liquid surface, frequency families differ for foam/turbulence, and alignment to liquid-surface normal affects returned echo.

facts.statement: Both pulse and FMCW free-space radar level instruments transmit microwave energy through an antenna and evaluate reflected energy from the product surface to infer distance. A pulse instrument times the returned pulse; an FMCW instrument mixes the received signal with the transmitted sweep and evaluates the resulting beat frequency. The exact transmitter, receiver, processing, level-conversion, and output implementation is instrument-specific.

facts.statement: In a conventional ratio-control arrangement, a measured uncontrolled or wild flow is multiplied by the specified ratio (after required range or engineering-unit scaling) to form the setpoint for a secondary flow controller. If the chosen ratio is defined as controlled flow divided by wild flow, the idealized relation is F_c,sp = R F_w; changing which flow is numerator changes the definition of R, not the control principle.

This is an ideal model relation; practical implementation must be causal, proper, stable where required, and robust enough for model uncertainty and actuator constraints.

facts.statement: Feedforward compensation can act on a measured disturbance before its effect appears in the controlled-variable feedback error, but it depends on disturbance measurement and model accuracy. facts.statement: A typical feedback process-control loop senses a process output, scales or converts the measurement to a process-variable signal, compares it with the setpoint to form error, computes a controller output, and uses a final control element to change a manipulated input to the process. The specific final element need not be a valve; the signal types and functional blocks depend on implementation.

facts.statement: A conventional single-loop feedback controller reacts to setpoint changes and measured process-variable deviations. It does not precompensate a separately measured disturbance unless a feedforward path or equivalent additional logic is configured; measured-disturbance compensation is a distinct feedforward function. This does not mean a single loop cannot reject disturbances: feedback can correct the resulting PV deviation, including effects of unmeasured disturbances.

facts.statement: At a split-range transition, a gap/deadband in which neither final element moves can produce repeated switching or oscillation when the controller output traverses the gap; poor valve sensitivity near seat opening and discontinuous or mismatched process gain across the two ranges can worsen transition behavior. Characterization, carefully chosen overlap or deadband, appropriate tuning, and transition testing are possible remedies, but must be evaluated against the actual process because simultaneous action by different services can itself be undesirable.

facts.statement: In a conventional LVDT, moving the ferromagnetic core toward one secondary increases the magnetic coupling and induced voltage of that secondary while decreasing coupling and induced voltage in the other; moving through the centered null reverses which secondary has the greater induced voltage. In the linear magnetic operating regime this is equivalently described as a position-dependent change in the effective primary-to-secondary mutual inductances.

facts.statement: Temperature can affect an LVDT through both mechanical expansion, which changes the core-to-winding relation and can appear as a false displacement or zero shift, and electrical changes such as increased copper winding resistance/primary impedance and altered primary current, which can change scale factor or span. The magnitude and compensation are construction- and signal-conditioner-specific; TE notes that ordinary-range core magnetic-property effects are small rather than a universal dominant error.

facts.statement: An LVDT senses linear motion through AC-excited transformer windings and the position-dependent magnetic coupling of a movable ferromagnetic core, producing a differential secondary voltage. A strain-gauge displacement instrument instead infers motion from strain in a mechanical member or elastic element via a small resistance change in bonded gauges, commonly converted to voltage with a Wheatstone bridge. The latter requires a mechanical strain-to-displacement relationship and is not the same transduction mechanism as the LVDT.

facts.statement: In a ratio-control setpoint architecture, the desired controlled-stream flow setpoint is obtained by multiplying the measured wild-stream flow by the specified ratio, with both flows represented on a deliberately consistent engineering basis. If the actual ratio is computed by division, for example R=F_controlled/F_wild, its sensitivity to wild-flow measurement error is dR/dF_wild=−F_controlled/F_wild²; thus the calculation becomes ill-conditioned as the denominator approaches zero. Low-flow handling, division limits, or an alternate setpoint-ratio structure may therefore be needed where the operating envelope reaches low wild flow, but no universal cutoff follows from the general principle.

facts.statement: For a normally incident electric field traveling from air into a lossless, nonmagnetic dielectric with relative permittivity εr>1, the field reflection coefficient under the stated incident/reflected-field convention is Γ=(1−√εr)/(1+√εr)<0, corresponding to a 180° phase reversal of the reflected electric field. This physical sign is not a universal rule for the sign of an echo peak displayed by a level transmitter: Endress+Hauser's Levelflex documentation identifies level echoes as positive in its envelope curve while interference echoes may be positive or negative, and Emerson's Rosemount 5300 documentation defines product-specific positive/negative peak thresholds. Echo interpretation must follow the particular transmitter's signal-processing and display convention rather than peak sign alone.

verification_refs.supports_claim: For εr>1 the numerator is negative and denominator positive, so the electric-field coefficient is negative and the reflected field is phase-reversed by 180 degrees under this convention.

These methods change detection behavior: short legitimate pulses may be missed and configured filters add response delay. Therefore thresholds and delays must be selected against both nuisance-transition behavior and the required protective response time; no universal setting is implied.

facts.statement: Functional-safety guidance defines the objective as achieving or maintaining a defined safe state, and control-system guidance describes actuators taking a specified tripped state on loss of signal or utilities. The appropriate state is process- and hazard-dependent: it is not universally fail-closed or de-energized, and in some circumstances power must be maintained to preserve safety.

verification_refs.citation: UK Health and Safety Executive, Functional safety
verification_refs.locator: Functional safety overview; sensors, logic functions, and final elements used to achieve a safe state
verification_refs.supports_claim: HSE describes safety-related systems as detecting dangerous conditions and manipulating final elements such as valves to achieve a safe state; functional safety concerns correct operation of safety-related systems and other risk-reduction measures.

verification_refs.citation: UK Health and Safety Executive, Control systems
verification_refs.locator: Use of fail-safe principles; actuators and failure modes
verification_refs.supports_claim: HSE describes a fail-safe principle in which an actuator takes its tripped state on loss of signal or power, gives held-open spring-return as an example, and says dangerous failure modes must be determined for the overall safety system specification.

verification_refs.citation: UK Health and Safety Executive, Electrical power systems
verification_refs.locator: Fail-safe state on loss of electrical power
verification_refs.supports_claim: HSE says hazardous installations should be designed to fail to a safe state on loss of power, but explicitly notes that in some circumstances electrical power may need to be maintained to ensure safety.

facts.statement: A control sequence can be specified as a state-transition function from the current state and the complete evaluated input/event set to a next state. For deterministic behavior, the design must make the result unique for each evaluated state/input combination; time state, simultaneous conditions, and transition priority cannot remain implicit. IEC 61131-3 defines SFC programming elements, but does not by itself guarantee that every application chart is deterministic.

verification_refs.citation: PLCopen, Software Construction Guidelines: Structuring with SFC, v1.0
verification_refs.locator: § State diagram representation and formal definition, p. 45
verification_refs.supports_claim: PLCopen represents finite-state automata with a defined state set, event set, initial/final states, and transition tuples of the form <current state, enabling event, next state>. This supports specifying state transitions as mappings; uniqueness requires the application to resolve competing transitions and include all relevant state in the evaluated inputs.

verification_refs.citation: IEC 61131-3:2025, Programmable controllers – Part 3: Programming languages
verification_refs.locator: Official scope and description
verification_refs.supports_claim: IEC states that SFC elements are defined for structuring the internal organization of PLC programs and function blocks; the catalog description does not claim that every SFC application automatically has deterministic behavior.

facts.statement: Sequence-control implementations commonly model process operation as ordered or branched steps/states whose actions are executed while active and whose transitions advance when their conditions are satisfied. Documented industrial SFC/sequencer implementations also provide step timers or timeout/fault handling. This supports the Topic Pack's step/action/completion/time-supervision concept, but exact state structure, timer policy, and fault response are application- and implementation-specific rather than mandatory in every sequence.

verification_refs.citation: ISA InTech, Automating procedures in the continuous process
verification_refs.locator: State-based control, transitions, implementation modules, steps and verification criteria
verification_refs.supports_claim: ISA describes states as defined process phases, transitions as condition-driven, implementation modules as containing steps and criteria to determine whether the intended result was achieved, and SFC steps as states that call associated tasks.

verification_refs.citation: Rockwell Automation Library of Process Objects Reference Manual, PROCES-RM006E-EN-P, Sequencer Object (P_Seq)
verification_refs.locator: § Main-Step Configuration, pp. 30-37
verification_refs.supports_claim: Rockwell documents per-step actions based on input conditions, step completion inputs, branching, and a step-fault timer that triggers a fault when completion exceeds its configured time.

facts.statement: ISA process-control guidance describes permissive logic as allowing a device to start or stop in automatic mode based on a set of conditions. Therefore a permissive is a condition gate for an operation; how many conditions are required, their Boolean combination, and whether the gate applies to start or a later transition are specified by the particular application. No universal permissive expression is asserted.

verification_refs.citation: ISA InTech, Passive loopback process simulation
verification_refs.locator: Device control logic attributes: permissive logic
verification_refs.supports_claim: ISA describes permissive logic as allowing start/stop in automatic mode based on a set of conditions.

verification_refs.citation: Siemens, Advanced Permissive Sequencing – Non-linear logic with SIMATIC S7 Safety Matrix, Entry ID 109770865
verification_refs.supports_claim: The example sequence requires startup release and an inactive sequence state before accepting its start signal; the document makes this specific interlock logic an application example rather than a universal Boolean formula.

facts.statement: In ISA's process-control example, an interlock is control logic that automatically shuts off a motor in an emergency, whereas a permissive condition allows an automatic start/stop action when specified conditions are met. Siemens' control-library example likewise uses an active interlock to place an object in its configured safe position and inhibit further state changes. These examples distinguish action/inhibit logic from alarm annunciation alone, but exact interlock semantics and action are application- and product-specific.

verification_refs.citation: ISA InTech, Passive loopback process simulation
verification_refs.locator: Device control logic attributes: interlock and permissive logic
verification_refs.supports_claim: ISA describes interlock logic as automatically shutting off a motor in emergencies and permissive logic as enabling operation under a set of conditions.

verification_refs.citation: Siemens, SIMATIC Control Function Library, System Manual, 09/2022
verification_refs.locator: §4.1 Common Blocks, Interlocks, p. 36
verification_refs.supports_claim: Siemens documents that an active interlock moves the function block to its configured safe position and prevents state changes.

facts.statement: In Siemens' documented Safety Matrix sequence example, a protection trip resets active effect steps and sequence states according to the application safety requirements; the example requires acknowledgement with the sequence stopped and no active trip criterion to prevent an automatic restart. This demonstrates a configured protective action overriding normal sequence progress and a possible latched/acknowledged reset policy. It does not establish one universal trip priority, stop state, latching rule, or manual-reset requirement for every process.

verification_refs.citation: Siemens, Advanced Permissive Sequencing – Non-linear logic with SIMATIC S7 Safety Matrix, Entry ID 109770865
verification_refs.supports_claim: The Siemens example resets sequence effect steps on protection trip and requires trip acknowledgement under defined stopped/no-active-trip conditions to prevent automatic restart.

facts.statement: A Rockwell process sequencer separates commanded outputs from configured input feedback: the inputs monitor device or logic signals and determine whether the desired state or combination of states has been achieved to end a step. Its step-fault timer can flag when step completion exceeds the configured time. This supports feedback-qualified completion and timeout detection; distinguishing a mechanical jam from a failed or disagreeing sensor requires additional application-specific diagnostics and is not guaranteed by the sequencer inputs and timer alone.

verification_refs.citation: Rockwell Automation Library of Process Objects Reference Manual, PROCES-RM006E-EN-P, Sequencer Object (P_Seq)
verification_refs.locator: § Functional Description, p. 9; § Main-Step Configuration, pp. 30-37
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manual states that sequencer inputs monitor device or logic signals to determine whether desired states have been achieved and end a step; it also documents a configurable step-fault timer for completion exceeding its set time.

verification_refs.citation: ISA InTech, Passive loopback process simulation
verification_refs.locator: Device control logic attributes and practical pump example
verification_refs.supports_claim: ISA describes monitoring motor auxiliary-contact feedback with a timer to check that the motor starts within a reasonable time, and uses delayed auxiliary-contact feedback to represent the physical device response.

facts.statement: SFC implementations define action behavior relative to step activation and deactivation. Siemens SIMATIC SFC documents initialization (first execution), cyclic processing, and termination (last execution), while noting that initialization or termination may be omitted. Rockwell SFC qualifiers similarly define actions that run while a step is active, pulse on activation or deactivation, or remain stored until reset. Rockwell's process sequencer also leaves a digital output at its previous state when that output is not configured in a step. Therefore action lifecycle and output release/retention must be explicit in the chosen controller implementation to avoid unintended retained commands; not every step must implement all entry/ongoing/exit phases.

verification_refs.citation: Siemens, SIMATIC SFC for S7 Sequential Function Chart, A5E00345250-01
verification_refs.supports_claim: Siemens describes initialization, cyclic execution and termination phases; step entry/exit and transition behavior; and notes initialization or termination may be absent. Its example demonstrates predecessor termination and successor initialization behavior.

verification_refs.citation: Rockwell Automation, Studio 5000 Logix Designer Online Help, Action and Boolean Action
verification_refs.locator: Qualifier table, N/P1/S/P/PO/R rows
verification_refs.supports_claim: Rockwell defines qualifiers for actions that start/stop with step activation, execute on activation or deactivation, or remain stored until reset.

verification_refs.citation: Rockwell Automation Library of Process Objects Reference Manual, PROCES-RM006E-EN-P, Sequencer Object (P_Seq)
verification_refs.locator: § Configuring the Sequence Steps, p. 35
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manual explicitly states that digital outputs not configured in a step remain at their previous states.

facts.statement: ISA's measurement text describes 1oo2 voting as initiating a trip when either input reaches its trip setting, which improves tolerance of a missed unsafe measurement but increases susceptibility to a spurious trip; 2oo3 requires two of three measurements to indicate the unsafe condition and is presented as a way to tolerate one measurement problem. Voting architecture therefore trades false-trip behavior against failure-to-trip protection and must be assessed for the particular safety function; the cited examples do not establish a universally best vote.

verification_refs.citation: Gregory K. McMillan, Essentials of Modern Measurements and Final Elements, Chapter 1: Essentials
verification_refs.locator: §1.5.1, discussion of 1oo2 and 2oo3 voting, printed pp. 41–42
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains the one-out-of-two trip behavior and false-trip tradeoff, and two-out-of-three response to measurement faults; does not declare one architecture universally optimal.

facts.statement: In Rockwell PlantPAx PINTLK, the first interlock condition raised is marked first-out, but if multiple conditions are raised in the same controller scan, all of those conditions are marked first-out. Thus a first-out display does not necessarily resolve a unique physical chronological cause when events are simultaneous at the implementation's scan resolution.

verification_refs.citation: Rockwell Automation, PlantPAx Process Interlocks (PINTLK), Studio 5000 Logix Designer documentation
verification_refs.edition_or_version: Studio 5000 Logix Designer v38.02 documentation; accessed 2026-10-11
verification_refs.locator: First Out section
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that the first raised condition is marked first-out and that multiple conditions raised in the same scan are all marked first-out.

facts.statement: Siemens SIMATIC S7 SFC defines a transition as conditions for passing control from one step to the next; multiple conditions can be combined with Boolean operators, and the Boolean result determines whether the next step is enabled. This supports modeling an SFC transition with explicit logical guards, while the exact condition set and execution semantics remain application- and platform-specific.

verification_refs.citation: Siemens, SFC for SIMATIC S7 (V9.0 SP7), Programming and Operating Manual A5E41356228-AG
verification_refs.locator: §5.6.4 What is a transition?, printed p. 43
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines transition conditions, Boolean combination, and enabling of the next step based on the logical result.

facts.statement: Rockwell PlantPAx PINTLK permits bypass only when the input is configured as bypassable, bypass is requested, and the downstream equipment instruction reports bypass enabled. Its documentation says Engineering typically configures which interlocks may be bypassed and Maintenance selects among those permitted options. This is a product-specific example of controlled bypass configuration and role separation, not proof that every system implements the same approvals, duration limit, or compensating measures.

verification_refs.citation: Rockwell Automation, PlantPAx Process Interlocks (PINTLK), Studio 5000 Logix Designer documentation
verification_refs.edition_or_version: Studio 5000 Logix Designer v38.02 documentation; accessed 2026-10-11
verification_refs.locator: Interlock Bypass section
verification_refs.supports_claim: Specifies bypassability configuration, bypass request, downstream bypass enable, and typical Engineering/Maintenance allocation of configuration and selection.

facts.statement: For the documented Fisher/Emerson sliding-stem globe-valve constructions, balanced plug geometry routes downstream pressure to act on both plug faces and thereby reduces, but does not necessarily eliminate, static unbalance force; a plug-to-cage seal can also limit upstream-to-downstream bypass leakage in the documented cage-style design. Actuator force assessment must use the construction-specific net unbalance area and shutoff differential pressure, together with required seat load, packing friction, and any application/construction-specific forces. The balanced/unbalanced label alone therefore does not establish zero residual force, shutoff class, or actuator size.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook—Refining, Chapter 3: Available Technologies
verification_refs.locator: §3.1.1, Balanced-Plug Cage-Style Valve Constructions, printed pp. 3-20–3-21
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes plug-to-cage seal limiting leakage, downstream pressure acting on both plug faces to reduce static unbalance, smaller actuator possibility, and application-dependent construction choices.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook—Oil and Gas, Chapter 2: Sizing and Selection
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 2, actuator sizing discussion, pp. 2-7–2-9
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines unbalance force from pressure differential and net unbalance area, notes balanced valves retain a small unbalance area, and separates seat-load, packing-friction, and application/construction force components.

facts.statement: Emerson/Fisher classifies control-valve designs by closure-member motion: sliding-stem designs move the closure member linearly into or out of the seating surface, while rotary designs rotate a ball, disk, or eccentric plug in the flow stream. The rotary shaft positions the closure member, whereas the linear-valve stem connects actuator motion to the closure member. This verifies the motion-based classification and its basic actuator-linkage distinction; it does not assert that motion class alone determines the correct valve, flow characteristic, or actuator sizing.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th ed., Chapter 1: Introduction to Control Valves
verification_refs.locator: §1.2 Sliding-Stem Control Valve Terminology and §1.3 Rotary Control Valve Terminology, printed pp. 18–25
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines linear-motion valve stem as connecting the actuator stem and closure member; describes rotary closures such as balls, disks, and eccentric plugs rotating to vary flow area, and rotary shaft/actuator lever motion.

facts.statement: For the NI LVDT signal-conditioning guidance, the AC excitation carrier is selected at least 10 times higher than the highest expected core-motion frequency so the carrier can be demodulated separately from the mechanical signal. The exact excitation frequency and voltage remain sensor/conditioner-specific and must stay within their specified operating limits; this is not a universal excitation-voltage prescription.

verification_refs.citation: National Instruments, Position & Displacement Measurement with LVDTs
verification_refs.locator: Excitation and phase-sensitive signal-conditioning discussion
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that the LVDT carrier/excitation frequency is generally selected at least 10 times higher than the highest expected core-motion frequency, and describes synchronous demodulation using the primary excitation reference.

verification_refs.citation: Analog Devices, AD698 Universal LVDT Signal Conditioner Data Sheet, Rev. D
verification_refs.locator: Features; excitation output characteristics; application information
verification_refs.supports_claim: Documents a conditioner-specific 20 Hz to 20 kHz oscillator and excitation output limits, supporting that permissible excitation settings are component-specific rather than one universal voltage/frequency value.

facts.statement: IEC 62443-3-2:2020은 IACS의 System under Consideration(SUC)을 정의하고 이를 zones와 conduits로 분할한 뒤 각 zone·conduit의 risk를 평가하고 target security level과 보안요구를 문서화하도록 요구한다.

verification_refs.citation: IEC 62443-3-2:2020, Security for industrial automation and control systems — Part 3-2: Security risk assessment for system design
verification_refs.locator: Official standard scope/requirements summary
verification_refs.supports_claim: IEC states that the standard establishes requirements for defining an IACS SUC, partitioning it into zones and conduits, assessing risk for each, establishing target security levels for each, and documenting security requirements.

facts.statement: An actuator and its linkage must provide the output motion and load form required by the valve: sliding-stem valves require linear stem thrust over the specified travel, while rotary-shaft valves require output torque over their rotation. A linear actuator may operate a rotary valve only through a suitable motion-converting linkage or actuator design, whose coupling and lost motion must be considered.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Actuators, Product Bulletin D103540X012
verification_refs.locator: Actuator Designs; sliding-stem actuators; rotary actuators
verification_refs.supports_claim: States actuator designs are configured for either sliding-stem or rotary bodies using linkages or motion translators; sliding-stem actuators connect rigidly to valve stems, while rotary actuators convert diaphragm/piston linear movement to the rotation required by rotary valves and must couple to the valve drive shaft with limited lost motion.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th ed., Chapter 1: Introduction to Control Valves
verification_refs.locator: §1.2–1.3, sliding-stem and rotary control valve terminology
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines linear valve stem and rotary shaft/actuator lever arrangements, establishing the distinct motion and linkage requirements for sliding-stem and rotary control valves.

facts.statement: A pneumatic rack-and-pinion valve actuator uses rack/pinion engagement to convert piston or rack linear travel into rotary output and is commonly applied to quarter-turn ball, butterfly, and plug valves. Selection must use the specific actuator's output torque throughout the required rotation and direction at available operating pressure, and respect the actuator's maximum operating pressure; these ratings are model- and configuration-specific.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Pneumatic Rack and Pinion Actuators
verification_refs.locator: What is a Rack & Pinion actuator?; Common Rack and Pinion Applications
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains rack-and-pinion conversion of linear rack force into pinion rotation and identifies quarter-turn ball, butterfly, and plug valve automation as common applications.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Bettis, Actuator Selection Procedures, Sheet I
verification_refs.locator: §4.2 Bettis Rack and Pinion, Spring-Return, Fail-Clockwise Actuators; torque selection steps
verification_refs.supports_claim: Requires actuator torque to exceed valve torque at corresponding positions and directions, provides start/end pressure and spring torque ratings, and directs users not to exceed the selected actuator's maximum operating pressure.

facts.statement: A butterfly valve uses a rotating disk for quarter-turn flow control. Fisher/Emerson describes the design as lightweight and compact, particularly in larger sizes, and the handbook notes minimum installation space and economy at larger sizes. Butterfly valves may serve throttling or on/off duty, but application-specific disk/seat design affects control and shutoff behavior; high-performance butterfly designs are not generally intended for precision throttling unless a suitable characterized design is selected.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th ed., Chapter 3: Valve and Actuator Types
verification_refs.locator: §3.1.3.1 Butterfly Valve Bodies
verification_refs.supports_claim: States butterfly bodies require minimum installation space, offer economy particularly in larger sizes and flow capacity per investment dollar, may be used for throttling or on/off control, and require consideration of potentially large operating torque. It distinguishes offset designs and describes the effect of disk/seat geometry on seal life, torque, and shutoff.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th ed., Chapter 10: Isolation Valves
verification_refs.locator: §10.1.11 Butterfly Valves
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes butterfly valves as simple, lightweight, compact, and inexpensive particularly in larger sizes; identifies a quarter-turn circular disk, metal or resilient seating, and flow-regulation capability.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, High Performance Butterfly Valves
verification_refs.locator: What are high performance butterfly valves?; Common Applications
verification_refs.supports_claim: Identifies the rotating disk and quarter-turn operation, high capacity, and use for throttling or isolation; limits general-service HPBV use to applications not requiring precision throttling and notes that characterized contours can expand control range.

facts.statement: A full-port ball valve presents little or no flow restriction when fully open and can permit pigging when it is not attenuated. In throttling service, a full-port ball may rotate through an initial portion of travel before absorbing significant process energy, which can add process-control lag; a reduced-port or attenuated design may be more suitable depending on the required duty. Thus the low-restriction/pigging advantage does not make full-port construction universally best for precision throttling.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th ed., Chapter 3: Valve and Actuator Types
verification_refs.locator: §3.1.3.5 Full-Port Ball Valve Bodies
verification_refs.supports_claim: States full-port ball valves present little or no restriction and allow pigging when not attenuated. It also explains that a full-port ball may rotate 15–20 degrees before absorbing significant energy, which relates to process-control lag, and contrasts reduced-bore/attenuated options for throttling control.

facts.statement: For the Fisher Multiport Flow Selector described in the cited handbook and product manual, a rotating plug selects one of eight inlet lines for diversion/testing through a test outlet while the other seven continue to a common group outlet. The arrangement provides compact selection/testing without interrupting the other lines' production. The cited construction includes a body, bonnet, rotor plug, and actuator, with the bonnet supporting the plug and providing tight sealing; the exact porting and isolation capability must be checked against the selected product configuration rather than generalized to every multiport valve.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th ed., Chapter 3: Valve and Actuator Types
verification_refs.locator: §3.1.3.6 Multi-Port Flow Selector
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes eight input lines, diversion/testing of one line through a rotating plug while the other seven continue to a common outlet, compact selection/testing without interrupting other production, and body/bonnet/rotor plug/actuator construction with tight sealing.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Multiport Flow Selector Instruction Manual D104239X012
verification_refs.locator: Description, p. 2
verification_refs.supports_claim: Specifies eight inlets, one test outlet, one group outlet, and continuous flow during sampling/testing of individual oil wells.

facts.statement: Control-valve screwed/threaded, bolted-flange, and welded end connections form different pipe joints and therefore have different removal/maintenance implications and service limits. The cited Fisher handbook describes screwed ends as common on smaller valves and potentially complicating body removal; flanged valves as readily removable; and welded ends as difficult to remove from the line, with connection design, materials, and applicable pressure-temperature ratings governing suitability. End-connection selection should therefore consider maintainability and piping integrity together with the specified service conditions, not assume a universal preference.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th ed., Chapter 3: Valve and Actuator Types
verification_refs.locator: §3.2.1 Screwed Pipe Threads; §3.2.2 Bolted Gasketed Flanges; §3.2.3 Welded End Connections
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes threaded joints as typically small-valve connections with body-removal maintenance complications and elevated-temperature limitations; flanged valves as readily removable with service limits defined for their flange type; and welded ends as difficult to remove, limited to weldable materials, and available as socket- or butt-weld constructions. It describes distinct sealing geometries and connection-specific service ranges.

facts.statement: Electric valve actuators use an electric motor with gearing to deliver valve output torque or thrust; selection must match the specific valve duty and actuator ratings, including power supply, operating speed, duty/modulation capability, hazardous-area approval, and the required behavior on loss of power. Manufacturer examples include continuous/modulating electric actuators and designs with mechanical, spring, or battery-based fail-safe options, so electric actuation is not limited to applications lacking instrument air. Fail-safe behavior and ratings are product/configuration-specific and must not be assumed from the power source alone.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Bettis TorqPlus Electric Valve Actuator product documentation
verification_refs.locator: Product description and key features
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes geared electric output with torque ratings, weatherproof/explosion-proof housings, open-close, continuous-duty and modulation applications, and a mechanically driven fail-safe option.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Bettis HQ-Series Quarter-turn Electric Valve Actuator product documentation
verification_refs.locator: Key Features; optional battery pack and proportional control unit
verification_refs.supports_claim: Lists a battery pack for emergency fail-safe operation and a modulating proportional control unit with explicitly rated duty cycle and starts per hour, showing that duty and loss-of-power behavior are design-specific.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Biffi, Fail Safe Electric Actuators Model EFS2000v4 Instruction Manual
verification_refs.locator: §2.2 Main parts description
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes a multi-turn electric actuator and epicyclic gear reduction for torque increase, plus a spring-return mechanism that moves the valve to its defined fail-safe condition on an ESD signal or power failure.

facts.statement: Hydraulic valve actuators can provide high thrust/torque, and hydraulic positioning stiffness can be high in an appropriately designed actuator/system; stiffness is not an unconditional property and depends on cylinder geometry, stroke, trapped fluid volume, and system design. Hydraulic systems use a hydraulic power source/control circuit and cylinder or rotary actuator; some fail-safe designs use an accumulator or other stored-energy path to move the valve to a defined safe position after power/supply loss. Hydraulic leakage, fluid condition/contamination, filters, and stored pressure require model-specific inspection and maintenance. These properties and fail-safe circuits are design-specific, not universal to every hydraulic actuator.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Hydraulic Actuators overview
verification_refs.locator: Hydraulic Actuator FAQ: definition, benefits, fail-safe mechanisms
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines hydraulic actuation as conversion of hydraulic energy to mechanical valve motion, identifies high torque/thrust for large/heavy/high-pressure valves, and states that some designs incorporate fail-safe return on power loss or system malfunction.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Bettis, Electro-Hydraulic Operator Installation, Operation and Maintenance Manual VCIOM-15345-EN
verification_refs.locator: §6 Operation, hydraulic circuit component descriptions
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes hydraulic pump/control components, optional accumulator providing hydraulic power, accumulator speed control, pressure relief, and de-energized solenoid action causing spring return to the configured fail-safe position.

verification_refs.citation: HAWE Hydraulik, Stiffness of Actuators
verification_refs.locator: Actuator stiffness discussion for hydraulic motor and cylinder
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that hydraulic actuator stiffness depends on compressed-oil-column effects, actuator dimensions, piston/rod area, stroke, and enclosed pipeline fluid volume; identifies conditions under which a cylinder can be stiff and conditions that reduce stiffness.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Biffi RPHS Hydraulic Actuators Installation, Operation and Maintenance Manual MAN 605 Rev. 4
verification_refs.locator: §5 Maintenance, periodic maintenance and hydraulic pressure discharge warnings
verification_refs.supports_claim: Requires inspection for hydraulic leakage and oil level, filter and condensate servicing where fitted, qualified maintenance, and discharging cylinder/control-unit/accumulator pressure before disassembly.

facts.statement: For the double-ported globe valve construction described by Fisher/Emerson, two flow ports can provide higher capacity than a single-ported body of the same line size, and opposing dynamic forces tend to balance, potentially reducing actuator sizing demand. The two seating interfaces cannot generally be assumed to seat equally at the same time: the cited handbook reports metal-to-metal Class II shutoff as typical, with Class III possible, and PIP explains simultaneous seating as difficult. Therefore force balance is partial and tight shutoff capability is limited relative to the cited single-ported construction; exact leakage class remains design- and test-specific.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th ed., Chapter 3: Valve and Actuator Types
verification_refs.locator: §3.1.1.4 Double-Ported Valve Bodies
verification_refs.supports_claim: States double-ported bodies normally have higher capacity than single-ported bodies of the same line size; dynamic force tends to balance as flow opens one port and closes the other, potentially permitting a smaller actuator; metal-to-metal seating usually provides Class II shutoff, although Class III is possible.

verification_refs.citation: Process Industry Practices, PIP PCECV001, Guidelines for Application of Control Valves, Technical Revision July 2022
verification_refs.edition_or_version: July 2022 technical revision; accessed 2026-10-11 (public mirror of PIP document)
verification_refs.locator: §4.2.2 Post-Guided, items 4–6, printed p. 14
verification_refs.supports_claim: States double-ported valves cannot provide the same shutoff as single-ported valves because seating both plugs simultaneously is nearly impossible (Class II versus Class IV); also describes partial force balancing by opposing differential forces and lower positioning force.

facts.statement: For sliding-stem globe-style control valves, Fisher/Emerson describes distinct cage-, top-, stem-, top-and-bottom-, and port-guiding arrangements, each locating the plug relative to the seat through different guide surfaces. Guiding is required for plug/seat alignment and effective control. Guide choice and condition should account for application side loads and resulting vibration, friction, and wear: Fisher's sourcebook documents guide-surface wear and instability/vibration concerns for particular constructions, while measured globe-valve research establishes that transverse stem loads can be relevant to wear of valve/actuator guidance parts. These effects and the preferable guide style are construction- and service-specific, not a universal ranking.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th ed., Chapter 3: Valve and Actuator Types
verification_refs.locator: §3.6 Valve Plug Guiding
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines cage, top, stem, top-and-bottom, and port guiding geometries and states that accurate guiding is necessary for plug/seat alignment and efficient process-fluid control.

verification_refs.citation: Fisher Controls, Control Valve Sourcebook: Power & Severe Service, 4th ed., Chapter 1 Control Valve Selection
verification_refs.edition_or_version: 2004 fourth edition; accessed 2026-10-11 (public mirror of Fisher sourcebook)
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 1, sections on guiding, wear, and high-pressure-drop liquid-service guidelines
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes plug/cage and post/bushing wear, guide wear leading to seat leakage, side-load support needs, and construction-specific vibration/vertical-instability concerns; notes cage guiding can provide substantial guidance and shielding in described applications.

verification_refs.citation: Jerome Ferrari, Measurement Of The Fluid Flow Load On A Globe Valve Stem Under Various Cavitation Conditions

Response speed, physical dimensions/installation, maintainability, and life-cycle cost may also be decision factors. Their relevance and weighting depend on the process and project; no single valve-actuator type is universally optimal.

facts.statement: Process-control structure selection should consider the control objectives and constraints, available measurements and manipulated variables, relevant disturbance paths and process dynamics, interactions among loops, and implementation/economic constraints such as instrumentation and existing system capabilities. These are engineering selection considerations, not a universal fixed checklist or a claim that every factor has equal weight; the applicable factors and trade-offs depend on the process and project basis.

facts.statement: A piping and instrumentation diagram (P&ID) is a process-flow-diagram representation of the technical realization of a process, using graphical symbols for equipment, connections, and process measurement and control functions. Its content and detail are governed by the applicable diagram standard and project conventions; it communicates functional/documentation information and is not a substitute for every detailed instrument or construction document.

A P&ID represents the technical realization in greater process-connection and measurement/control-function detail. The exact content level depends on the governing standard and project conventions; the distinction is purpose and relative detail, not a claim that every PFD contains the same data or that every P&ID contains every construction detail.

facts.statement: A P&ID is generally a functional schematic of piping, equipment, instruments, and their relationships rather than a scaled physical layout. For physical positioning and construction dimensions, use the applicable plot plan, layout, piping, or construction drawings and project document rules.

The standard also defines dedicated symbols for other connections such as filled-system capillary tubes. These meanings are standard- and project-legend-dependent; line style alone must not be interpreted as a universal code across drawings.

Exact graphic symbols and tag conventions follow the applied ISA edition and project legend.

facts.statement: For DOE nuclear facilities within the scope of DOE-STD-1073-2003, configuration-management assessments compare documented design and system requirements, system documentation such as drawings and procedures, and the physical facility configuration. The documents selected for a specific P&ID review should therefore be those applicable to the system and controlled by the facility's configuration-management process; no fixed universal checklist of every possible engineering register is implied.

The resulting controlled documentation is to be field- and design-verified against the as-built configuration. This is a scoped configuration-management method, not a universal requirement to use one named punch or redline workflow at every site.

The change review should identify affected process-safety information, including P&IDs, and revisions must be made permanent in the applicable drawings and manuals; P&ID updates are therefore part of change control when the change affects their content.

OSHA identifies P&IDs as diagrams that may describe equipment/instrumentation relationships and other relevant information, and expects required P&IDs to be completed before startup; their usefulness depends on keeping affected information current.
