facts.statement: In technical-document terminology, P&ID denotes a piping and instrumentation diagram representing a process system, while PID in control theory denotes proportional-integral-derivative control/controller behavior. The acronym PID is also used by ISO terminology for process and instrumentation diagrams, so the bare string PID alone is ambiguous; identify the meaning from the drawing/document context, explicit expansion, tag/legend, and applicable project convention rather than treating the token by itself as proof of either meaning.

facts.statement: For globe or angle control-valve bodies, the bonnet is the pressure-retaining closure at one end of the body, provides passage for the moving plug stem or shaft, and normally houses the packing box. Bonnet style and trim-access arrangement depend on the valve construction; these functions should not be generalized to rotary bodies that may house packing in the body and use no bonnet.

facts.statement: In multiloop process control, a manipulated variable or final element in one loop can affect other controlled variables, so loop interaction can change closed-loop dynamics and performance. In override/selective structures, multiple controllers may share one actuator, with selector logic granting actuator authority to one controller at a time; control direction, output limits, tracking/anti-windup, and transfer between active controllers must be configured for the actual process so an inactive or saturated controller does not cause windup or a disruptive transition. Pairing, decoupling, or other coordination are options when interaction materially affects performance, not universal requirements for every pair of loops.

facts.statement: In post-guided sliding-stem globe valves, the post/bushing guide supports plug alignment through travel. Fisher documents product-specific post-guided designs that stabilize the plug and reduce vibration and trim wear, while side loads and guide geometry remain construction- and service-dependent. As a mechanical inference, for a rigid plug supported by two guide reactions separated by span L, a transverse force F applied with eccentricity e creates moment M=F·e and a reaction couple of magnitude M/L; therefore guide span and support location can change local guide reaction/contact loading, but do not by themselves determine the externally generated hydraulic side force. This inference does not establish a universal optimum guide length or wear rate.

facts.statement: NIST's production-scheduling review defines scheduling as assigning activities to resources over time and identifies machines, operators, tools, fixtures, and raw materials as resources; relevant constraints include task duration, release/due dates, precedence, transfer/setup times, resource availability, and resource sharing. ISA-95-based operations-management guidance describes dispatching within agreed limits using local availability and current conditions. Microsoft documents finite-capacity scheduling as respecting available/reserved resource capacity and finite-material availability in its product. Together these sources support considering real resource and sequence constraints in a feasible short-term schedule, while dispatch priorities remain a plant policy that should be consistent with governing delivery/priority commitments.

facts.statement: Lean Enterprise Institute defines WIP as items between processing steps and distinguishes buffer stock used to protect downstream customers from short-term demand increases that exceed production capacity; it cautions that inventory should be reduced only after considering variability and upstream capability. Little's Law relates long-run average WIP to throughput rate and time in the system, so under a stable boundary and unchanged throughput, higher average WIP implies longer average flow time. In a documented MIT Sloan case study of one manufacturing division, high WIP occupied floor space, carried cost, delayed quality feedback, and increased cycle time; those observed effects are context-dependent rather than a universal rule that every increase in buffer WIP harms every production system. This supports managing WIP, throughput, cycle/flow time, and buffers together rather than treating these measures as interchangeable.

These sources support feeding actual equipment availability, capability, tooling, and planned downtime into production resource planning. They do not prescribe a universal equipment-maintenance strategy or MTBF/MTTR KPI; those maintenance-policy decisions are outside this production-scheduling fact.

Within that scope the requirements call for Control Plans for Ford parts, traceability of special characteristics and their control approach through the specified FMEA/SCCAF/Control Plan chain, approval for changes to specified inspection frequencies, and current operator work instructions containing reaction steps for nonconformances. The source therefore supports these controls for the defined Ford supplier scope, not a universal requirement that every manufacturer use the same CTQ labels, sampling scheme, document template, or approval route.

facts.statement: NIST/SEMATECH describes a control chart as plotting a quality characteristic against sample number or time, with center/control limits; an out-of-control point or non-random pattern warrants investigation for assignable causes, with the chart's associated out-of-control action plan (OCAP) guiding response. Statistical control limits characterize process behavior and are not the product specification/acceptance limits. A series appearing within limits alone does not establish process stability if it is non-random. Separately, Ford's IATF CSR effective 15 June 2026 requires its suppliers to retain process-control/product-inspection data and reactions to specification-outside readings, prevent nonconforming product shipment, and pursue root-cause correction/prevention within that customer scope. Chart use, signal rules and product containment/disposition remain process/customer-specific; a control-chart signal alone is not proof that a product is nonconforming.

facts.statement: TE Connectivity describes free-core LVDTs with radial clearance and no coil contact, and explains that the LVDT responds primarily to axial core position; its tutorial also distinguishes free-core from guided-core and spring-loaded constructions. NewTek similarly treats alignment and side-load limits as installation considerations, while noting some misalignment need not degrade measurement. Therefore radial misalignment is construction- and magnitude-dependent; the evidence does not support claiming that every radial offset causes zero shift, hysteresis, or repeatability error.

verification_refs.supports_claim: HSE requires procedures to state success/failure criteria and safe test conduct, including management arrangements, operating restrictions and competence; maintenance procedures include post-maintenance reinstatement and proof testing.

facts.statement: A configured Fisher FIELDVUE lock-in-last accessory assembly can retain actuator pressure after loss of adequate supply pressure; the retained valve position depends on actuator exhaust speed and the installed switching/locking arrangement, so this behavior is not inherent to every relay or package.

verification_refs.locator: Introduction and Lock-in-Last on Loss of Supply Pressure, PDF pp. 1–2; Figures 1–2
verification_refs.supports_claim: Emerson states that after supply pressure falls below a minimum, a locking device activates and prevents remaining actuator air from venting; it notes locked-in position depends on actuator exhausting speed and shows distinct single-acting and double-acting assemblies using switching/trip valves.

facts.statement: Positioner direct/reverse action, actuator air-pressure action, actuator spring-return motion, and the valve assembly's fail-open/fail-closed result are distinct properties that must be checked together for a selected package. Fisher documentation defines positioner action by output-pressure response, describes the 657 actuator's air and spring stem motions, and shows that resulting fail-open/fail-closed behavior depends on whether the valve is push-down-to-close or push-down-to-open.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Fisher 3582 and 3582i Positioners and 582i Electro-Pneumatic Converter Instruction Manual, D200138X012
verification_refs.locator: §5.1 Principle of Operation; §5.2 Direct/Reverse Action; §3.5 Direct/Reverse Action
verification_refs.supports_claim: The positioner manual describes its direct/reverse action as a positioner output/pressure response and treats selection separately from the valve/actuator's movement and calibration.

verification_refs.locator: Description and Figure 2, PDF pp. 2–3; Discussion of Bench Set, PDF pp. 5–6
verification_refs.supports_claim: The manual states that Fisher 657 is a direct-acting spring-opposed diaphragm actuator, illustrates air pushing the stem down and spring lifting it up, and separately refers to positioner manuals.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Fisher 657 and 667 Diaphragm Actuators Bulletin D100087X012
verification_refs.locator: §657 and §667 descriptions, PDF p. 3
verification_refs.supports_claim: The bulletin explains that the spring-driven actuator stem direction produces fail-open for push-down-to-close valves and fail-closed for push-down-to-open valves; the complementary actuator configuration likewise maps fail action according to valve plug action.

facts.statement: For a reflective direct time-of-flight measurement with colocated transmit and receive reference, the measured delay is the light pulse's round-trip travel time; under the ideal propagation model, target distance is d = c·Δt/2, where c is light propagation speed in the measurement medium.

verification_refs.citation: OMRON TECHNICS, Development of a TOF Sensor for Long-Range and Stable Wide-Angle Detection
verification_refs.locator: §2.1 Operating principle of ToF, dToF, Eq. (2)
verification_refs.supports_claim: OMRON states that dToF directly measures the round-trip time of projected light and derives d=c·Δt/2, with Δt defined as the delay from pulse projection until return.

verification_refs.citation: Analog Devices, Time of Flight System for Distance Measurement and Object Detection
verification_refs.locator: Time-of-flight principle, lines 14–15
verification_refs.supports_claim: ADI describes emitted light reflected from the object, defines the emission-to-reception delay as proportional to twice the distance, and gives d=(c×Δt)/2.

facts.statement: A typical active optical noncontact measurement chain emits light, interacts optically with a target, receives the reflected or interrupted light, converts the received-light change into an electrical signal, and processes that signal to infer a target state or distance within the selected sensing method.

verification_refs.citation: OMRON Industrial Automation, Overview of Photoelectric Sensors
verification_refs.locator: What Are Photoelectric Sensors?
verification_refs.supports_claim: OMRON describes an emitter and receiver; target interruption or reflection changes received light, which the receiver converts to electrical output.

verification_refs.citation: NIST, Laser triangulation displacement measurement in diffusion flames
verification_refs.locator: §1, functional principle, PDF p. 3
verification_refs.supports_claim: NIST describes laser emission to a target, reflected spot reception by lens and detector, signal-conditioning electronics, and geometric distance inference.

facts.statement: In a photoelectric sensor, the receiver detects a change in received light caused by interruption or reflection at the sensing object and converts that change into an electrical output for subsequent detection logic.

verification_refs.citation: OMRON Industrial Automation, Overview of Photoelectric Sensors
verification_refs.locator: What Are Photoelectric Sensors?
verification_refs.supports_claim: OMRON states that the receiver detects received-light change when emitted light is interrupted or reflected by the object and converts it to electrical output.

facts.statement: In transmitted-beam photoelectric sensing, the emitter and receiver are mounted opposite one another; an object is detected when it interrupts the beam. This mode can provide longer sensing distance and greater operating margin than retroreflective or diffuse modes, subject to product and application conditions.

verification_refs.citation: Rockwell Automation, Sensor Technology and Application Basics Reference Manual, C117-RM001
verification_refs.locator: §Sensing Modes; Transmitted beam sensing, PDF pp. 11–14
verification_refs.supports_claim: Rockwell describes opposed emitter and receiver, beam interruption for detection, and product-mode comparisons showing transmitted-beam sensors can have the longest sensing distances and highest operating margin.

verification_refs.citation: OMRON Industrial Automation, Overview of Photoelectric Sensors
verification_refs.locator: What Are Photoelectric Sensors?; Through-beam classification
verification_refs.supports_claim: OMRON confirms the emitter/receiver photoelectric architecture and classifies through-beam sensors as a distinct sensing mode.

facts.statement: A retroreflective photoelectric sensor houses its emitter and receiver together, directs emitted light to a reflector, and detects an object when the object interrupts the return beam. Polarized retroreflective designs can reject many shiny-object reflections because the receiver accepts the polarization state returned by the depolarizing reflector rather than specular reflections that preserve polarization.

verification_refs.citation: Rockwell Automation, Sensor Technology and Application Basics Reference Manual, C117-RM001
verification_refs.locator: §Retroreflective and Polarized Retroreflective, PDF pp. 15–19
verification_refs.supports_claim: Rockwell describes emitter/receiver in one housing, reflector-return beam interrupted by the target, and crossed polarizers distinguishing depolarized reflector returns from most shiny-object reflections.

facts.statement: Diffuse-reflective photoelectric sensing places the emitter and receiver at the sensor and detects light scattered back from the target; detection margin depends strongly on target and background reflectivity, surface orientation and geometry.

verification_refs.citation: Rockwell Automation, Sensor Technology and Application Basics Reference Manual, C117-RM001
verification_refs.locator: §Diffuse, PDF pp. 20–22
verification_refs.supports_claim: Rockwell states that the target surface scatters emitted light toward the receiver and discusses how object/background reflectivity and surface orientation affect sensing margin.

verification_refs.citation: OMRON Industrial Automation, Overview of Photoelectric Sensors
verification_refs.locator: Photoelectric Sensor classifications
verification_refs.supports_claim: OMRON identifies diffuse-reflective sensing as a distinct sensor type using target reflection.

facts.statement: Reflective direct optical time-of-flight measures the delay from transmitting a light pulse until its reflected return is received; this measured interval is the pulse's round-trip travel time.

verification_refs.citation: OMRON TECHNICS, Development of a TOF Sensor for Long-Range and Stable Wide-Angle Detection
verification_refs.locator: §2.1 Operating principle of ToF, dToF, Eq. (2)
verification_refs.supports_claim: OMRON describes direct ToF as measuring the round-trip delay between pulse projection and its return from the target.

facts.statement: Indirect time-of-flight intensity-modulates emitted light and estimates propagation delay from the phase difference between the transmitted modulation reference and received reflected modulation; for a single frequency, d=c·φ/(4πf_m) under the stated round-trip model and wrapped phase convention.

verification_refs.citation: OMRON TECHNICS, Development of a TOF Sensor for Long-Range and Stable Wide-Angle Detection
verification_refs.locator: §2.1 Operating principle of ToF, iToF, Eq. (1)
verification_refs.supports_claim: OMRON states that iToF intensity-modulates a laser, measures transmitted/received phase difference, and derives d=c·θ/(4πf).

facts.statement: In laser triangulation, projected light reflected from the target is imaged through a receiving lens onto a position-sensitive detector; calibrated sensor geometry maps the observed spot position to target distance or displacement within the sensor's measurement range.

verification_refs.citation: NIST, Laser triangulation displacement measurement in diffusion flames
verification_refs.locator: §1, functional principle and Fig. 1, PDF p. 3
verification_refs.supports_claim: NIST describes target illumination, reflected-spot imaging through a collection lens onto a PSD, geometric distance inference, and range/standoff determined by sensor geometry.

facts.statement: For a calibrated laser-triangulation sensor geometry, a change in target depth changes the imaged spot coordinate on the detector, and that coordinate is converted to distance or displacement using the sensor's geometry model.

verification_refs.citation: NIST, Laser triangulation displacement measurement in diffusion flames
verification_refs.locator: §1 and Fig. 1, PDF p. 3
verification_refs.supports_claim: NIST explains that reflected spot position at the detector and geometric relationships determine distance, and illustrates the lens/PSD/target geometry.

facts.statement: With coherent laser illumination of a rough surface in laser triangulation, interference among scattered light components creates a granular speckle intensity pattern; this pattern makes the imaged spot centroid or position uncertain and contributes random measurement error. The effect depends on surface and optical-system conditions and has no universal magnitude.

verification_refs.citation: E. F. J. de Kock et al., Laser line triangulation for fast 3D measurements on large gears, The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology
verification_refs.locator: §4.3 Measurement deviation, lines 250–254
verification_refs.supports_claim: The paper attributes random error to coherent laser speckle, describes bright/dark speckles from phase interference, and states that random speckle makes exact CCD laser-image centroid determination uncertain; speckle appearance depends on coherence, apertures and surface roughness.

verification_refs.citation: R. G. Dorsch, G. Häusler, and J. M. Herrmann, Laser triangulation: Fundamental uncertainty in distance measurement, Applied Optics 33(7), 1306–1314
verification_refs.locator: Abstract and full-article description
verification_refs.supports_claim: The authors identify speckle noise from coherent illumination of rough surfaces as a limiting uncertainty source in laser-triangulation distance measurement and derive its dependence on optical parameters.

facts.statement: In single-frequency iToF, measured phase is periodic, so distinct distances can map to the same wrapped phase and create a finite unambiguous range. Measurements at multiple modulation frequencies can support phase-unwrapping and extend the unambiguous range, but the resulting range and performance depend on implementation.

verification_refs.citation: OMRON TECHNICS, Development of a TOF Sensor for Long-Range and Stable Wide-Angle Detection
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines iToF as phase measurement of intensity-modulated light and gives d=c·θ/(4πf); a phase measurement repeating modulo 2π therefore yields a finite distance interval for a single modulation frequency.

verification_refs.citation: J. Droeschel et al., Multi-frequency Phase Unwrapping for Time-of-Flight cameras, IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS), 2010
verification_refs.locator: Abstract and §II, Phase Unwrapping
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes ToF distance as proportional to measured phase modulo the modulation wavelength, states that longer distances wrap into the sensor's non-ambiguity range, and demonstrates multiple modulation frequencies for identifying and correcting phase wraps.

facts.statement: Protective/equipment grounding provides a safety path for fault current and must remain permanent and continuous; signal or circuit ground is a measurement reference whose relation to earth depends on the equipment and measurement configuration. facts.statement: For analog DAQ noise troubleshooting, NI recommends examining the signal spectrum (for example with an FFT), surveying the measurement setup and environment, and establishing a device baseline; disconnecting components one at a time can help localize the source. The sequence is a diagnostic method for the described DAQ context, not a mandatory universal plant procedure. After a correction, confirm the measurement against the original application conditions and device specifications.

verification_refs.citation: National Instruments, Diagnosing & Reducing Measurement Noise in Analog Signals

facts.statement: For analog-noise troubleshooting, preserve baseline raw signal data or spectral evidence and record the relevant setup/operating context before changing the measurement configuration or applying mitigation; compare follow-up measurements under comparable conditions. NI describes FFT/setup inspection and baseline checks as diagnostic tools, while event timestamps can be correlated with recorded power disturbances as candidate evidence. This is an evidence-based troubleshooting recommendation, not a mandated record format or permission to alter protective-earth connections.

facts.statement: After an analog-noise troubleshooting change, recheck the signal under application-appropriate and safe conditions, compare with the documented baseline, and check the result against the measurement-device specifications. Tests such as UPS transfer or deliberate noise-source switching are installation-specific and should be performed only when supported by the design and an approved safe procedure; they are not universal acceptance steps.

facts.statement: For energy-performance monitoring, an organization defines energy performance indicators (EnPIs) and baselines appropriate to its processes. Production output, product mix, operating hours, and other significant relevant variables can affect energy consumption; therefore, a simple energy-per-unit ratio may be useful but may need normalization or a model when comparing performance across materially different operating conditions or product mixes.

Cause categories for lateness are organization-specific rather than a universal required taxonomy.

facts.statement: ISO 22400-2 describes manufacturing operations management as covering production, quality, inventory, and maintenance operations, with activities including detailed scheduling, dispatching, execution management, resource management, tracking, data collection, and analysis. Production planning considers capacity and resources such as workforce, materials, and equipment in response to demand. The standard describes KPIs by formulas/elements/time behaviour/units and notes that organizations define context-specific thresholds and actions. The particular mix and priority of safety, quality, delivery, cost, and resource goals is organization- and product-specific, not a universal priority prescribed by the standard.

facts.statement: For active laser triangulation under the far-field approximation d >> f, the geometric mapping is d ≈ f b/u, where b is the baseline, f the imaging lens focal length, and u the detector spot coordinate. Propagating spot-coordinate uncertainty δu gives δd ≈ d² δu/(f b). For fixed distance and δu, a longer baseline or focal length reduces this modelled distance uncertainty, while uncertainty grows quadratically with distance. This idealized geometry is not a product performance specification.

verification_refs.locator: Active triangulation, Eqs. (3)–(4)
verification_refs.supports_claim: Gives d=f x/x′ under d >> f and δd=d²/(f x)×δx′; states that uncertainty at a given distance is reduced by longer baseline, longer focal length, and higher-resolution detector.

verification_refs.locator: §1 and Fig. 1, p. 3
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes laser-spot projection and image-detector geometry used to infer distance; serves as independent triangulation-geometry cross-check, not as the source of Hamamatsu’s uncertainty formula.

facts.statement: For the direct-ToF pulse receiver described by Hamamatsu, with a given telescope aperture, received return-light amount depends on target distance and reflection characteristics including color, orientation, and surface smoothness. At a fixed distance, these target characteristics can therefore change the received return-pulse amplitude. This is a configuration-specific signal-amplitude statement, not a universal SNR or uncertainty formula for all optical sensors.

facts.statement: In active triangulation, shadowing occurs when the projector light cannot reach a target point, while occultation occurs when reflected light from that point cannot reach the camera/receiver. Reducing the baseline can reduce occultation, but the cited geometry incurs increased distance uncertainty. These are line-of-sight and geometry effects in the described triangulation setup.

verification_refs.citation: Hamamatsu Photonics, Measuring distance with light
verification_refs.locator: Active triangulation, Fig. 4 and discussion of occultation/shadowing
verification_refs.supports_claim: The source distinguishes projector shadowing from receiver occultation and states that a shorter baseline can reduce occultation with increased distance uncertainty.

facts.statement: For the described pulsed direct-ToF round-trip model in a medium of refractive index n, distance is d=ct/(2n) and timing uncertainty δt gives approximate range uncertainty δd≈cδt/(2n). The source identifies detector jitter, pulse rise-time variation, electrical noise, and threshold-crossing levels as contributors to timing variation in its example. Propagation speed alone therefore does not guarantee high ranging accuracy.

verification_refs.supports_claim: The source gives d=ct/(2n), δd≈cδt/(2n), and describes detector jitter, rise-time variation, electrical noise, and threshold levels as timing variation sources.

VIM states accuracy is not a quantity and is not assigned a numerical quantity value. These terms must not be conflated.

facts.statement: 반사형 Direct optical ToF는 왕복 광 비행시간 t와 매질 굴절률 n으로 d=ct/(2n)을 계산하고, 초음파 pulse-echo는 왕복 음향시간 t와 음속 c_s로 d=c_s·t/2를 계산한다. 따라서 두 방식 모두 왕복시간에서 편도거리를 얻지만 전파속도와 반환 신호(광반사/음향 에코)가 다르다. 탱크 ullage의 기체 경로에서는 음속이 기체 종류·온도·증기압의 영향을 받는다. 이는 비교 개요이며 초음파 보상·설치·에코 진단의 상세는 초음파 Topic 소유 범위다.

facts.statement: AMCW ToF range camera에서 한 receiving pixel이 direct return과 다른 경로의 global/multiple returns를 함께 받으면 위상·거리 추정에 multipath distortion이 생길 수 있다. 특히 넓은 조명 아래 투명체의 여러 장면점에서 온 반사가 한 pixel에 들어오는 경우 잘못된 depth map을 만들 수 있다. 이는 해당 ToF camera와 장면의 조건부 오차이며 모든 광학 ToF 센서나 모든 표면에서 같은 크기·방향으로 발생한다고 일반화하지 않는다.

verification_refs.supports_claim: After gas sizing, directs use of the sizing result to calculate Cg for Fisher aerodynamic-noise prediction; relates Cg to Cv and xT, and defines the relevant critical pressure regime and service-condition calculations.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th edition, Chapter 5: Control Valve Sizing
verification_refs.locator: §5.15 aerodynamic noise prediction and §5.16 noise control
verification_refs.supports_claim: Noise prediction depends on valve geometry and service conditions, including pressure regimes and flow; noise-control treatment and specialized low-noise trim are further design evaluations rather than outputs of gas capacity sizing alone.

facts.statement: Internal acoustic noise in a closed control-valve system can transmit through the fluid and excite pipe-wall vibration that radiates sound externally.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook—Oil and Gas, Chapter 5: Control Valve Noise
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 5, Noise Control, closed-system transmission discussion
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that, in closed systems, process sound travels through the valve and adjacent piping; the in-fluid sound field excites solid boundaries, whose vibration radiates sound into the ambient environment.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th edition, Chapter 5: Control Valve Sizing
verification_refs.locator: §5.16 Noise Control, path treatment
verification_refs.supports_claim: Separates noise generation inside the pipe from sound transmitted through pipe walls to the external environment and describes path treatment for that transmission.

facts.statement: Certain multi-path or drilled-hole control-valve trims split a large turbulent flow into multiple smaller jets or noise sources, changing acoustic-source behavior.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Noise-Attenuation Technologies for Control Valves, D351989X012
verification_refs.locator: Whisper Trim III Cage and V260/V280 attenuator product descriptions
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes multi-path/multi-stage trim passages that break a large turbulent stream into many small independent jets and a drilled-hole attenuator that separates flow into multiple smaller jets.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Whisper Trim I Cage product documentation
verification_refs.locator: Product Description and Key Features
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that this model-specific cage uses multiple specially shaped, sized, and spaced orifices to reduce noise for gas, vapor, or steam; the evidence does not establish a universal reduction for other trims.

facts.statement: Inline silencers, pipe insulation or heavy-wall pipe, and acoustic enclosures are distinct noise-path attenuation treatments used in applicable control-valve systems.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook—Oil and Gas, Chapter 5: Control Valve Noise
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 5, Noise Control, source and path treatment sections
verification_refs.supports_claim: Separates source treatment from external path treatment and lists heavy-wall piping, acoustic insulation, insulated boxes/buildings, and inline silencers for suitable gas systems.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th edition, Chapter 5: Control Valve Sizing
verification_refs.locator: §5.16 Noise Control, path treatment and silencer discussion
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes in-line silencers, acoustical materials, pipe treatment and insulated enclosures/buildings as ways to attenuate sound transmission, with efficacy depending on installation and treatment extent.

facts.statement: Documented multi-stage low-noise trim distributes pressure reduction among stages and uses passage geometry/expansion areas to manage gas velocity and reduce acoustic power conversion.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 6th edition, Chapter 5: Control Valve Sizing
verification_refs.locator: §5.16 Noise Control, multistage trim and velocity management
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes multistage pressure reduction as dividing stream power among stages and lowering acoustic conversion efficiency; it also describes expanding flow areas for velocity management.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook—Oil and Gas, Chapter 5: Control Valve Noise
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 5, Figure 5-1, two-stage cage trim and pressure-drop discussion
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes a two-stage cage trim for high pressure-drop ratios, with restrictions sized and spaced to control jet interaction; these are design examples rather than universal numeric stage limits.

facts.statement: Control-valve aerodynamic noise arises from turbulent gas or steam flow and, in high-pressure-ratio or choked regimes, can include noise-producing interactions of shock waves and turbulence in the jet and downstream flow.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Whisper Trim III Cage product documentation
verification_refs.locator: Product Description
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that aerodynamic noise is generated by turbulence created in vapor, gas, or steam flow as it passes through a control valve, and scopes the cited trim performance to properly sized applications.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook—Oil and Gas, Chapter 5: Control Valve Noise
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 5, aerodynamic noise discussion
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes aerodynamic control-valve noise as arising from turbulent gas flow and discusses its dependence on pressure drop, flow rate, pressure ratio, trim, piping, and downstream pressure.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual: Gas and Steam Flow
verification_refs.locator: §4.3.1 Aerodynamic noise generation; §4.3.2 Aerodynamic noise prediction
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that throttling gas or steam produces aerodynamic noise; at choking, shock-wave and turbulence interactions are major noise sources, while at low pressure ratios turbulence is the stated cause.

facts.statement: In liquid control-valve cavitation, vapor bubbles form as local pressure falls and collapse when pressure recovers; this collapse can generate high noise and vibration as well as damage.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Cavitation in Control Valves
verification_refs.locator: Understanding Cavitation in Control Valves; Definition
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines cavitation as formation and collapse of vapor bubbles in liquid flow, explains pressure-drop formation and downstream collapse, and identifies high noise, vibration, and material damage as possible effects.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Catalog 12, Section 3: Hydrodynamic Noise
verification_refs.locator: Hydrodynamic Noise, Introduction, p. 3-5
verification_refs.supports_claim: Identifies cavitation as formation and subsequent collapse of vapor bubbles in liquid flow and attributes associated noise and damage to bubble collapse; distinguishes persistent-bubble flashing as producing little hydrodynamic noise.

facts.statement: In high-pressure-ratio or choked gas/steam control-valve flow, interactions between shock waves and turbulence in the jet or downstream flow can be important aerodynamic-noise sources; this mechanism is not asserted for every gas condition.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual: Gas and Steam Flow
verification_refs.locator: §4.3.1 Aerodynamic noise generation, §4.3.2 Aerodynamic noise prediction
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that choking makes shock-wave/turbulence interaction a main noise source, that high pressure ratios make turbulent shock interactions a major source, and that shock waves can form a compression-wave chain at a control-valve outlet.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook—Oil and Gas, Chapter 5: Control Valve Noise
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 5, Aerodynamic Noise Prediction, pp. 5-3–5-4
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines distinct aerodynamic noise-generation regimes based on vena-contracta and downstream pressure, requiring regime-specific acoustic efficiency rather than a single mechanism for all conditions.

facts.statement: Gas/steam choking occurs when sonic velocity is reached at the vena contracta and, after the fully choked limit at fixed inlet pressure and valve opening, a further pressure-drop increase does not increase flow; it is a finite-flow regime used to select the applicable aerodynamic-noise model, not zero flow.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual: Gas and Steam Flow
verification_refs.locator: §4.1 General; §4.3.1 Aerodynamic noise generation; §4.3.2 Aerodynamic noise prediction
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines gas choking by sonic vena-contracta velocity and states the fully choked flow limit at fixed inlet pressure; also defines different noise mechanisms and prediction regimes by flow condition.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook—Oil and Gas, Chapter 5: Control Valve Noise
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 5, Aerodynamic Noise Prediction, pp. 5-3–5-4
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that IEC aerodynamic noise prediction uses five regimes determined by vena-contracta/downstream pressure relationships and computes regime-specific acoustic efficiency.

facts.statement: Aerodynamic-noise generation and prediction depend on flow velocity/sonic regime and the valve, trim, and downstream piping geometry; the prediction method uses service conditions and accounts for piping transmission when estimating external sound pressure.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual: Gas and Steam Flow
verification_refs.locator: §4.1 General; §§4.3.1–4.3.2 Aerodynamic noise generation and prediction; §4.5.1 Velocity control
verification_refs.supports_claim: Relates gas compressibility to flow/speed-of-sound regime, identifies choked shock/turbulence noise, and explains velocity management through valve trim and expanding flow areas.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook—Oil and Gas, Chapter 5: Control Valve Noise
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 5, Aerodynamic Noise Prediction, pp. 5-3–5-4
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that the method uses measurable valve geometry and service conditions, converts vena-contracta velocity and mass flow to stream power, accounts for pipe-wall transmission loss dependent on pipe material, size, shape and frequency, and calculates SPL at an observer location.

facts.statement: External sound-pressure level is a point/observer quantity that depends on source-to-observer distance and direction, and measurement or prediction conditions must account for the acoustic environment, reflecting surfaces, and noise-path treatments such as enclosures.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook—Oil and Gas, Chapter 5: Control Valve Noise
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 5, Aerodynamic Noise Prediction, pp. 5-3–5-4; external noise treatment discussion
verification_refs.supports_claim: Distinguishes acoustic power from measurable sound pressure, calculates SPL at a reference/observer point, states that SPL decreases with observer distance, and describes external boxes/buildings as path treatment.

verification_refs.citation: ISO 3744:2025, Acoustics — Determination of sound power levels of noise sources using sound pressure
verification_refs.locator: §1.1 General; §1.3 Test environment
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines sound-power estimation from sound-pressure measurements over an enveloping measurement surface; specifies reflecting-plane/test-environment conditions and environmental corrections, demonstrating that measurement location/surface and environment cannot be omitted.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual: Gas and Steam Flow
verification_refs.locator: §4.4 Atmospheric venting
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that vent sound pressure decreases with observer distance and that observation direction affects radiated noise because of source directivity; environmental and barrier conditions add propagation attenuation.

facts.statement: Noise generated by process flow through a control valve and noise from pneumatic actuator-system exhaust are distinct sources that should be diagnosed separately; positioner/booster/quick-exhaust configurations can vent air separately from the process stream.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson/Fisher, Control Valve Sourcebook—Oil and Gas, Chapter 5: Control Valve Noise
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 5, Sources of Valve Noise, pp. 5-1–5-2
verification_refs.supports_claim: Classifies control-valve process noise into mechanical vibration, aerodynamic noise from gas flow, and hydrodynamic noise from liquid flow.

verification_refs.citation: Schneider Electric/Foxboro, VBS200 Volume Booster Series Quick Guide, QG EVE0602 A-(en)
verification_refs.locator: §2.2.4 Tapped Exhaust; §3.2 Operation
verification_refs.supports_claim: Identifies noise created by exhausting air from the volume-booster/actuator pneumatic circuit and recommends an exhaust silencer; the booster is controlled by the positioner and connected to the actuator, separate from process fluid flow.

verification_refs.citation: SMC, IP8001 Electro-Pneumatic Positioner Operation Manual, ANo.IP8S-OM00013
verification_refs.locator: §3, Simple Balance Current Adjustment, p. 19
verification_refs.supports_claim: Uses an audible change in positioner exhaust noise as an indication during the model-specific balance-current adjustment, demonstrating that a pneumatic-positioner exhaust source can be distinguished from process-flow noise.

facts.statement: A field-noise result is interpretable only with its measurement position/distance, frequency weighting, representative operating or exposure conditions, and any background/environment correction required by the selected measurement method recorded.

verification_refs.citation: OSHA Technical Manual, Section III, Chapter 5: Noise
verification_refs.locator: Section III, noise measurements, sound level meters and field records
verification_refs.supports_claim: Directs recording source description, measurement distance, exposed workers, A- and C-weighted levels, frequency spectrum when used, duration, microphone location, and noise-source/time context.

verification_refs.citation: ISO 9612:2025, Acoustics — Determination of occupational noise exposure — Methodology
verification_refs.locator: Scope and methodology summary; §§7–8 (work analysis and measurement strategy)
verification_refs.supports_claim: Specifies A-weighted and optionally C-weighted occupational exposure measurements, requires observation/analysis of exposure conditions to control measurement quality, and provides uncertainty methods.

verification_refs.citation: ISO 3744:2025, Acoustics — Determination of sound power levels of noise sources using sound pressure
verification_refs.locator: §1.1 General; §1.3 Test environment
verification_refs.supports_claim: Requires a defined enveloping measurement surface in a stated reflecting-plane environment and provides corrections within limits for imperfect test environments; this supports recording method-required environmental correction context, not indiscriminate correction of every field measurement.

verification_refs.citation: CDC/NIOSH, Eliminate or Reduce Noise
verification_refs.locator: Comparing the noise levels of tools
verification_refs.supports_claim: Recommends keeping the sound-level-meter microphone at the same distance and recording for the same duration when making comparative noise measurements.

facts.statement: A control-valve noise prediction is method- and scope-dependent; identify the prediction method and edition, its applicable fluid/valve scope, and the reference or observation condition for the reported sound-pressure level.

verification_refs.citation: IEC 60534-8-3:2010, Industrial-process control valves — Part 8-3: Noise considerations — Control valve aerodynamic noise prediction method
verification_refs.locator: Scope and edition summary
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines an aerodynamic external sound-pressure prediction method restricted to single-phase dry gases/vapours, states valve configuration applicability and a downstream-pipe assumption, and notes edition-specific technical changes. This demonstrates that method edition, applicability and reference conditions matter.

verification_refs.citation: ISA-75.17-1989, Control Valve Aerodynamic Noise Prediction, ISA product description
verification_refs.locator: Product description and scope summary
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes the ISA document as a method for compressible-fluid aerodynamic control-valve noise and resultant noise outside/downstream of the pipe; it expressly excludes mechanical vibration, unstable flow and other unpredictable behavior. It is not evidence that this historic ISA edition is equivalent to the IEC edition.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual
verification_refs.locator: Appendix K, Noise prediction aspects
verification_refs.supports_claim: Identifies the method used in the manual's control-valve sizing calculations as mainly based on VDMA 24422 (1979) and IEC 60534-8. This supports identifying the manufacturer calculation method rather than treating every vendor output as the same method.

verification_refs.citation: Valmet, Flow Control Manual: Gas and Steam Flow
verification_refs.locator: §4.3.2 Aerodynamic noise prediction
verification_refs.supports_claim: Describes the predicted atmospheric sound-pressure level and its observation-point distance/direction dependence, supporting explicit reference or observation conditions for reported SPL.

facts.statement: Liquid flow through a control valve can generate hydrodynamic noise from normal turbulence; IEC 60534-8-4 treats normal turbulence and liquid cavitation as noise-generation mechanisms within its hydrodynamic prediction method.

verification_refs.citation: IEC 60534-8-4:2015, Industrial-process control valves — Part 8-4: Noise considerations — Prediction of noise generated by hydrodynamic flow
verification_refs.locator: Scope and edition summary
verification_refs.supports_claim: The standard establishes prediction of noise generated by liquid flow through a control valve and says noise may be generated by normal turbulence and liquid cavitation; its method is validated by test data.

facts.statement: Occupational noise exposure criteria are tied to the applicable jurisdiction and exposure duration/averaging method; project or employer criteria should also be checked when they apply. Do not treat one jurisdiction's limit or a valve SPL prediction as a universal occupational exposure limit.

verification_refs.citation: CDC/NIOSH, Understanding Noise Exposure Limits: Occupational vs. General Environmental Noise
verification_refs.locator: What is the NIOSH recommended exposure limit?
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines NIOSH's occupational REL as 85 dBA over an 8-hour TWA and describes how allowable time changes with level; explicitly distinguishes occupational exposure limits from general environmental noise criteria.

verification_refs.citation: U.S. OSHA, 29 CFR 1910.95 Occupational noise exposure
verification_refs.locator: §1910.95(b), Table G-16, Permissible Noise Exposures
verification_refs.supports_claim: Sets permissible noise exposure values by duration per day and specifies measurement/combination rules, demonstrating the duration and regulatory framework are essential to applying the limit.

verification_refs.citation: UK Health and Safety Executive, Assessing noise risks for larger / more dynamic sites
verification_refs.locator: Exposure action values and daily/weekly personal exposure
verification_refs.supports_claim: Uses UK-specific daily or weekly personal exposure action values (80 dB and 85 dB), distinct from the cited U.S. OSHA and NIOSH frameworks; supports jurisdiction-specific selection and warns against a universal limit.

facts.statement: For a fixed service, selecting sufficient effective flow area can help limit outlet velocity, but oversizing a control valve can force low-travel operation and compromise usable rangeability and control performance; size against the full operating cases rather than noise velocity alone.

verification_refs.citation: Baker Hughes, Masoneilan Noise Control Handbook (2021)
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that outlet velocity must be limited to prevent noise regeneration and identifies choosing a valve size adequate to ensure proper outlet velocity as one method; the handbook also explains that the appropriate approach depends on the application.

verification_refs.citation: Emerson, Control Valve Handbook, 6th edition
verification_refs.locator: Chapter 2, Control Valve Performance; oversized-valve performance and turndown discussion
verification_refs.supports_claim: Explains that an oversized valve may reach system capacity at low travel, flatten the installed flow response at higher travel, and lose usable turndown/rangeability when throttling at the low end. The cited handbook's examples do not establish a universal numeric rangeability for every installation.

facts.statement: For a credible fail-open gas-valve scenario, calculate the resulting fully-open flow using the scenario's coincident upstream/downstream pressures and gas-sizing inputs, and check whether critical/choked flow limits apply. The maximum credible upstream pressure and minimum downstream pressure are paired only if they can occur together in that scenario.

verification_refs.citation: Fisher/Rosemount, Control Valve Primer, Chapter 5: Valve Sizing Made Easy
verification_refs.locator: pp. 24–26, especially p. 25 'What Are the Right Flow Conditions?'
verification_refs.supports_claim: The primer gives gas-flow relations in terms of absolute upstream and downstream pressures, temperature, gas properties and valve coefficients; distinguishes subcritical/critical flow; and explicitly asks whether a fail-open valve's resultant flow could exceed downstream relief capacity. It stresses selecting correct process conditions, including pump head at the maximum flow to be passed, static head, and line/equipment pressure losses.

verification_refs.citation: IEC 60534-2-1:2011, Industrial-process control valves — Part 2-1: Flow capacity — Sizing equations for fluid flow under installed conditions
verification_refs.locator: Scope and sizing-equation description
verification_refs.supports_claim: The standard provides installed-condition flow equations for compressible and incompressible control-valve flow. The scenario-specific pairing requirement is an engineering application of those equations, not a claim that the standard prescribes one universal maximum/minimum pressure pair.

verification_refs.citation: API Standard 521, Pressure-relieving and Depressuring Systems
verification_refs.locator: Scope description for pressure-relieving system design guidance
verification_refs.supports_claim: Identifies API 521 as guidance for pressure-relieving and vapor-depressuring system design. The detailed fail-open scenario calculation remains governed by the applicable edition, process scenario analysis, and site relief basis; this citation is not used to claim a universal outlet-credit or relief-load rule.

facts.statement: ISO 14224:2016 defines corrective maintenance as restoration after fault detection, preventive maintenance as action to limit degradation/reduce failure probability, condition-based maintenance as preventive maintenance based on physical-condition assessment, and predictive maintenance as forecasting future entity state from defined historical data and known future operating parameters. The standard's scope is petroleum, natural gas, and petrochemical industries; these definitions do not prescribe an asset-specific strategy mix or interval.

verification_refs.citation: ISO 14224:2016, Petroleum, petrochemical and natural gas industries — Collection and exchange of reliability and maintenance data for equipment
verification_refs.edition_or_version: Edition 3, 2016; ISO page states confirmed in 2022 and remains current; accessed 2026-10-11
verification_refs.supports_claim: The official ISO Online Browsing Platform preview defines condition-based maintenance as preventive maintenance based on physical-condition assessment (§3.7); corrective maintenance as restoration after fault detection (§3.8); predictive maintenance as future-state forecasting estimated/calculated from defined historical data and known future operating parameters (§3.77); and preventive maintenance as limiting degradation/reducing failure probability (§3.78). ISO's catalogue scopes the standard to petroleum, natural gas and petrochemical industries and confirms the 2016 edition remains current. The standard does not prescribe a specific plant's strategy selection or interval.

facts.statement: ISO 14224:2016 defines a maintenance plan as a structured and documented set of tasks comprising the activities, procedures, resources, and duration needed to perform maintenance. This definition does not prescribe universal asset-specific tasks, inspection intervals, safety measures, or shutdown windows.

verification_refs.citation: ISO 14224:2016, Petroleum, petrochemical and natural gas industries — Collection and exchange of reliability and maintenance data for equipment
verification_refs.edition_or_version: Edition 3, 2016; ISO page states confirmed in 2022 and remains current; accessed 2026-10-11
verification_refs.locator: §3.54 (maintenance plan)
verification_refs.supports_claim: The official ISO Online Browsing Platform defines a maintenance plan as a structured and documented set of tasks comprising the activities, procedures, resources, and duration needed to perform maintenance. The ISO catalogue scopes the standard to petroleum, natural gas and petrochemical industries and confirms the 2016 edition remains current.

facts.statement: Metrological traceability is a property of a measurement result relating it to a reference through a documented unbroken chain of calibrations, each contributing to measurement uncertainty; traceability alone does not establish fitness for purpose. NIST sets no universal recalibration interval; accuracy needs, contract/regulation, instrument stability, environment and measurement history can affect interval selection.

verification_refs.citation: NIST Policy on Metrological Traceability
verification_refs.locator: Policy Statement and traceability definition
verification_refs.supports_claim: Defines traceability of a measurement result through a documented unbroken chain of calibrations, each contributing to uncertainty; explicitly warns traceability alone does not guarantee fitness for purpose.

verification_refs.citation: NIST, Recommended Calibration Interval
verification_refs.locator: FAQ: whether NIST requires or recommends a set recalibration interval
verification_refs.supports_claim: States that NIST generally specifies no set interval; relevant factors include customer accuracy requirements, contract/regulation, instrument stability, and environmental factors. It recommends measurement assurance/history to determine and refine intervals when external requirements do not set them.

facts.statement: Risk analysis considers consequences and their likelihood. ISO 55001:2024 asset-management decision-making uses defined criteria and appropriate methods; it does not prescribe one universal criticality-factor list or weighting for all instrumentation assets.

verification_refs.citation: ISO 31000:2018, Risk management — Guidelines
verification_refs.locator: Risk assessment process and risk-analysis concepts
verification_refs.supports_claim: ISO 31000 frames risk in relation to objectives and risk analysis considers consequences and their likelihood; the specific assessment criteria are established in context, not as a single universal asset-maintenance factor list.

verification_refs.citation: ISO 55001:2024, Asset management — Asset management system — Requirements
verification_refs.locator: §4.5 asset-management decision-making and value; §6.1.2 risk; §6.2 planning
verification_refs.supports_claim: The 2024 standard adds an asset-management decision-making framework with defined criteria and appropriate methods, and addresses risk and resourcing. The standard allows organizational asset scope and criteria; it does not mandate a fixed factor list for instrument-maintenance criticality.

facts.statement: Within ISO 14224:2016's petroleum, natural gas and petrochemical scope, equipment identification numbers identify equipment function and physical location; reliability/maintenance data include equipment taxonomy and relevant equipment attributes. The standard excludes complete equipment data sheets and additional on-service data an operator may separately consider useful, so it does not define a universal complete instrumentation asset-register schema.

verification_refs.citation: ISO 14224:2016, Petroleum, petrochemical and natural gas industries — Collection and exchange of reliability and maintenance data for equipment
verification_refs.edition_or_version: Edition 3, 2016; ISO page confirms current; accessed 2026-10-11
verification_refs.locator: §§3.91–3.92; catalogue abstract and scope notes on equipment data
verification_refs.supports_claim: The official ISO browsing preview defines identification number as a unique code identifying equipment function and physical location (§3.91), and taxonomy as systematic classification (§3.92). The official catalogue says the standard collects equipment taxonomy and attributes, while excluding complete equipment data sheets and additional on-service data that an operator may consider useful.

facts.statement: Within ISO 14224:2016's petroleum, natural gas and petrochemical scope, collected reliability/maintenance data include equipment data, failure data such as cause and consequence, and maintenance data such as action, resources used, maintenance consequence and downtime in a standardized format. The standard excludes additional on-service data operators may consider useful and does not prescribe every site's work-order authorization, permit, test, restoration or closeout workflow.

verification_refs.citation: ISO 14224:2016, Petroleum, petrochemical and natural gas industries — Collection and exchange of reliability and maintenance data for equipment
verification_refs.edition_or_version: Edition 3, 2016; ISO page confirms current; accessed 2026-10-11
verification_refs.locator: Catalogue abstract, data categories and exclusions; §§3.50–3.54 definitions
verification_refs.supports_claim: The official ISO catalogue enumerates equipment data, failure data (cause/consequence), and maintenance data (action, resources, maintenance consequence, downtime) in the standardized collection/exchange scope; it expressly excludes additional on-service data an operator may consider useful and methods for applying RM data.

facts.statement: ISO 14224:2016은 석유·천연가스·석유화학 산업의 신뢰성·정비 데이터 교환을 위해 고장 원인과 결과 등 failure data 범주 및 표준 형식을 제시하며, 정의된 failure mode를 정량·정성 분석에 활용할 수 있다고 설명한다. 이 표준은 분석·적용 방법 자체를 규정하지 않으므로 Bad Actor 기준, RCA 의무조건, 개선조치 환류 절차는 사업장·프로그램별로 정해야 한다.

verification_refs.citation: ISO 14224:2016, Petroleum, petrochemical and natural gas industries — Collection and exchange of reliability and maintenance data for equipment
verification_refs.edition_or_version: Edition 3, 2016; ISO page confirms current; accessed 2026-10-11
verification_refs.locator: Official catalogue abstract: §§48–52 and listed failure-data categories/exclusions at §§60–88
verification_refs.supports_claim: ISO describes standardized RM-data collection for the petroleum, natural gas and petrochemical industries; lists failure cause/consequence categories; says normative failure modes can serve as a reliability thesaurus for quantitative or qualitative applications; and expressly excludes methods for analyzing and applying RM data.

facts.statement: 미국 OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147 적용범위에서 위험에너지에 노출될 수 있는 설비 정비 전에는 고용주가 에너지관리 절차·교육·정기점검을 갖추고, 권한 있는 작업자가 격리 상태를 확인해야 한다. 잠금/표찰 해제와 재가동 전에는 설비 구성품의 운전상태와 작업구역·작업자 안전을 확인하고 영향받는 작업자에게 통지한다. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 적용 공정에는 별도로 해당 공정의 안전작업수칙과 작업별 교육·협력사 통제가 적용된다. 이는 해당 규정의 범위에 한정되며 모든 정비에 공통인 작업허가·SIS bypass 승인·기능시험 체크리스트를 뜻하지 않는다.

verification_refs.citation: U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 29 CFR 1910.147 — The control of hazardous energy (lockout/tagout)
verification_refs.edition_or_version: Current eCFR text as published by OSHA; accessed 2026-10-11
verification_refs.supports_claim: The regulation requires an energy-control program with procedures, training, and periodic inspections for covered servicing/maintenance; authorized employees verify isolation before work; before release, the work area/equipment condition and employee safety are checked, and affected employees are notified before restart.

verification_refs.citation: U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 29 CFR 1910.119 — Process safety management of highly hazardous chemicals
verification_refs.supports_claim: For covered processes, employers implement safe work practices including control of hazards during LOTO and control of maintenance/contractor personnel; employees receive task-relevant safe-work training, and covered maintenance and contract employees have defined training and coordination duties.

facts.statement: ISO 14224:2016 및 ISO/TR 12489는 MTTR(mean time to repair, 고장품을 수리하는 데 필요한 기대시간)과 MTTRes(mean time to restoration, 고장 검출·수리 시작 전 경과·실제 수리·운전복귀 가능 상태가 될 때까지의 시간을 포함)를 구분한다. ISO 14224에서 검출시간은 0이거나 알려지지 않을 수 있으므로 지표에 사용할 표준 정의와 시작·종료 경계를 명시하고, MTTR과 전체 복구시간을 같은 뜻으로 혼용하지 않는다.

verification_refs.citation: ISO/TR 12489:2013, Petroleum, petrochemical and natural gas industries — Reliability modelling and calculation of safety systems
verification_refs.edition_or_version: 2013 edition; ISO Online Browsing Platform preview accessed 2026-10-11
verification_refs.locator: §§3.1.31–3.1.35, especially notes to MTTR and the MTTRes/MRT/MART time components
verification_refs.supports_claim: ISO/TR 12489 defines MTTR as expected time to repair a failed item; distinguishes fault detection time from detection-to-restoration time; explains that MTTR in ISO 14224 excludes or cannot collect detection time while IEC usage can mean restoration; and defines MTTRes as detection plus pre-repair delay, active repair, and time until the component is available for return to operation.

verification_refs.citation: ISO 14224:2016, Petroleum, petrochemical and natural gas industries — Collection and exchange of reliability and maintenance data for equipment
verification_refs.edition_or_version: Edition 3, 2016; French Online Browsing Platform preview; accessed 2026-10-11
verification_refs.locator: §§3.63–3.64, MTTR and mean time to restoration definitions; Note 4 to §3.63 on detection time
verification_refs.supports_claim: The ISO 14224 preview defines MTTR as expected time to repair a failed entity and MTTRes as detection, time before repair, effective repair, and time until available for return to service; it notes detection time is zero or unknown in collected data.

facts.statement: 영국 HSE Offshore Petroleum Regulator의 functional-safety inspection guide는 offshore SIS 구성품의 정비·수리·시험을 연기할 때 사업자가 정의된 deferral 관리절차를 두고, 검토·승인 역할, 위험평가, 검토·모니터링을 정하며, 예상 연기기간에 따른 위험감소 영향과 여러 SIS 구성품의 누적위험을 고려하도록 권고한다. 이는 해당 offshore SIS 지침이며 모든 산업·모든 정비에 동일한 연기기한·임시보호조치·승인체계를 법적 보편요건으로 두지 않는다.

verification_refs.citation: UK Health and Safety Executive, Offshore Petroleum Regulator, Functional Safety Inspection Guide
verification_refs.locator: p. 30, Deferrals and Success Criteria
verification_refs.supports_claim: The guide recommends that dutyholders define a process for SIS maintenance, repair, and test deferrals, specify review/approval roles and risk assessment/monitoring, and consider the effect of anticipated duration on achieved risk reduction and cumulative risk across deferred SIS components.

facts.statement: 미국 OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 적용 공정의 기계적 건전성 대상 설비에서 허용한계를 벗어난 결함은 공정안전정보에 정의된 한계를 기준으로 추가 사용 전에 시정하거나, 안전한 운전을 보장하는 필요한 조치를 취한 상태에서 안전하고 적시에 시정해야 한다. 이 규정은 모든 산업의 동일한 우선순위 산식·Work Order 형식·재시험 절차를 정하지 않는다.

verification_refs.citation: U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 29 CFR 1910.119 — Process safety management of highly hazardous chemicals
verification_refs.supports_claim: For the listed equipment in covered PSM processes, inspections and tests follow recognized and generally accepted good engineering practices and are documented; deficiencies outside acceptable limits, defined by process safety information, are corrected before further use or safely and timely when necessary measures assure safe operation.

facts.statement: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3은 OT 구성 변경을 배포 전에 기록·시험·승인하고 변경을 추적하며 운전 영향을 고려하도록 권고한다. NIST SP 1339(2026)는 OT backup을 변경관리에 통합하고 정기 생성·시험 및 복구연습에서의 검토를 권고한다. 이는 지침이지 모든 정비작업 전후의 baseline 확인이나 backup 생성을 일괄 요구하는 것은 아니며, 변경통제 범위·영향받는 기록·backup 대상과 주기는 조직 및 시스템별로 정한다.

verification_refs.citation: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security
verification_refs.edition_or_version: Final, September 2023; current publication page accessed 2026-10-11; Rev. 4 is only an initial public draft
verification_refs.locator: §6.2.4.2, pp. 111–112: approved baseline, document/test/approve changes, central tracking considerations, tool operational impacts; §6.2.4.3, pp. 112–113: verify/test backups and include backup procedures in configuration/change management
verification_refs.supports_claim: NIST says organizations should document approved OT baseline configurations; describes an SDLC approach to document, test and approve changes before deployment; suggests central tracking and validation; warns configuration tools may affect OT operations; and recommends maintaining/testing backups, verifying reliability/integrity where possible, and including backup procedures in configuration/change-management processes.

verification_refs.citation: NIST SP 1339, OT Backup Quick Start Guide
verification_refs.locator: Official abstract: OT backup management integrated with change management, regular creation, testing, and review during recovery exercises
verification_refs.supports_claim: NIST states effective OT backup management involves integrating backups into change management, creating them regularly, testing them, and reviewing them during recovery exercises.

facts.statement: ISO 55001:2024는 조직이 적용대상 자산을 정하고 자산관리시스템을 수립·실행·유지·개선하도록 요구하며, 자산관리 의사결정에서 비용·위험·성과의 균형을 고려한다. ISO 55000:2024는 자산수명주기 전반의 가치 실현을 강조한다. 이는 지속개선의 관리 틀을 제공하지만, 특정 KPI·교정 OOT·예비품 지표의 정기 검토와 정해진 후속조치·주기를 모든 조직에 동일하게 처방하지 않는다.

verification_refs.citation: ISO 55001:2024, Asset management — Asset management system — Requirements
verification_refs.locator: Official catalogue description: scope determined by organization; establish, implement, maintain and improve AMS; lifecycle performance/risk/expenditure balance
verification_refs.supports_claim: The official ISO 55001:2024 page describes requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining and improving an asset management system; says the organization determines applicable assets; and describes balancing asset lifecycle performance, risk and expenditure to meet organizational goals.

verification_refs.citation: ISO/TC 251, ISO 55001 — Asset management system requirements, published-standard overview
verification_refs.locator: Clauses 4.5 asset-management decision-making and value; 6.2.3 planning and balance of cost, risk and performance; clause 10 improvement and predictive action overview
verification_refs.supports_claim: The ISO/TC251 overview describes asset-management decision criteria and methods, planning to resource objectives while balancing cost/risk/performance, and management review considering risk, opportunity, decision-making and improvement. It does not define the anchor's specific OOT/KPI/spares loop as a universal procedure.

verification_refs.citation: ISO 55000:2024, Asset management — Vocabulary, overview and principles
verification_refs.locator: Official catalogue preview and FAQ: asset life cycle, organizational objectives, continual improvement and value realization
verification_refs.supports_claim: The ISO 55000:2024 catalogue describes managing assets through their life cycles to realize value and align asset-management objectives with organizational objectives.

facts.statement: ISO 14224:2016은 석유·천연가스·석유화학 산업의 RM 데이터 최소 범주(장비 taxonomy·속성, 고장 원인·결과, 정비조치·자원·결과·downtime), 표준 교환 형식 및 데이터 품질 지침을 제시한다. 이는 일관된 데이터 교환과 신뢰성·가용도 분석을 지원하지만, CMMS/EAM 사용·모든 사업장별 필드·KPI/RCA 결과의 재현성을 보장하지 않는다.

verification_refs.citation: ISO 14224:2016, Petroleum, petrochemical and natural gas industries — Collection and exchange of reliability and maintenance data for equipment
verification_refs.edition_or_version: Edition 3, 2016; ISO page confirms current; accessed 2026-10-11
verification_refs.locator: Official catalogue abstract: scope, standardized format, data quality control/assurance, minimum collected data, categories and exclusions
verification_refs.supports_claim: The official ISO catalogue says ISO 14224 defines minimum RM data and a standardized exchange format in the petroleum, natural gas and petrochemical scope; lists equipment taxonomy/attributes, failure cause/consequence, maintenance action/resources/consequence/downtime; describes data quality control and assurance; and excludes additional operator-specific on-service data and methods for analyzing/applying RM data.

verification_refs.citation: R. Østebø et al., OTC-28705-MS, ISO Standards to Enable Reliable, Safe and Cost-Effective Technology Development, Project Execution and Operational Excellence, 2018
verification_refs.locator: pp. 11–12, malfunction reporting, structured input, field validation and RM data quality management
verification_refs.supports_claim: The ISO/TC67 paper describes one ISO 14224 implementation using taxonomy, picklists, field validation and quality assurance/control for standardized failure/maintenance records. It is implementation guidance/example, not evidence that every site must use a particular CMMS workflow.

facts.statement: In the NASA SWE-085 release-management guidance, a software release process identifies release configuration items and their versions/revisions, defines creation and verification of a master copy, and checks delivery copies against that master; the project establishes applicable storage, handling, delivery, release, and maintenance procedures. This supports controlled identity and copy-consistency checks, not a universal requirement that every plant use an identical release workflow or a particular checksum tool.

verification_refs.citation: NASA Software Engineering Handbook, SWE-085: Release Management
verification_refs.locator: Requirement 5.1.8; §§3.1–3.2, release scope, configuration-item versions/revisions, master-copy verification and delivery-copy comparison
verification_refs.supports_claim: The handbook calls for procedures for storage, handling, delivery, release and maintenance; identifying release scope and CI versions/revisions; documenting how a master copy is created and verified; and verifying delivered copies against the master, giving checksum validation as an example. The project-specific procedure remains applicable.

verification_refs.citation: NIST CSRC Glossary, Baseline Configuration (citing NIST SP 800-128)
verification_refs.locator: Baseline configuration definition
verification_refs.supports_claim: A configuration baseline is a formally reviewed and agreed specification at a point in time, changeable only through change-control procedures, and used as a basis for future builds, releases and changes. This is corroborative configuration-management context, not an OT-specific release procedure.

facts.statement: 형상관리에서는 승인된 형상 문서가 실제 제작·설치된 구성(as-built)을 반영하도록 대조·조정한다. OT 백업은 복구에 필요한 설정정보를 포함해 목록화하고 신뢰성·무결성을 가능한 경우 확인한다. 백업은 시점이 기록된 복구 사본이므로 현재 온라인 형상과 항상 동일하다고 가정하지 말고 버전·시점 및 차이를 추적한다.

verification_refs.citation: NASA-HDBK-1004, Functional Configuration Audit and Physical Configuration Audit (FCA/PCA) Documentation
verification_refs.locator: Appendix A.11, Description/Use
verification_refs.supports_claim: NASA defines PCA as an audit of configuration documentation and quality-control records to ensure the as-built configuration complies with the as-designed configuration defined in documentation. This supports as-built/documentation reconciliation, within the handbook's project context.

verification_refs.citation: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security
verification_refs.locator: §6.2.4.3, OT-Specific Recommendations and Guidance; Appendix E backup storage
verification_refs.supports_claim: NIST recommends a list of maintained backups including configuration information and recommends verifying backup reliability and integrity if technically possible. It does not say a backup must be identical to the current online state.

verification_refs.citation: NIST SP 1339, OT Backup Quick Start Guide
verification_refs.locator: Official abstract and backup inventory guidance
verification_refs.supports_claim: NIST states OT backup management involves integrating backups into change management, creating them regularly, testing them, and reviewing them during recovery exercises; it calls for identifying files and configuration information needed to restore the environment.

facts.statement: OT 백업 범위는 자산·위험·복구목표와 의존성을 기준으로 정한다. 필요한 경우 프로그램·로직·설정정보, I/O 목록, firmware, HMI 파일, license key, vendor 도구, OS/VM image와 지원 문서·소프트웨어를 식별하고, 백업을 날짜·시간 및 자산 식별정보와 함께 관리한다. integrity 확인과 비운전계 restore 시험은 적용 가능한 기술·위험 조건에 맞춰 수행한다.

verification_refs.citation: NIST SP 1339, OT Backup Quick Start Guide
verification_refs.locator: pp. 1–2: identify assets critical to operations; identify backups per asset; manage procedures; backup integrity testing and restoration
verification_refs.supports_claim: NIST says to identify files, software, and spares needed to restore the environment (examples include program/logic/configuration files, I/O lists, firmware, HMI files, license keys, vendor tools, OS/VM images, and supporting software); set backup frequency/media/location by information-change rate, system type and risk; label media with system name/date/time; maintain backup integrity; and conduct recurring restore tests on non-production systems to validate media and functional integrity. This is guidance, with scope and procedures adapted to the operating environment and safety requirements.

verification_refs.citation: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security
verification_refs.locator: §6.2.4.3, OT-Specific Recommendations and Guidance; Appendix E backup storage
verification_refs.supports_claim: NIST recommends identifying relevant OT backups including installation media, license keys and configuration information, verifying reliability/integrity if technically possible, and selecting backup plans by risk and operational context.

facts.statement: 미국 OSHA PSM 적용 공정에서는 like-for-like replacement를 제외하고 공정화학물질·기술·설비·절차 변경 및 적용 공정에 영향을 주는 시설 변경을 서면 MOC 절차로 통제한다. 변경 전 기술적 근거, 안전·보건 영향, 절차 수정, 변경 기간과 승인 요건을 검토하고, 영향받는 운전·정비·계약 인력에게 가동 전 알리고 교육하며, 필요한 공정안전정보·운전절차를 갱신한다. 별도로 NIST OT 지침은 OT 변경의 문서화·시험·승인 후 배포를 권고한다. 적용 범위는 각 규정·지침과 사업장 절차에 따른다.

verification_refs.citation: 29 CFR 1910.119(l), Process safety management of highly hazardous chemicals
verification_refs.locator: Paragraphs (l)(1)–(5)
verification_refs.supports_claim: The rule requires covered employers to establish written MOC procedures for changes other than replacements in kind to process chemicals, technology, equipment, procedures, and facility changes affecting a covered process. Before a change, procedures address technical basis, safety/health impact, operating-procedure modifications, time period, and authorization; affected operating, maintenance and contract employees are informed/trained before startup; PSI and operating procedures are updated when affected.

verification_refs.citation: OSHA Appendix C to 29 CFR 1910.119, Compliance Guidelines and Recommendations for Process Safety Management (nonmandatory)
verification_refs.locator: Appendix C, Management of Change guidance on temporary changes
verification_refs.supports_claim: The nonmandatory appendix explains temporary changes are subject to MOC provisions and recommends defining and monitoring their time limits and returning equipment/procedures to original or designed conditions at the end of the temporary change. This is interpretive guidance within OSHA PSM scope.

verification_refs.citation: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security
verification_refs.locator: §6.2.4.2, Configuration Change Control, pp. 111–112
verification_refs.supports_claim: NIST recommends an SDLC approach to document, test and approve changes before deployment to OT and suggests centralized change tracking/documentation to support testing and approvals. It is guidance and not a universal regulatory MOC mandate.

facts.statement: OT migration planning의 baseline으로 현재 asset/configuration inventory를 사용한다. NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3는 asset 식별정보와 vendor·model·location, 설치된 software·firmware version 및 system/data interconnection 정보를 관리하고 구성요소 추가·제거·변경 시 inventory를 갱신하도록 권고한다. 정확한 inventory는 risk, vulnerability 및 obsolescence tracking을 돕는다. Custom logic, 운전절차, license, spare와 기타 숨은 의존성의 조사는 현장별 추가 확인이며 NIST의 완전한 migration checklist라고 단정하지 않는다.

verification_refs.citation: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security
verification_refs.locator: §6.1.1 Asset Management, §6.1.1.1 Mapping Data Flows, §6.1.1.2 Network Architecture Documentation, §6.1.3 Risk Assessment, and §6.2.4.2 Configuration Change Control, pp. 91–92, 94, 111–112
verification_refs.supports_claim: NIST recommends OT asset inventory including identifiers and hardware details such as vendor/model/location, installed software and firmware versions, and vendor/update information; it calls for inventory updates when components are added, removed or changed. It describes data-flow and network-interconnection documentation and states accurate inventory supports risk assessment, vulnerability management and obsolescence tracking. Applying that inventory as a migration-planning baseline is an engineering use of the guidance; NIST does not prescribe the anchor's former exhaustive list of custom logic, procedures, licenses, spares and hidden dependencies as a universal migration checklist.

facts.statement: HHS EPLC Data Conversion 가이드는 데이터 변환에서 source-target mapping과 blank/new-code/부적절 값 처리 규칙을 계획하고, 표본 변환 및 위험도에 맞는 모의 전환을 수행한 뒤 target data의 format·completeness·accuracy를 검증·조정하며 duplicate를 제거하도록 안내한다. 이는 해당 IT 데이터 변환 가이드의 실무 권고이며, 모든 OT Migration에 체크섬·단위/인코딩 검사·record-count 대조 또는 운전 의미 검증을 동일하게 요구하는 보편 규격은 아니다. 프로젝트별 추가 검증항목은 데이터 유형·공정영향과 인수기준으로 정한다.

verification_refs.citation: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Enterprise Performance Life Cycle Framework Practices Guide: Data Conversion, v1.0
verification_refs.edition_or_version: EPLC Practice Guide v1.0; archived guide; accessed 2026-10-11
verification_refs.locator: pp. 1–3: mapping and business rules, sample/mock conversion, validating/evaluating conversions, format/completeness/accuracy, duplicate elements
verification_refs.supports_claim: HHS describes planning field mapping and business rules for blank, new or inappropriate entries; test sample conversions and risk-dependent full mock conversions; reconcile converted data for format, completeness and accuracy; and eliminate duplicates. The source is an IT practice guide and is treated as an example, not an OT-wide normative standard.

facts.statement: HHS EPLC Data Conversion 가이드는 프로젝트가 parallel operation과 one-time cutover 중 실행방식을 정하고, 구 시스템을 archive할지 계속 운영할지 계획하도록 안내한다. 가이드의 계획항목에는 데이터의 양·유형·품질, criticality, application dependencies, 위험, 비용과 일정이 포함된다. 이는 해당 IT data-conversion 가이드의 project-planning example이며, 모든 OT Migration에 같은 방식 선택지나 최적화 산식을 의무화하지 않는다. 구체적 전환방식과 허용정지시간은 현장 요구·위험·승인 기준으로 정한다.
